routine_announcement.title: WATERMAN WAY - Working Together, Group Chooses Name for New Cambridge Street
routine_announcement.author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
routine_announcement.content:
WATERMAN WAY - Working together, group chooses name for new Cambridge street

 August 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 742
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - It's official: Waterman Way will be the name of the new road at Cambridge Harbor.The name choice was not a solo decision. Residents gathered at Cambridge Harbor Tuesday evening to vote on the name of the new road parallel to the water that intersects Aurora Street and Dorchester Avenue.The name-choosing event gave residents the chance to hear the three options and pick their favorite. As they voted on their favorite name, attendees enjoyed a free scoop of ice cream from the Scottish Highland Creamery and even got a chance to try their luck at a raffle for free Cambridge Harbor merchandise.Matt Leonard, executive director of Cambridge Waterfront Development said the new street that is closest to the park will be the perfect street to close off and use for events once it is paved."We can have food trucks, we can have art shows, we can have music festivals," Leonard said. "So this will blend seamlessly into this activated park that we're going to have." On Tuesday evening, community members were given three options for the new name: Sailwinds Plaza, Waterman Way and Harbor Way. Everyone got the opportunity to vote on their favorite name using a QR code or by simply telling BCT Design Group Principal Bob Northfield their choice. BCT Design Group has been helping Cambridge Waterfront Development with the naming process.Votes were tallied during the event so that the winning name could be shared before the event ended.Betsey Harrington, who voted for the winning name, said Waterman Way is "traditional" for Dorchester County.Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer also said he voted for Waterman Way. Pfeffer said it "pays heritage" to the county, whose seal depicts a waterman and a farmer.While neither voted for the winning name, Chesapeake College Cambridge Center Director Lorelly Solano and Chesapeake College Director of Development Amber McGinnis were excited to vote on Tuesday."We are neighbors and active members of the community," Solano said. "So we're excited to support our partners and see the community grow." The three names that community members voted on are all in the theme of maritime heritage.Cambridge Waterfront Development, with the help of BCT Design Group, put out an online survey in June for community members to rank different themes that the street name would be created from.The survey, which closed July 1, gave the community four themes to rank. The three other themes were Rose Hill, roses and light/sources of light.McGinnis said she is happy that the Cambridge Waterfront group has tried to listen to and involve the community in its decision-making process."There are so many times that partners have come in and haven't really considered the community," McGinnis said. "And I do feel like Matt and that group has really tried to integrate community needs and wants, realizing they can't make everyone happy. And so the fact they're even just getting input on the naming of the street, I think it validates that they're happy to have the community engaged." Leonard said Cambridge Waterfront Development is a "community-first organization." "When it comes to things that we can get direct input from the community on, like a name, we think they should be a part of it," he said. "And it just gives them the real buy-in. It gives us real input as to what matters to the community. So as we focus more and more on the actual development of the buildings and the uses, we have a better understanding of what matters to the community." His organization's mission is to develop the harbor in partnership with the community so that it is a benefit to the community. Leonard called the relationship with the community "a continued conversation." "If we continue to put out really good accurate information, timely information, and listen to what the community says," Leonard said, "the people who are commenting will be more and more positive over time and more bought in to the whole thing." McGinnis said that she thinks a lot of people in Dorchester County have a connection to the Cambridge Harbor area."I think to see this property be revitalized with some new and interesting ideas - workforce development, economic development, tourism - bringing in the old and the new identities of the county is really exciting." 
 
 Caption: MAGGIE TROVATO/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Matt Leonard, executive director of Cambridge Waterfront Development speaks to a crowd of people before giving them the opportunity to vote on what to name the new street at Cambridge Harbor Aug. 8.

routine_announcement.content:
About this story and its author, WHCP's Jim Brady

 September 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: A8 | Section: News 
 
 171
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - For journalists, sometimes it just takes one comment to launch an investigative project.For Jim Brady, that comment was about Dorchester County's audits."I had heard from someone, I can't remember who, that the county's audits were messed up," said Brady, who spent more than three decades in journalism and nearly two more in the technology industry before moving to Cambridge."That's all I knew. And so I started talking to fellow producers and volunteers at the radio station." Brady eventually got in touch with Eugene Lauer, a Cambridge resident who was working with a group called Dorchester Citizens for Better Government on a charter petition. Via Maryland's Public Information Act, Lauer had already requested and received an auditor's report which details "many of the problems in the finance department and the county government." From there, Brady went to county officials and commissioners."The story just came together that way," he said.Brady has been doing pieces for the MidShore MidDay program at WHCP, which is where his story first aired earlier this week.

routine_announcement.title: 'It's going to carry us into the future' - U.S. Constitution celebrated at Talbot County Courthouse
routine_announcement.author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
routine_announcement.content:
'It's going to carry us into the future' - U.S. Constitution celebrated at Talbot County Courthouse

 September 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 7 | Section: News 
 
 531
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Star-Spangled Banner, performed by 35 students from Easton Middle School, resounded in the area surrounding the Talbot County Courthouse Saturday, Sept. 16.The band's rendition of the national anthem kicked off the second annual Constitution Day celebration in Easton. A crowd gathered to listen to speeches, enjoy Rita's Italian Ice and learn more about the Constitution of the United States.The event was hosted by the Mid-Shore Constitution Alliance.Along with speeches from an array of people - from elected officials to students - actor Darius Wallace performed a re-enactment of Frederick Douglass speaking about freedom and the Constitution.Wallace received a standing ovation for his performance.Easton resident John Miller was especially impressed with Wallace's performance."That took great appreciation of our freedoms and made us aware of how important our freedoms were and what slavery means and that there is still work to do," Miller said.Miller said it's important that the Constitution is still acknowledged today because it's "where our government gets its power." Speakers at the event, who talked about the importance of the Constitution, included Maryland State Sen. Johnny Mautz; Tarence Bailey Sr., founder and president of The Bailey-Groce Family Foundation; Joseph Prud'Homme, a professor in Religion, Politics, and Culture at Washington College; Zach Affeldt, a student at Washington College; William Fachet, a student at University of Maryland College Park; Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble and Ron James, a Veterans of Foreign Wars member.Mautz talked about his experience delving into the Constitution at law school."Never did I think that the Constitution was fun or exciting until you start to talk about free speech," he said. "And then we're into the good stuff." Mautz said that without free speech protections in the Constitution, we wouldn't be standing here today.Bailey spoke about the Constitution being important for everyday life during his speech."I think it's very important, especially for youth, that they learn the Constitution, know what's in it and know what applies to them," he said.Michelle Ewing, co-director of the Mid-Shore Constitution Alliance, said the mission of the organization is to educate the public and raise awareness about the U.S Constitution. She said the group offers scholarships to graduating seniors and non-traditional students who want to go back to school."We want to get the youth involved and informed," she said.At the end of his speech, Mautz talked about the importance of the Constitution today."We have to go back to the Constitution and use the Constitution to fix the problems, not tear it apart," he said. "It's gotten us to where we are. It is going to carry us into the future."

routine_announcement.title: Mayor's Prayer Breakfast Set for Oct. 26
routine_announcement.content:
Mayor's prayer breakfast set for Oct. 26

 September 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 14 | Section: News 
 
 617
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Thursday, Oct. 26, from 7-9 a.m., Easton's 40th annual Mayor's Prayer Breakfast will be held at the Tidewater Inn in Easton. This year's breakfast will feature Claudia Reyes, occupational therapist, and Linda Brown, culinary arts lead teacher at Talbot County Public Schools.Music will be provided by Katherine Tooley, Immanuel Lutheran Church in Easton.Claudia Reyes was born in Guatemala City in Central America and immigrated to the United States at age 7. Having always walked the path of life by faith, she has trusted in God's provision and faithfulness since personally knowing Christ as her personal Savior at the age of 15. She devoted herself to a Christian youth ministry as a teenager and attended Mount Saint Mary's University in Los Angeles, California.Married for 29 years with four children, she and her husband Eliud Reyes have had a passion for serving Hispanic youth ministries. The family moved to Maryland's Eastern Shore and Claudia has currently been serving as a pastor's wife at the First Hispanic Baptist Church in Easton.Since 2003, she and her husband have continued to help youth navigate through the most challenging times of their life by presenting the gospel of Jesus Christ and helping youth grow in their walk with Christ. She currently serves as the volunteer coordinator for extended young adult ministry at the Talbot County Detention Center and is involved in many outreach and community events across Talbot County to help bring cultures together.Reyes shares, "God has called me to service Him to the unprivileged and poor, through local and global mission trips, including New York, Mexico, El Salvador and Indonesia. Through this spiritual work, I am reaching out to those in desperate spiritual need and making God known as the only Savior, healer, and waymaker in transforming lives." Linda Saathoff Brown, a lifetime active member of Immanuel Lutheran Church, serves the Lord in the church, family, and community.Faithfully attending worship, studying the Word in Sunday School, confirmation and Bible classes, singing in the church choirs, engaging in church and community service outreach missions and building fellowship are among the ways the family helped to build and support the church over these many years.Throughout her career of 47 years of leading students on their educational journey with the Talbot County Public Schools, Brown impacts the lives of hundreds of students, living her faith in the everyday school setting. She also serves as a volunteer leader in the 4-H program and in many community and state organizations.Last fall, her active life was suddenly altered after a major life-threatening fall that left her likely paralyzed. Through the tragic injury, she received glimmers of hope, medical talent, and amazing grace, filled with the power of Prayer, the power of Faith, the love of friends, and the relentless dedication and love of her family.She shares, "From the waters of baptism as an infant, Jesus has been walking with me and I with Him. My statement of faith is as large and old as the Apostles and Nicene Creeds and as personal as Christ Jesus died for me. I confess Jesus as my Lord and Savior. Indeed, He is the author and finisher of my saving faith, a gift given to me by the Holy Spirit who called me out of darkness into His marvelous light." Tickets to the 2023 Mayor's Prayer Breakfast may be purchased at the Easton Town Office and the Dairy Queen beginning October 1. The cost is $20 a person and seating is limited. No tickets will be sold at the door. Tickets must be purchased ahead of time. For further information, contact Kathy Ruf at 410-822-2525.

routine_announcement.title: 200 Years of Federalsburg - Bicentennial Celebrated with Gala Dinner
routine_announcement.author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
routine_announcement.content:
200 years of Federalsburg - Bicentennial celebrated with gala dinner

 September 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 22 | Section: News 
 
 1005
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG - There was much glittering finery at the Federalsburg Bicentennial Gala party at the Lion's Club on Sept. 23.Although tropical depression Ophelia was in full force just outside, the only hitch for the 90 guests who attended was that the band canceled.But the party went on with Spotify playing the tunes, and there was much good chat among friendly neighbors, politicians and business leaders.One guest, Carol Evans, was really in the mood as it was her birthday too. She showed up in a silver 1963 Rolls Royce complete with a driver.Evans said, "I rented the Rolls because I have been a business person in Federalsburg for a number of years.This is my last hurrah, and it is also my birthday. Wasn't it nice of them throw me a party? We did a bit of touring from Williston to Federalsburg.We honked the horn and waved and people gave us the thumbs up. I hope Federalsburg can make it through with this type of upscale event."Mayor Kimberly Abner welcomed guests from the rain at the entrance dressed in black sequins. She pointed the way to tables, hors d'oeuvres and cocktails. Inside the Lion's Hall was transformed into a warm and welcoming space. Not only did the people come to celebrate, they came to connect and chat.President of the Preston Commission Savannah Winston was there."It's exciting because the town of Preston is right next door to the town of Federalsburg.So we are neighbors.Preston is from 1892. We have some time to go. We are going to enjoy tonight networking and socializing and admiring everyone in their beautiful dresses. Mayor Kim and her team are great neighbors."Amber Korell, town manager of Preston, added, "We are excited to be here to get entertained and wined and dined."Not only were there government folks like all of the Caroline County commissioners, who sat together, but there were some big employers who sponsored the event.One was co-owner Wayne Cole who works at WIN Transport."It is important for our company to give back to the community. My business partners agree with me so that is why we are here tonight.We bought a table and some of our employees are here. It is just a terrific event. We are happy to be a part of it. This is a formal event that is celebrating 200 years. Our little community is celebrating its 200th anniversary. We have a great turnout here," Cole said.Some guests were born and raised in Federalsburg and had came a long way to be here for this bicentennial celebration.Nancy Downie said, "My family moved to Federalsburg when I was 3. So that is 47 years ago. After living in Colorado I moved back. I am a day care provider. I love seeing everyone so dressed up.It's beautiful."Sister of Downie and Federalsburg Town Council member Debbie Sewell said, "I came back here to raise my kids. This is perfect for me.These are my extended family.""I love this town. I really do. I am excited about what the town can be. We have kind of lost that and I am so proud to be a part of that with them. I am proud that people like Kim and Debbie are on the council. It has made me look at Federalsburg with new eyes. It is flourishing and things are getting better all the time. I am president of the Lion's Club. I belong to the Historical Society. Now that I am retired I can get involved in it all," Denise Nagel said.There were three sisters who were all dressed up to the nines. Deborah Sewell, Nancy Downie and June Cuddy all have roots in Federalsburg."My husband and I moved back. We wanted to be here after he finished medical school in Baltimore. We came back. There is something about how I feel when I am in Federalsburg. It is where I want to be," said Sewell.Cuddy said, "I remember being at the carnival and the nickel toss. It was the highlight of the summer. And getting sand burrs getting stuck to my leg. Ouch!" Downie said that she was not only Miss Caroline County but also Miss Federalsburg.She remembered the fishing contest put on by the Jaycees."Even if they are not your neighbor, they are your neighbor. It doesn't matter what, now we are in, what district we live in. If you need a helping hand, we will help.We don't let our town folk fall," Downie said.David Ricks is president of Men For Change and a member of the Lion's Club."The town has been around for 200 years. I feel like the town is really trying to move forward right now, which is a good thing for everybody. There is a lot of poverty so we need better jobs, but I feel like the town is really trying to get us better jobs," he said. "If we give them the opportunity to work, our kids won't leave. I love the town. When I was young I played baseball around here.I coached Pop Warner Football.Coached basketball. I love this town."Abner took the microphone and acknowledged all the politicians and former politicians and law enforcement.And corporate sponsors like the Preston Automotive Group and Safe House, WIN Transport, Trigas and Oil and M&M Carnot."Our musician canceled this evening, but we are able to pivot, and we have a wonderful playlist, and we we will still be dancing and having a great time," Abner said. "It will be a fancy night."

David Ricks, president of Men for Change, said that although there is poverty, that the town is trying to give better opportunities.

Amber Korell, left, is the town manager of Preston and Preston President of the Commission Savannah Winston said they love being the town next to Federalsburg.

routine_announcement.content:
Winter Festival to be 'bigger and better'

 September 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 19 | Section: News 
 
 251
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Based on Ridgely's successful Winter Festival last year, the town's Board of Public Works Director David Crist asked the Caroline County Commissioners for help managing public safety this year.The commissioners agreed to lend the needed assistance for this year's festival scheduled for 4 to 9 p.m. Saturday, Dec. 9. The rain date is Dec. 16.Crist said the town's first Winter Festival in 2022 was anticipated to be "a very small event - 1,000 to 2,000 people maybe."However, "going off the drone footage, we had 10,000 to 12,000 people," Crist said. "Now we're figuring that we have to do it every year, and we're going to try to do it bigger and better every year. But we can't do it by ourselves."Crist said the second festival is "already doubled from last year" with 80 vendors, 15 food trucks and an acre devoted to children's amusements lined up.Caroline County Director of Public Works Ryan White and Director of Emergency Services Mark Sheridan walked into the hallway outside the meeting room to work out some details after Crist's appeal.The town promotes the festival as "home of Caroline County's largest Holiday Light Display and the 2022 Winner of APG Media's Best of the Best Chesapeake Awards for Best Seasonal Attraction, Best Festival/Fair and Best Local Event."

routine_announcement.title: 'We just want to feed 'em' - St. Michaels Community Center gives out turkeys for the holidays
routine_announcement.author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
routine_announcement.content:
'We just want to feed 'em' - St. Michaels Community Center gives out turkeys for the holidays

 November 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 590
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - A small line formed outside of the St. Michaels Community Center's temporary location on Talbot Street in the late afternoon on Monday.While some people waited to pick up their usual grocery items from the food pantry, others came for a hefty frozen turkey, pie, a sack of potatoes and a large bag of canned and dry items - all the fixings for a delicious and plentiful Thanksgiving dinner.Food Bank Director Amy DeWitt said that the SMCC has been handing out these "Thanksgiving boxes" to people who might not be able to afford a full Thanksgiving dinner for at least six years."(With) the cost of food nowadays, I think a lot of people just can't afford to go out and buy a turkey," DeWitt said. "And I think it's very important for them to have a meal they can prepare at home for their family." From 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. on Monday, DeWitt and her small team handed out all the turkey day classics for residents to cook on Thursday."The boxes are like an addition to what they already have at home," Mark Singleton, DeWitt's assistant, said."So just to push things along, maybe even press the meal for another day or two." In addition to the Thanksgiving boxes, the SMCC is hosting an eat-in community dinner on Wednesday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Walk-ins are welcome. Those in attendance will be served turkey and gravy from Ava's Pizzeria and Wine Bar as well as cornbread stuffing, garlic mashed red skin potatoes, green bean casserole, dinner rolls and homemade apple and pumpkin pies.DeWitt estimated that they will serve between 150 and 175 prepared meals on Wednesday. She said she had around 75 people taking home Thanksgiving boxes this year.One of those people, Theo Bees, is making Thanksgiving dinner for his mom and himself this year."I love to cook," he said.Bees, who was working as a caretaker but is now taking care of his 92-year-old mother, said he plans to cook the entire meal.Bees said he would love it if everybody could celebrate Thanksgiving with their family."People need to be with family," he said, "every holiday." Kerri Clear, executive chef at the SMCC, who is making most of the dishes for Wednesday's community dinner, said the community is very supportive of what the community center does to help residents."We get a lot of donations," Clear said, "a lot of interest from the community." DeWitt said that all of her clients are "very thankful" for the special holiday meals that the SMCC hands out.Singleton said each person appreciates what they do."They show us every time they come in," he said."They're really thankful." And Dewitt, Clear and Singleton are just happy to help out in the community."We just want to feed 'em," DeWitt Said. 
 
 Caption: MAGGIE TROVATO/STAR DEMOCRAT

routine_announcement.content:
Town keeping watchful eye on Centreville mill

 March 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 199

 No direct action on the town's part is planned at this time regarding the dilapidated mill located adjacent to Mill Stream Park on Route 213, running through Centreville."We are in continued conversations with the owner on addressing any issues at the property," Centreville Town Council President Ashley Kaiser said.
The mill is privately owned by Charles Geschwilm of Easton. Geschwilm has been very cooperative with the council, and has been very open to discussion and communication and regularly meeting with town officials, Kaiser said.
Council member Jeff Kiel said the owner of the mill had a structural engineer review the structure who stated it was structurally sound, but noted, "metal is falling off the building."
With fears lessened the structure will fall into the roadway, the owner is now working to have a contractor repair the metal of the building to prevent exposure to the elements and maintain structural integrity.
The mill owner has been doing some repair himself and is currently seeking professionals for roof work, according to Kaiser, who said the town will work to identify contractors and to assist as it can.
"There is no option where the mill just stays how it is right now in perpetuity," she said.

routine_announcement.author: Tom McCall
routine_announcement.content:
Hundreds of children gather thousands of eggs on courthouse lawn

 March 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 451
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — About 150 children waited with anxious excitement on the Talbot County Courthouse lawn shortly before 10 a.m. Saturday for the arrival of a very famous rabbit and the start of the Easton Economic Development's annual egg hunt.There were lots of multi-generational families gathered.
Erica and Christian Mackendrick came with their 2-year-old son Noah.
"It is Noah's first time. We are going to see the bunny and the fire truck, hopefully get some eggs," Erica said. "It is fun to get out, see other kids and celebrate Easter and have a good weekend."
Dorothy Rudny came with her three grandchildren — Cooper, Charlotte and Magnolia.
"I am excited because I want candy," said Charlotte. "I just like picking up the eggs."
At 10 a.m. sharp, the Easter Bunny arrived in style aboard a red fire truck, with Donald "Bunky" Spies at the wheel. There was a palpable excitement in the air.
Then, the kids were off searching.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook said, "It is so much fun seeing the community out and all the kids. It is a beautiful day. Easton Economic Development does a great job hosting the event. It is one of the things that makes Easton a great place to raise your family. We loved this event when my kids were little. It is like a big family reunion."
Holly Dakarske, executive director of Easton Economic Development, said that volunteers had set out more than 5,000 filled Easter eggs earlier Saturday morning.
They contained a mix of candies and trinkets, like erasers, tattoos and stickers, she said.
"We have done (the egg hunt) the last three years since we took it over, but I think it has been over a decade (since the town first started holding the event)," Dakarske said. "Every year it is the fire engine with the bunny and the mayor."
She seemed pleased with her team's effort to fill the lawn with thousands of eggs.
"It goes so fast. It the fastest event ever," Dakarske laughed. "The kids pick up the eggs in seconds, and it takes us an hour and half to put them out. It is cool to see all the families come out and the kids are dressed up for Easter and watch them take a picture with the bunny. It is wholesome, small town kind of stuff."
Val Dambrosio, Visitor Center coordinator for Easton Economic Development, said she had an "eggcellent" week stuffing eggs ahead of the event.
For Dambrosio, the best part of the event is seeing the creative Easter baskets that local children carry to collect eggs in. "I have yet to see two of the same," she said.
Whether they got a basketful or just a few eggs, everyone seemed happy. There was not one egg left on the green.

routine_announcement.title: National Vietnam War Veterans Day observed in Chestertown
routine_announcement.author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
routine_announcement.content:
National Vietnam War Veterans Day observed in Chestertown

 April 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 351
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — On Good Friday, Memorial Park in downtown Chestertown filled with Vietnam War Veterans, their families and residents, to honor the veterans for their sacrifice.The March 29 event, Kent County's third National War Veteran's Day, saw a turnout of 240.
Veteran and organizer Peter Sweetser said 35 veterans stepped forward to receive their pin, a handshake and verbal affirmation, thanking them for their service.
As Sweetser put it, soldiers in Vietnam had a unique experience compared to other war veterans being that when they returned from their tour they were mistreated.
Alongside Sweetser, Kent County Commissioners Ron Fithian, Albert Nickerson and John Price proclaimed March 29 as Vietnam Veteran's Day.
They, as well as Chestertown Mayor David Foster, recognized Gold Star family members and spouses who lost veterans after the war.
Keynote speaker Larry Wilkerson, retired army colonel and chief of staff for former U.S. Secretary of State Colin Powell, put forth examples of bravery in the conflict.
He not only used examples of American soldiers enduring the pain and loneliness war created. He used examples of the opposition as well, how in tearful, emotional movements both sides came together, bonding over losses suffered.
Wilkerson then talked about a soldier who fought bravely, not just in Vietnam but also against pancreatic cancer.
"That's the Vietnam War for me. So many Americans, so many brave men and women, and so much pain and agony, for what," he said.
All veterans who stepped up were anonymous, with the exception of Sfc. Samuel Tiller, age 95, who had received a Bronze Star and a Purple Heart for his bravery in Vietnam from April 12 to 14, 1964.
Sweetser, who noted that this is a private ceremony between the Department of Defense and the veterans, was pleased with the results.
"It was a great day of celebration for veterans who served nearly 50 years ago, supported by a large crowd of family, friends, and Kent and Queen Anne's County residents. Those men and women who answered the call to duty by their country, along with the MIA/POWs and the Gold Star families of that war and all wars, will never be forgotten," he said.

routine_announcement.author: Maggie Trovato
routine_announcement.content:
Oxford clerk-treasurer takes oath of office

 April 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 294

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Town of Oxford has a new employee in its office.Vickie Sharp was sworn into the role of clerk-treasurer at a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday. Commission President Tom Costigan administered the oath of office.
After Sharp was sworn in, Costigan introduced Sharp. He said that she previously worked for the Town of St. Michaels. According to the Town of St. Michaels website, Sharp was the town's finance clerk and Water Department and billing clerk.
"We're thrilled to have her with us, and we expect great things," Costigan said to Sharp.
The clerk-treasurer is a new position for the Town of Oxford.
According to the job posting on the town's website, Sharp will be tasked with directing and managing the town's finances under the town manager's direction and implementing policy set by the Commissioners of Oxford. The clerk-treasurer will act as the chief financial officer of the town.
The creation of this position was talked about at a Jan. 11 commissioners meeting, when Commissioner Katrina Greer said she wanted to discuss the possibility of hiring someone to take on the town's financial duties.
At the Jan. 11 meeting, Greer said this could address a material weakness detailed in the town's audit for the town's lack of internal controls. This has been a finding in town audits going back to 2016.
"This would take some burden off the manager and enable us to comply with the audit recommendation of having multiple people performing financial roles," she said at the meeting.
Town Manager Cheryl Lewis said she had shared this idea with the commissioners originally because hiring more employees is the way to solve the internal controls issue.
"Admittedly most towns our size can't afford more staff," Lewis said at the Jan. 11 meeting. "Oxford is not in that situation, per se."

routine_announcement.title: Community Wishes Library Director a Fond Farewell
routine_announcement.author: Will Bontrager
routine_announcement.content:
Community wishes library director a fond farewell

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 365
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — It was a heartfelt goodbye for Executive Director of the Kent County Library Arnessa Dowell on Friday.She's leaving for Guam, where a new job awaits her as supervisor librarian at Andersen Air Force Base.
In the new position, Dowell said she'll take with her the values she has learned in Kent County since she started early in 2021, such as the importance of building partnerships in a close-knit community.
As executive director during the Covid-19 lockdowns, she was celebrated for her dedication under trying circumstances in a rural library system.
Natalie Hagan, director of technical services commended Dowell.
"She nearly doubled our staff since the time she was here," she said.
Hagan also pointed out that Dowell exercised creativity under a system with limited resources.
Dowell dealt with the logistics of those issues while having to relocate both the Galena and Rock Hall libraries during her tenure.
In a brief farewell speech, Dowell expressed how important libraries are to her.
At one point in her life, during financial turmoil, her job at a library was a refuge, offering her hope for future endeavors.
Dowell reflected on the time she had in the Kent County community. She was thrilled with the development of the KCPL Cares program, a quarterly free giveaway initiative that lets the library connect with and support the community in a variety of ways.
It was birthed out of the pandemic. Dowell and staff kept seeing a need in people's lives. They gave away Kindles, COVID kits, cold weather clothing and other necessities.
With a ready smile, Dowell said, "Thank you to everyone for your support, mentorship, advice, hugs and laughs. I just really appreciate it. I'm immensely proud of my staff. It was challenging and I've grown so much as a leader because of it."
The community showed appreciation back to her as well.
While they enjoyed tacos and a sumptuous red velvet cake courtesy of Happy Chicken, Cynthia Saunders president of the Friends of the Kent County Public Library, presented Dowell a portrait of the Chestertown waterfront.
Hagan, on the search committee for the new executive director said the library already has a few applicants for the position and expects to have many more in the nationwide hunt to fill Dowell's shoes.

routine_announcement.title: County Turns Out for Talbot Day Celebration
routine_announcement.author: Tom McCall
routine_announcement.content:
County turns out for Talbot Day celebration

 April 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 622
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Over 150 members of the Talbot County community, clad in purple and red, gathered on the Talbot County Courthouse lawn Thursday evening to celebrate those who make Talbot County a better place.Citations, volunteer awards and poster-making recognitions were given in honor of Talbot Day, an annual celebration of the county and the people who live and work there.
Established in 1983 by unanimous proclamation of the County Council, April 25 has been recognized as the official birthday of Talbot County. In 2023, the tradition was revitalized with the designation of "Talbot Day," aimed at fostering community engagement and celebration of the county's rich heritage, according to a press release from the county.
"We are just trying to follow through on what we started back in 1983, which was a proclamation that designated April 25 as Talbot County's birthday. We want to celebrate and what you see here is just amazing for our first go at it. It is heartwarming to see," said County Council Member David Stepp, who offered a prayer of hope at the celebration. He also thanked the staff for putting it all together, from setting out chairs, to getting cupcakes to hanging banners.
The courthouse was bedecked in the colors of the county's flag — purple and red — for the celebration.
Community members sang and read poetry, and the sheriff's office presented the flags.
The Allegro Academy's women stood up and offered an endearing a capella renditions of "In Meeting We Are Blessed" and "Connected." Rows and rows of young children from BAAM lined up in front of the crowd and recited a poem in unison. Some teens from BAAM recited words written by famed abolitionist Frederick Douglass about his pursuit of knowledge and how he taught himself to read.
Mayor Megan Cook came up to the lectern to address those gathered.
"Happy Talbot Day, everyone," she said. May we continue to push each other forward towards our even brighter tomorrow," Cook said.
Council members Keasha Haythe and Lynn Mielke presented the names for the Citizen and Service Awards. The service awards celebrated volunteers who have lifted up Talbot County.
Mielke underscored the impact of these individuals, highlighting their invaluable contributions across various sectors of the community.
"Each nominee makes Talbot County a better place to live, work and visit. Each individual shares their expertise, time and effort assisting to fill the gaps in many different sectors and the needs of our community," Mielke said.
The nominees were: Dr. Judi Gieske, Lizette Hannegan, Laura Heikes, Diana Mautz (posthumously), Michelle Moaney, Dana Newman, Syrinthia Ann-Foster Johnson, Sherye Nickerson, Krisa Paquin, James Redman, Susan Roecker, Susan Sherman, and Angeline Sturgis.
Stepp presented the winners of the poster contest. Winners were: Division 1 (Age 0-11), Paige Smith with her poster entitled "Lighthouse and Heron"; Division 2 (Age 11-18), Makayla Moore with her poster entitled "Bay to Beach" and Josephine Shaw with her poster entitled "Home"; and Division 3 (Age 19+), Lisa Ghezzi with her poster entitled "Buzzing Bees".
The highlight of the evening came with the announcement of the "Citizen of the Year" award, the honor posthumously bestowed upon Diana Mautz for her exceptional service and unwavering dedication to the Talbot County community.
"Through sailing she touched the lives of thousands of children and was also an invincible force shaping the St. Michael's Business Association, helping to transform the local economy into a booming destination for visitors from around the world," Mielke said.
In a touching tribute, Diana's children, Johnny and Danny Mautz, accepted the award on her behalf from the County Council and State Del. Chris Adams.
As the Easton High School band played "Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy" there was cake, cupcakes and lemonade served up by Clay Stamp, the county manager, well into the evening — a celebration befitting Talbot County's birthday.

routine_announcement.title: Dorchester County Council, County Employees Thank Powell
routine_announcement.author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
routine_announcement.content:
Dorchester County Council, county employees thank Powell

 May 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 603
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — With a newly-hired county manager set to begin Monday, May 20, the Dorchester County Council and county employees acknowledged and thanked Jeff Powell at a council meeting May 14 for serving in the role of interim county manager.Powell, who was previously on the County Council from 1994 to 1998, took on the role of interim county manager in January 2023.
Before leading a standing ovation for Powell, County Council President Lenny Pfeffer talked about Powell's leadership. Pfeffer said Powell joined the county at a challenging time and led the way toward stability.
"I don't know how we can repay him for all the stuff that he's done," Pfeffer said. "Not too many people want to jump onto a sinking ship."
Council member Ricky Travers said that when the current council took office, "it was a mess."
"But that young man over there had vision and still has vision," Travers said about Powell. "Every time I talk to him, I'm just awed at how he can connect the dots."
Council member William Nichols, who served on the County Council when Powell did, said it's been a pleasure working with Powell for the second time.
"If you could stay, I'd like to see you stay," Nichols said. "But I understand."
County employees also expressed their thanks to Powell during the meeting. The county's Economic Development Director Susan Banks said she has been with the county for 10 years, and when Powell came in, he quickly made changes "that everyone felt."
"You will be missed big time," she said.
Airport Director Steve Nuwer thanked Powell for the respect and opportunities he has given him. Nuwer said he's witnessed Powell make tough decisions that aren't always popular.
"But you get down to the reason for the decision that you made, and it's the right thing to do," Nuwer said.
Finance Director Karen Tolley thanked Powell for not being afraid to "take the hard punches" when it comes to making those unpopular decisions. She talked about Powell's ability to listen to any employee, no matter the time.
"You don't always get that higher up," she said, later adding, "The reason is you want us to do the best job possible."
At the meeting, Powell expressed his appreciation.
"I can't leave here and not call out the people that work for this county," he said. "Especially the department heads. And Sandra Tripp-Jones, who's been an incredible help to me as we move this rock a little bit up the hill. But sincerely, thank you."
Powell said the county is in better shape, but there is still a lot of work to do. He said he thinks Jerry Jones, who has been named the next county manager, is the right person to take the job.
"I've talked to Jerry a couple times," Powell said. "I've told him that I'll be readily available where ever he needs, transition-wise."
Jones, who was appointed to the role by the county council, previously served as secretary and as superintendent of the Maryland State Police under former Gov. Larry Hogan's administration.
At the meeting, Council Vice President Mike Detmer read a quote from a 1998 newspaper article. The quote, a statement made by a county official, talked about the progress the county has made with its new comprehensive plan and zoning ordinance. It said the county needs to expand its efforts to "protect productive farmland" and keep growth near population centers that have central water and sewer services.
"So that's something, Mr. Powell, that you said in 1998 that is just as apt today as it's ever been," Detmer said before expressing his appreciation for Powell's efforts in the county manager role.
"Thank you for stepping up to the plate," Detmer said.

routine_announcement.content:

 Author/Byline: JIM JOHNSON jjohnson@chespub.com | Section: Local News

 ST. MICHAELS — A tableau of Americana walked, rolled and pedaled down Talbot Avenue in St. Michaels on Thursday in the 48th annual Independence Day Children's Parade.Hundreds participated, dressed in red, white and blue. The street was lined with residents and visitors, who cheered the children and their families as they walked past.
Brian Collison, a Denver resident who was visiting his aunt and uncle in town, set the tone as he played patriotic songs on his trumpet along the parade route.
Six-year-old Maizi Koehne was typical of many of those participating. Maizi was bedecked in red, white and blue, including stars and stripes pinwheels attached to her headband. She and her sister Ava were visiting their grandparents. They come every year from their home in Plano, Texas, and participate in the parade.
Easton resident Bodey Richardson dressed as Uncle Sam and marched in front of the Boy Scout Troop 741 color guard at the front of the parade. He flashed thumbs up signs and waved to those watching.
The parade had an international flavor — although somewhat ironic considering the holiday celebrates America's independence from England. British citizen David Brown carried his 4-year-old son, Charlie, on his shoulders. David married American Emily Roiter, the daughter of recently elected St. Michaels Commissioner Alexis Roiter.
David and Emily live in London. He told how he has thrown Fourth of July parties in the past for his wife featuring hot dogs and red, white and blue bunting.
Ten-year-old Mitchell Boyd, dressed in a colonial outfit, walked the parade with his parents, April and Rob, and his sister, Addy. The Boyds live in Washington, D.C., and have a second home in St. Michaels.
Following the parade, the St. Michaels Volunteer Fire Department grilled hamburgers and speeches were given in front of the St. Michaels Museum. Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher talked about Revolutionary War patriot Matthew Tilghman. Recently retired Police Chief Anthony T. Smith read the Declaration of Independence, and St. Michaels Museum Secretary Jo Ann Manning gave the invocation.
"May the changes we want to see begin with each of us," Manning said.

 GREENSBORO — The Town Hall building in Greensboro is currently closed due to a bat infestation found over the weekend.The town initially discovered a swarm of bats on Friday morning. On Saturday, the town said in a Facebook post that a bat was found in the building during a normal pest control checkup.
"Since the attic isn't typically checked, this issue has unfortunately grown," the town wrote. Town Manager Tammy Kelledes said multiple bats were found both dead and alive in the building.
The town added that the closure is for health reasons since bat droppings pose risks.
"It can carry harmful fungi that, when inhaled, can cause histoplasmosis — a respiratory disease that can be severe, especially for those with weakened immune systems," the town wrote.
Kelledes told The Star Democrat that the building will be closed until at least next week, though the town is still "conducting as much business as usual."
Residents can go to Meeting Hall at 111 S Main Street for assistance, which is located across the parking lot from Town Hall.
They can also reach the town by calling 410-482-6222 or emailing greensboro@greensboromd.com.

routine_announcement.content:
Betterton dedicates late restaurant owner with bench in his honor

 August 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News

 BETTERTON — While Betterton Day was in full swing, Saturday, Aug. 3, up the hill a bench was dedicated to the late Francis Marzella, restaurant owner for over 52 years.His wife, Maureen and their son, Michael, christened the bench, situated near the Betterton Volunteer fire house, and across from their restaurant, Marzella's By the Bay.
Almost 50 people came out to pay their honors to Francis. Leading the dedication was Dick Story, a close friend.
Francis died in the early hours, Tuesday, March 19, after putting in a shift at the restaurant. He worked hard, but also in these years here, he enjoyed the slower paced lifestyle of Kent County, specifically in Betterton.
His son coming in from California, told the Kent County News, this was just the place for his parents after decades of serving students at Ursinus College in Pennsylvania. There, the demand never stopped. Alumnus have fond memories of eating at his establishment.
During the bench ceremony, under the shade of a maple, Maureen recalled with humor the time they discovered Betterton.
They were being shown real estate in Kent County when they came across the road sign pointing to the town.
At first sight, Maureen knew right away that old firehouse was special.
"We saw it, and I wanted it, and I was surprised my husband didn't shoot it down. He said if we can get it at a reasonable price, you got it. And you know what ... I never want to leave."
Michael thanked all the people for coming out to honor his father.
"This community has been wonderful to my parents, and it's been a great place to spend their retirement years."
Maureen added some background. When Francis and Maureen purchased the firehouse in 2002, they just so happened to have a worker who got accepted into Delaware State, training as an airplane pilot.
He needed a place nearby to stay and needed a job. Not only did the old firehouse work for that, it helped eventually develop Marzella's by the Bay, opening it for business on weekends.
That place eventually drew the owners in 2013, as Kent County tends to do, with the loveliness found on the Eastern Shore.
Francis and Maureen moved from college town to beach town in 2013, where they've ingratiated themselves to the community ever since.
Nothing explains any better their dedication to the town than a message from the Betterton Volunteer Fire Department during an emergency in January 2019.
"On behalf of the Betterton Vol. Fire Company members, I would like to thank Frank and Maureen Marzella for getting up and opening their business 2 a.m. this morning during the major Apartment building fire that Betterton Vol. Fire company had. Mr. and Mrs. Marzella fed over 45 Firefighters with pizza, sandwiches, and coffee and then stayed open the rest of the day serving all the customers that dine there everyday."
From Francis and Maureen's early start as restaurant owners, they've showed that kind of dedication to their community.
It's what they've done ever since 1960, when they sold a one-size, 12-inch pizza for $1.25 each, at a pizza shop in Collegeville, Pennsylvania. The first location had only two tables.
After a decade they moved to 488 Main St. across from Ursinus College, quickly building a legacy, where they extended their menu.
Always adapting, they expanded, shipping their products nationwide because Ursinus College alumni couldn't shake those indelible memories and savory dishes from their college years.
Then in 2013, the couple approaching their 70s, longing for a quieter life, moved to Howell Point Road, in Betterton, deeming the restaurant, Marzella's by the Bay.
There they had the freedom to reduce their hours, and meet the ever-growing demand for their delicious strombolis.
The family atmosphere, warmth and witty, whimsical stories from Maureen combined with Francis' tradition of excellent food continues to this day.
That was evident with the amount of support at the bench ceremony. Story said it didn't take long to find a way to pay for the bench, the plaque and fly Michael in from California.
"This is really so nice," Maureen said, overwhelmed by the attentiveness.
Story said that they'd be honored for Maureen to christen the bench, the first "sit."
With a smile, and a slow shake of her head, Maureen pointed out that technically that wasn't true. She wasn't the first. Earlier she saw some cute little boys sitting on it.
Which she said was all right too.
Francis probably would have wanted it that way, she replied. She added that as much as the community misses her husband, she misses him even more.
Marzella's continue to serve great food. They're open from Tuesday to Sunday, offering pizza, hearty sandwiches and more.
The bench, like Marzella's, is open for business as well, Story announced.

 Cambridge — Dorchester County Chief of Staff Donna Lane was thanked at her final County Council meeting as a county employee.During the meeting, Council President Lenny Pfeffer announced that Lane has taken a job with the state. In her 18 years and nine months as a county employee, Lane served a variety of positions, from administrative assistant to acting county manager.
Pfeffer, who called the news "bittersweet," thanked Lane for being a valuable resource in the county, as well as a friend.
"Even before I was elected, when I would sit in the audience and I'd have questions about how the county works, I'd come to you, and you would give me answers, and I greatly appreciate that," he said to her.

Before the meeting ended, County Attorney Chip MacLeod said that over the years, he's always copied Lane on emails.
"Knowing that whatever happens, if Donna knows I've sent this email, there's going to be a record and we'll figure something out," he said.

routine_announcement.content:
Veterans Day brings together Marylanders who served for breakfast at American Legion

 November 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 CAMBRIDGE — Serving in the U.S. Army gave Gov. Wes Moore (D) the chance to see parts of the country and world he never knew existed.The experience also gave him the opportunity to create lasting bonds with people different from him.
"I can tell you that some of my best friends on this planet are people who society tells me I shouldn't even be talking to," he said during a Veterans Day breakfast at American Legion Post 91 in Cambridge. "And these are my brothers now. And my sisters."
Before shaking hands with Maryland veterans and serving them breakfast, Moore — who was deployed to Afghanistan in 2005 — talked about the military's ability to unite people and the importance of unity in a time of division.
"I could not tell you the political affiliation of people that I served with," he said. "Because we didn't talk about it. ... Because it didn't matter. We fought for each other."
Moore said he and the people he served with had one goal: Making sure they got home. He talked about standing with each other and fighting for each other, even when disagreements arose.
There is a lot society can learn from veterans, he said.
"This Veterans Day, I think it becomes incredibly important that we hold those values dear and that we understand that even in the darkest moments, that it's faith that is what's going to drive us through," he said.
In his speech, Moore also talked about Maryland's efforts to support veterans. He mentioned tax relief for veterans as well as the Time to Serve Act, which extends military leave for state employees who serve in the National Guard or Reserve.
Along with Moore, American Legion Department of Maryland Commander David Heredia and Maryland Secretary of Veterans and Military Families Anthony Woods spoke at the breakfast event that drew an array of American Legion members from different posts.
Woods announced grant awards to the American Legion through the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund. He said Post 70 and Post 193 would receive funding for capital projects.
"This is a beautiful post right here," Woods said about Post 91. "But we want to invest in those posts because we know the role that the posts play in building community amongst our veterans."
The state is also giving $10,000 to the American Legion Department of Maryland to be invested in the American Legion's Be The One campaign, a national effort to reduce veteran suicide rates through offering supports and resources to veterans and working to destigmatize mental health support.
Steve Williams, who served in the U.S. Air Force from 1964 to 1968, said medical care and homelessness are two of the most important issues when it comes to supporting veterans. He said he thinks Moore is "pretty well on top of" what the issues affecting veterans are because Moore is a veteran.
Williams, who is the judge advocate for Post 91, said the event went "wonderfully."
"Seeing the different Legion posts all come together with state officials, you don't see that very often," he said. "I'm Really, really proud of it."
Post 91 Commander Rich Colburn said there were no Democrats, no Republicans and no independents in attendance at the event Veterans Day morning.
"Just veterans," he said.

routine_announcement.title: Iota Alpha Alpha Provides Turkeys, Meals to Hundreds of Easton Families
routine_announcement.author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
routine_announcement.content:
Iota Alpha Alpha provides turkeys, meals to hundreds of Easton families

 November 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 417
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Hundreds of turkeys and packaged meals were handed out to Easton residents Saturday afternoon on Glenwood Avenue.Iota Alpha Alpha, an Easton chapter of the national Omega Psi Phi fraternity, organized the distribution, which was held at the American Legion Blake-Blackston Post 77. Residents lined up around noon Saturday to pick up turkeys and meals.
Doug Rogers, a member of Iota Alpha Alpha, and Mayor Megan Cook each spoke at the start of the distribution.
"This is a great opportunity to give back to your community," Cook said.
She thanked the local organizations for their contributions that will help Easton residents not just the week of Thanksgiving, but throughout the entire holiday season.
Rogers said organizations such as the Dock Street Foundation, Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, Neighborhood Service Center and Building African American Minds Center were important partners with Iota Alpha Alpha for the event.
"This truck, it was filled to the brim," Rogers said of the truck that held the meals and turkeys. "… We passed out over 200 turkeys and 200 certificates for meals. And if people don't come and pick up those turkeys, it's great, because we're going to give the overflow to the Neighborhood Service Center. If they don't eat today, they'll eat next week."
The men of Iota Alpha Alpha joined with sister organizations and community members to not just pass out food, but to give away winter clothing to those in need as well.
It was the chapter's first Thanksgiving distribution at Blake-Blackston Post 77. Rogers said he hopes it continues and grows in future years.
Founded in 1911 at Howard University, Omega Psi Phi is predicated upon public service, Rogers said. A motto of the fraternity is "friendship is essential to the soul," something Rogers says the Easton chapter strives to do in the local community.
"When we start talking about giving, we start talking about (what) the Lord calls us to do, (He) calls us to serve people," Rogers said. "We're a service organization first and foremost. We're called to serve people. The little bit that we can do, the little bit that we can gather, is about serving God as people. So that's at our core."
Rogers said Saturday's cheerful and upbeat turkey and meal distribution was an example of the Iota Alpha Alpha chapter carrying out its mission and helping local residents in need during what can be trying times.
"It makes us feel good as men, is that we're able to stand up and be able to serve," Rogers said. "… We're living our creed."

 QUEEN ANNE'S COUNTY — There is still time to be part of the Christmas magic to ensure new toys and goods for local children through the QAC Christmas Angels this season.Local nonprofit QAC Christmas Angels works year round to ensure every child in Queen Anne's County has a merry Christmas and upcoming community events invite everyone to once again be part of the magic.
In its fifth year of spreading holiday joy, QAC Christmas Angels currently serves 1,500 county children and is continually growing, providing not only clothing and toys, but essentials such as hygiene kits, blankets and pillows to support families in the community that are going without due to circumstances beyond their control, organizer Linda Austin said.
Community collaboration has ensured the success for the QAC Christmas Angels for the holiday season and this year is no different, including upcoming SantaCon 2024 festivities.
While it's not a reindeer, El Jefe Mexican Kitchen/Tequila Bar will be home to a mechanical bull Dec. 7 from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m., $5 or a new toy donation will provide the opportunity to see how long you can hang on for a wild ride.
An escape room inviting everyone to "save Christmas" will take place at Kent Island Resort Dec. 12. Starting at 5:30 p.m., the evening includes dinner, a glass of champagne, dessert, a cash bar and a unique Christmas themed escape room.
Tickets are $75 per person or $65 per person with a table of eight and more information can be found at shoreupdate.com/savechristmas.
All designated proceeds will go toward QAC Christmas Angels to benefit county children.
QAC Christmas Angels falls under Queen Anne's Advocates for Youth, and with a 100% volunteer crew that operates out of a donated space, it is immensely proud of having no overhead, Austin said.
"Every dollar goes to the kids," she said.
QAC Christmas Angels are continuously collecting new goods and seeking volunteers and sponsorships to get a head start on next year's planning, Austin added.
Monetary contributions, no matter how small, are greatly appreciated. Amazon Wishlist and Paypal donation links are available through the QAC Christmas Angel Facebook page.
The QAC Christmas Angels were recently presented with a $15,000 donation from the county commissioners, who lauded the nonprofit for its dedication.
"We have seen tremendous support from the community," Austin said.
More information about the QAC Christmas Angels and how to get involved can be found by contacting Austin at 410 829-3136 or contacting linda.austin@longandfoster.com.

routine_announcement.title: Wind Causes Snow Drifts on Mid-Shore, Make Clearing Roads More Difficult
routine_announcement.author: Maggie Trovato
routine_announcement.content:
Wind causes snow drifts on Mid-Shore, make clearing roads more difficult

 January 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 575
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Thursday afternoon, Grand Rental Station of Easton employee Zach Kilmon sat atop a green tractor and cleared snow off the facility's driveway.It was not the first time Kilmon had been out to clear snow in front of the building that day. With strong winds blowing through the Mid-Shore, snow has been drifting into the roads, making conditions difficult on drivers and on public works departments.
With the next bout of snow expected Friday night, public works departments on the Mid-Shore are trying to address those snow drifts.
Dorchester County Manager Jerry Jones said they have plowed every road in the county.
"Every road in the county has been touched multiple times," he said. "But with this prevailing, strong, 20-plus mile-per-hour northwest wind, you can go through and them a half hour later, there's drifts again."
According to the National Weather Service, wind gusts Friday night were anticipated to reach as high as 29 miles per hour in Cambridge and 30 miles per hour in Easton.
Talbot County Manager Clay Stamp said snow drifts are having a significant effect on the county's back roads.
"We're working hard with our road crews to address that," he said. "And we've activated our farm community to join our county resources to try to address the re-drifting of these roads. And it's just an uphill battle until the wind decreases."
Stamp said the rural community has been very helpful with clearing roads using tractors, which has freed up county resources.
"As a rural community, we're very proud of our farm community for stepping up when the community is in need with that heavy equipment," he said.
Jones said that in Dorchester County, a lot of contractors have offered assistance in clearing roads.
"And we have certainly welcomed their offers and gotten them into the queue to try to help us manage these roadways," he said.
Kilmon said Grand Rental Station of Easton has rented out tractors to "a good few" people interested in clearing snow. He said he witnessed a few cars get stuck in ditches Thursday in front of his workplace on Centreville Road.
As they try to address snow drifts, both Talbot and Dorchester counties are preparing for the predicted snowfall Friday evening. According to the National Weather Service Thursday, about an inch of accumulation is possible in Easton and two inches of accumulation is possible in Cambridge.
Stamp said Talbot County's crews are prepared for the additional snow. He said the county wants to stress to the community that it's better for drivers to stay off the roads if they're able to and allow road crews to clear snow. He said drivers should also avoid the snow drifts if possible.
"I think our roads crew (members) are often unsung heroes," Stamp said. "They work well into the night, day in and day out, to try to get these roads open. We appreciate the public's patience."
Jones said Dorchester County's road crews are working as much as they can and the county is monitoring potential precipitation on Friday.
"We've got a lot of road here," Jones said. "I think it's 570-some miles that we're responsible for. So we're certainly doing the best we can to get that all done. And we're certainly working with State Highway (Administration) in trying to leverage that relationship as well where we can. I think right now, we just need mother nature to ease up on us and give us a break so we can get on top of it and get it cleared up."

routine_announcement.content:
Caroline Cares connects community with services at Resource Day

 January 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News

 Denton — Multiple vendors at Caroline Cares Community Resource Day Wednesday were reminded how amazing it is to do community work and help others.His Hope Ministries Youth Director Desiree Jefferson distributed winter clothes at the event. She was one of many vendors who had previously attended the event not to distribute resources, but to receive them.
"It's really refreshing to be able to give back," Jefferson said. "Just a couple years ago, I was somebody that was coming through the doors and receiving services myself, so it's good to see that we can help families in need."
The Caroline Cares Community Resource Day featured around 40 vendors providing information, help and food to the community.
"This is what it's all about," said Stephanie Johnson, His Hope Ministries' executive director and board member for Resources Day. "Just getting all the resources in one building so that it can be kind of an easily accessible for those who need them the most. Being able to bring those providers under one roof, on a specific day, to get those services out to everybody who needs them is huge."
One of the main focuses for Resource Day is providing many different types of help for many different people.
Some attendees face expenses they can't afford or are just in a bad financial situation, and some people are homeless. Resources Day helped with a variety of situations.
Directors expect 100 to 150 county residents experiencing homelessness to attend Resources Day every year, and they have a plan to make sure homeless residents can find shelter.
"With this particular event, they have access to walk around, talk to the vendors and see what exactly what their services are that they provide," Johnson said. "However, like when it comes to those who are actually experiencing homelessness, we have a separate room set aside for them to really dig into what their needs are and see how we can connect them with services."
Caroline County Public Schools officials attended, providing information for children on enrollment in school and many different resources for mental and physical health. United4Caroline provided free diapers for families with infants.
Chesapeake College's nursing program provided free blood pressure checks for all people in attendance. Nursing students gained experience and enjoyed serving the community.
"Oh, I love this, and I'm actually from Denton myself, so to give back to the community is amazing," Katie Reuwer, an assistant professor at Chesapeake College, said. "It's a great experience for the students to really learn about community service and helping others. I've already had some really good feedback from the students about how much they enjoy it."
Staff from Studio 107 Hair Salon in Kent Island and Edwards All Star Barbershop in Denton enjoyed providing free haircuts and styles at Resource Day, something both shops provide every year.
"There's no better feeling," Lisa Milligan, owner of Studio 107, said. "You're helping people that are maybe down on their luck or they're just getting out of jail or they're just going for jobs. It's every aspect, older people that can't afford to get their hair cut especially in this economy. So it's great to give back."

routine_announcement.title: Oxford Moves Forward with Website Update
routine_announcement.author: Maggie Trovato
routine_announcement.content:
Oxford moves forward with website update

 January 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 318
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Town of Oxford is getting a major update to its website.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting Tuesday, the commissioners awarded a contract to CivicPlus to develop an updated website that includes a direct resident messaging platform.
Commissioner Katrina Greer called the move "exciting."
"It'll be much easier to use," she said. "The old WordPress site was really clunky and difficult to use, so this will be drag-and-drop technology."
Greer said with the new site, users should be able to get where they need to go within two clicks, "which is simply not true right now."
Town Manager Holly Wahl said with this update, the town will be able to forward its current website to a government domain. She said with a direct resident messaging platform, the town will no longer have to use Constant Contact, an online platform it has been using to get information out to residents.
Wahl said all of the messages the town sends out will also populate on the updated website.
Residents who have been using Constant Contact will not have to do anything to stay in the loop. Wahl said all of the users subscribed via Constant Contact can be uploaded as subscribers to the new website. She said those who were not previously using Constant Contact will be able to subscribe to town updates from the updated website.
The mobile-friendly and ADA-compliant website will cost the town $3,598 to initiate. This price is approximately 50% less than the original quote the town received. Wahl said that cost will be covered in the town's existing fiscal year 2025 budget.
Wahl said she hopes to have the updated website up and running within the next two months.
"I'm aiming for six to eight weeks to get a base site set up so that agendas can be clear, meeting minutes are easy to locate (and) all of the boards and commissions have a page that's easy to navigate," she said.

routine_announcement.title: Easton Farmers Market Retains Downtown Spot for 2025
routine_announcement.author: Konner Metz
routine_announcement.content:
Easton Farmers Market retains downtown spot for 2025

 March 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 540
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Easton Farmers Market is set to remain at its normal downtown spot this season, though the location drew concerns at a recent town meeting.The market's public assembly permit was approved by the Easton Town Council March 18, allowing the market — operated by the Avalon Foundation — to run Saturdays from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. on North Harrison Street behind Goodwill in the town's parking Lot 5.
But some business owners expressed worry about the farmers market limiting downtown parking on Saturday mornings.
Steve Mangasarian, owner of Breakfast in Easton, said at the March 18 Town Council meeting that there have been parking and trash disposal issues stemming from the farmers market.
In an interview, Mangasarian said while he's not against the market and acknowledged it has "many good actors," he believes the Avalon is not doing enough to police market vendors.
"We feel as if we have a right as taxpayers to be entitled to some parking spaces, to be entitled to the secure use of our dumpsters, and accessibility to our parking lot," Mangasarian said. "And nobody at the farmers market seems to worry about these merchants who are being negatively impacted by the market."
Marie Nuthall, the Avalon's outdoor event coordinator , argued the downtown location is crucial for community connection. The market has been in the same spot for more than 30 years, Nuthall said.
"Over that time, families get to know where to find us, generations, their kids, so forth," she said. "Longevity and consistency is very, very important to us."
"The town has a vested interest in the farmers market being there, because we are part of a tourism draw," she added.
Nuthall said vendors sign memorandums of understanding at the beginning of each season outlining proper garbage disposal standards and parking regulations.
"We do everything that we can to be really good neighbors to all the neighboring businesses," Nuthall said.
The public assembly permit first went through the Easton Police Department before it hit the Town Council desk. While the Easton Police Department recommended approval for the North Harrison Street location, it also suggested an alternative spot at the District Court parking lot on Dover Street.
That lot is larger and would prevent downtown parking from being unavailable on Saturday mornings, according to EPD recommendations.
Easton Sgt. Patrick Sally said while the Harrison Street setup is "as safe as it ever has been," the department explored another option because an unofficial parking lot on Washington Street at the site of the former Safeway is soon to be under construction.
In an interview, Sally said the district court lot may be more of a "long-term" consideration. "It is a safety concern because there (are) a lot of people that do walk there," Sally said of the current downtown location.
Crossing guards are typically stationed at the current location during peak hours to assist pedestrian traffic on Harrison Street and Brewers Lane.
Nuthall said it's a relief to have the market remain in Lot 5 this year. She said "if a move is inevitable" in the future, she hopes the market and vendors "have buy-in" during that decision-making process.
"It should be something that is done thoughtfully and collaboratively," Nuthall said.
The Easton Farmers Market kicks off its 2025 season Saturday, April 12, and runs through December.

routine_announcement.title: 70 Children Attend Flashlight Easter Egg Hunt in Caroline County
routine_announcement.author: Ahmad Garnett
routine_announcement.content:
70 children attend flashlight Easter egg hunt in Caroline County

 April 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT | Section: News 
 
 336
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Kids enjoyed fun and special prizes at Denton Elementary Thursday for Caroline County Parks and Recreation's flashlight Easter egg hunt.Although the event was postponed from the week prior due to rain, Parks and Recreation program specialist Lynn Davis doesn't think the attendance was affected. Seventy kids aged 3 to 10 participated in the egg hunt, which Caroline County has been hosting the past 10 years.
"We love this. This is what we do it for," Davis said about having kids out for the event.
While traditional Easter egg hunts take place in the daylight, the Caroline County event has an added obstacle for egg hunters — darkness. The annual hunt takes place at dusk, and children use flashlights to help locate eggs on the elementary school's lawn.
Each age group had a special egg to look for. For ages 3 and 4, it was a soccer egg. For ages 5 to 7, it was a camouflage egg, and for ages 8 to 10, it was a football egg.
Each group had a separate time slot to capture the most eggs they could and go after the special egg. When a child found the special egg, they received a special prize, an Easter basket.
The event is fun for the children, but Parks and Recreation employees have fun as well.
"I found different patches of taller grass, leaves, branches and twigs," Parks and Recreations employee Liam Wallace said about hiding the eggs. "I kind of just hid it within those."
"It was just crazy. I wanted to see how happy they were out here, no elbows, no shoving, so safe fun," Halie Readores, another employee, said.
Lynn Zepp, a mother of two, brought her son, Weston, and daughter, Willow, to the egg hunt for their first year of participation.
"It was exciting," Lynn Zepp said. "We just got done with a baseball game, and we rushed over here because we wanted to try out the flashlight egg hunt."
When Weston and Willow were asked if they enjoyed the event, they said they had fun.
