routine_announcement.title: Childlene Brooks, Kenley Timms Win Awards at Talbot Day
routine_announcement.author: Konner Metz
routine_announcement.content:
Childlene Brooks, Kenley Timms win awards at Talbot Day

 April 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 533
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Childlene Brooks and Kenley Timms were honored Friday for their outstanding community service.During a Talbot Day ceremony, an annual celebration for the county's April 25 birthday, the county presented Brooks with the Lifetime Service Award and Timms with the Ripple Effect Award.
Brooks is manager of the Brookletts Place Senior Center, and Timms serves as commander of VFW Post 5118.
Talbot County Council members Lynn Mielke and Keasha Haythe spoke on the impact of the winners' work in the Talbot County community.
"Childlene's name is synonymous with service to Talbot County," Mielke said. "Through her leadership at Brookletts Place, her tireless volunteerism, she's guided, mentored and uplifted generations. Her service has not only filled gaps, but has built bridges."
"A Vietnam veteran and longtime VFW commander, Kenley's legacy is one of action and compassion," Haythe said. "Whether organizing welcome-home parades, helping homeless veterans, supporting first responders, or simply showing up for those in need, Kenley leads with heart. His efforts have not only made a difference, they've inspired movement."
Brooks volunteers for nonprofit organizations along with leading the Brookletts Place in its mission to serve the county's growing senior population. Timms recently organized a Welcome Home parade for Vietnam veterans and families, an event that brought hundreds to the streets of Easton.
A 1983 proclamation originally declared April 25 as the county's birthday. The County Council led a charge to reinvigorate Talbot Day by signing a new proclamation to create the holiday in 2023.
In all, the county recognized 17 nominees for community service, part of the new tradition.
Haythe noted that the county created the award ceremony to continue the tradition of a now-defunct state program dating back to the 1980s, which honored community service leaders.
"Although the statewide program ended in 2022, the Talbot County Council chose to carry the tradition forward," Haythe said. "We renamed it the Talbot Citizen and Service Awards, continuing its legacy of recognizing those who give their time and heart to our community."
Talbot Day also brought around 100 residents to the lawn of the Talbot County Courthouse to celebrate the county's history. Mike Mielke, a local farmer, waterman and historian, served as Friday's guest speaker.
Mielke said a range of local organizations, schools and volunteer groups make Talbot County a special place to live. He pointed out towns such as Oxford, St. Michaels and Easton for bringing a unique way of life to the Eastern Shore as well as being a "mecca for weddings."
And for unincorporated areas such as Tilghman Island or Neavitt, Mielke said it's a neat mix of residents.
"The people do get along, the newcomers and watermen and stuff," Mielke said. "They get along pretty darn well."
"It's still the land of pleasant living," Mielke said of Talbot County. "Talbot's my home, and I love it."
Talbot Day Poster Contest winners: Maddy Calabro, Division I; Toni Wilson, Brianna Johnson, Meyers Hannah and Leah Bell, Division III.
Talbot Citizen and Service Awards nominees: Carlton "Corky" Greene, Childlene Brooks, Christine Dorset, Daphan Smith, Della Andrew, Doris Dobson, Mary DeShields, Jennifer Stanley, JR Burkhardt, Karla Wieland-Cherry, Kenley Timms, Khalid Kurtom, Lonnelle Green, Nancy Andrew, Raymond Bonner, Sonny Diefenderfer, Virginia Capute
This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Talbot Citizen and Service Award nominee Sonny Diefenderfer.

From the publisher: Newspaper broadens outreach

 July 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Local News 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 This week marks a key milestone for our Star Democrat. We are engaging our community on a deeper level with two events in Easton. We want to continue to inspire and share, build and broaden, help and care about our community. These new events will help us do so.For our first connection, we have a public facing event to hyper-focus on a key element of our community — the power of women. This is a yearlong exercise in connecting, sharing, mentoring, modeling and caring about the women in our community.
It's a powerful and risky venture but one we believe is worthwhile. While we began with a Women to Watch as a keystone event in the spring, this is a summer speaker series with some key influencers, movers and shakers.
On the Easton Mid-Shore event panel we have Amber McGinnis, executive director of Chesapeake College Foundation; Morgan Foster, founder and CEO of The Pivot Process; Shania Gregory, the executive director of the YMCA-Easton; and Anne Altvater, group facilitator and owner, Campbell's Lane Farm. Their discussion on "mindfulness" will be moderated by Cassandra Vanhooser, Economic Development and Tourism Director for Talbot County. Join us at 8 a.m. on Aug. 7 at The Market at Dover Station. For more information go to apgchesapeake.com/summer-speaker-series-2025.
Our other new offering is an effort to collaborate with people in the Eastern Shore community through those whose unique perspective and insight is a valuable asset to share with our readers. In our first effort we are engaging Easton Mayor Megan Cook to write a column on the first Friday of each month about the view, the sights, and experiences with the community "from the Mayor's Chair." She will share her work, her thoughts and her interactions with the community so we can all be more aware of our local world and what the future may hold. I am sure it will be sometimes serious and other times humorous — but always sincere and informative. Mayor Cook may, from time to time, engage or partner with other key influencers in our town so be ready, you may be called on to be on the team.
These two efforts complement the Star Democrat's Reader Advisory Board that meets with us quarterly to give us perspective and insight into our coverage. They offer unedited truths and thoughts about what we do well and what we need to improve. It's a great bunch and we'll do them justice in another forum.
Thank you again and again for your support. It means the world to us.
Orestes Baez, Regional President
Adams MultiMedia/Chesapeake

routine_announcement.title: Autumn Block Party in Ridgely Approved for Second Year
routine_announcement.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
routine_announcement.content:
Autumn Block Party in Ridgely approved for second year

 August 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 444
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — The Autumn Block Party in Ridgely is back for another year, and committee members expect it to be better than last year.At their July meeting, the Ridgley Town Commissioners approved the block party for the second year.
The idea of the block party came from a conversation in a Facebook group last year started by committee member Anthony Duckery.
Committee member Holly Justice, commented on Duckery's post and they began conversations about creating an autumn block party for the youth in Caroline County.
After more conversations multiple members of the community Tina Hurley, Erin Wheeler and Chad Leister joined the committee.
At the end of the block party last year, the committee put out a poll to the community to see what could be better about the event. Extending the time was the biggest item the residents raised.
"People said that they would have liked it to be longer and a couple of other things, so we did decide this year to make it from 12 p.m. to 7 p.m. just to give people that weren't able to make it due to sports or whatever they had going on last year, they can maybe attend this year," Justice said.
Other changes include the amount of vendors and the resources those vendors provide for the community.
"We offer nonprofits the opportunity to set up information tables," Justice said. "We do not charge them a vendor fee because we get how difficult it is with for-profit. We wanted to give them a platform to tell people about their services."
Food and family fun will continue to be free at the event. The committee ensured the block party had many free components because they wanted children and families in the community to have something to enjoy without worrying about a price.
"This is something that we want to do, and we really are about trying to keep this a free event. That was key for us is making it free," Justice said. "... I didn't want for the block party to be something that people had to see if they could do. I wanted them to know they could do it and it not be finances that would keep them from it.
"I don't feel that children should be excluded from the fun things, and life in general, just because unfortunately this economy is crazy and everything is astronomically priced. I wanted to just be able to give them a day where no one had to worry."
The block party will include a DJ, bands, dance performances, free games, face paintings, sports tournaments, craft stations and more.
It will be held on Saturday, Sept. 13, from noon to 7 p.m. at Martin Sutton Park in Ridgely.

routine_announcement.title: Greensboro to Hold Annual Winter Clothes Drive on Nov. 21
routine_announcement.author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
routine_announcement.content:
Greensboro to hold annual Winter Clothes Drive on Nov. 21

 October 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 263
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — The Town of Greensboro is currently accepting donations of new or clean, gently used winter clothes items for its annual winter clothes drive.Town resident Cathy Spencer said the event started because she hates to see people cold.
"As a child I never liked being cold, and as I got older, I saw other people, and I hate to think of children being cold," Spencer said. "So, people are always willing to give things, and I figure a winter clothes drive would be the perfect way to get clothes that people donated out of the public so no one's cold this winter."
The town is accepting winter clothes such as coats, hoodies, sweatshirts, heavy sweaters, gloves, scarfs, winter hats, ski pants and snow boots in all sizes, but mainly children's sizes.
The distribution event is scheduled for Nov. 21 at the Greensboro Community Hall at 13781 Greensboro Road. The drive begins at 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. and then 4 p.m. until 7 p.m.
The town emphasizes that everyone is welcome to attend, no matter their address or income.
Donated items can be dropped of at Greensboro Town Hall during normal business hours or at 509 N. Academy Street in Greensboro.
"I'm a giver, so I love doing this," Spencer said. "It just makes me feel good to see them come in there. Everybody's laughing, everybody's smiling."
In addition to donations, the town is looking for a Spanish-speaking translator to help attendees who do not speak English.
Any person interested in being a translator for the drive should call the town at 410-482-6222 and ask to speak to Julie.

routine_announcement.title: Community Invited to 9/11 Day of Remembrance Ceremony
routine_announcement.content:
Community invited to 9/11 Day of Remembrance Ceremony

 August 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A5 | Section: News 
 
 510
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Easton Economic Development Corporation along with community partners the Town of Easton, Talbot County Government, Talbot County Department of Emergency Services and the Talbot County Chamber of Commerce Young Professionals invite the public to a Day of Remembrance Ceremony on Sept. 11, 2023.Throughout the summer, volunteers have been working together to help strengthen relationships between members of the community by supporting projects that exemplified the theme, "We Are One: Community Supporting Community." The project is one of many across the country that will pay tribute to the individuals lost and injured on September 11, 2001, as well as honor the first responders and the many others who have risen to service in a crisis. The purpose of this awareness effort is to empower the general public to be caring, responsive community members should their fellow citizens need their support and to be mindful of the work of first responders in their community.The Day of Remembrance ceremony concludes the summer events."Easton is a resilient community, one that has supported its citizens through hundreds of years, through the good and the challenging times," said Easton Mayor Megan Cook. "I am proud of the summer-long project that helped our neighbors get to know each other and reinforce the idea that everyone will reach out and lend a hand across the city in times of need." Projects throughout the year included citizen responder trainings, a community mosaic project, community conversations and creation of downtown banners illustrating the theme."We are so grateful to be in such a supportive community.Teaching our community how to keep themselves and their neighbors safe is the first step in making our community resilient and able to endure whatever may come our way," said Geneva Schaffle, Talbot Emergency Management coordinator.This year's ceremony will incorporate volunteers from several local towns in the area, including the Easton Middle School Band and representatives from the Talbot County School system, local law enforcement officers and fire department volunteers, and members of local churches.Keynote speaker and Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher will remark on the significance of the ceremony to the Easton community. Following the ceremony, the public is invited to a reception at the Talbot County Free Library, which will feature works of art created by program participants."We Are One: Caring for our Community" is funded through The Arc of The United States through a sub-grant from Ameri-Corps, a federal agency that engages millions of Americans in service and leads the nation's volunteer efforts for Patriot Day and the national 9-11 Day of Service and Remembrance Project.The ceremony will take place beginning at 8:30 a.m. at the Service Memorial on the corner of West and Dover streets in Easton. In the event of inclement weather, the ceremony will be moved to the Talbot County Free Library on Dover Street.More information about the event is available online at discovereaston.com/weareone.

routine_announcement.author: Maggie Trovato
routine_announcement.content:
Counties and towns prepare for snow on the Mid-Shore this weekend

 January 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 531
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With snow in the forecast this Sunday and Monday, Mid-Shore towns and counties are making plans and readying their snow plows."Every storm is different and unique," Easton Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh said. "But we feel that we're prepared and ready for the storm."
On Friday, the Talbot County Department of Emergency Services had a meeting with local towns to coordinate in preparation for the winter weather.
According to the National Weather Service forecast as of Friday afternoon, snow is likely to fall in Easton from Sunday night into Monday. The weather organization is expecting a "major winter storm" will bring snow and ice across the country, "from the Central Plains to the Mid-Atlantic" this weekend.
Sunday night, there is a 90% chance of precipitation in Easton with snow expected mainly after 1 a.m., according to the National Weather Service. On Monday, there is a 90% chance of precipitation in Easton with snow expected before 1 p.m. and then rain and snow likely. Monday night, there is a 50% chance of precipitation.
Talbot County Public Schools Communications Director Debbie Gardner said the district is monitoring the forecast to determine if closures will be necessary.
Dorchester County Emergency Management Division Director Jimmy Windsor said Dorchester County has warned all its departments of the predicted weather, including its Highway Division. He said the county's Highway Division is preparing its inclement weather plans.
Van Emburgh said on Friday that Easton was putting plows on the fronts of trucks and loading salt into the trucks that spread salt.
"And we have equipment that we're placing around town that we'll use to address alleys and some of the tighter spots that we plow," he said.
Windsor said it is important that residents make sure they take the usual winter preparedness precautions, such as making sure vehicles have gas in them. He said that residents who live in areas that are prone to power outages should make sure they have blankets and warm clothing in the event of an outage.
"And a supply of fresh water in case the power goes out and you're on well water and therefore you rely on the power for your water source," he said.
Van Emburgh said it's helpful if residents do not park their cars on main streets.
"When people park on the streets, we have to plow around the cars and sometimes that can — depending on how much snow we get — that can get tricky and then we plow the cars in," he said.
Van Emburgh also talked about the importance of not plowing snow from the sidewalks into the street.
"Because we then plow it back onto the sidewalk," he said, laughing. "It's just a battle. (Residents) plow it onto the street. We plow it back onto the sidewalk. And they get mad at us."
Van Emburgh said residents should plow snow off their sidewalks by starting in the center of the street and working toward a house or building so that the snow is plowed into a yard.
"Some properties don't have yards," he said. "But if you plow it out in the street, it's just going to get pushed back onto the sidewalk. So we ask that everything moves away from the center of the street."

 OXFORD - Oxford Commission President Tom Costigan dispelled rumors that a new secretary had been hired at the Oxford Town Office."There is no new secretary being hired," Costigan said at Tuesday's town meeting."And there was no consideration of hiring a new secretary or any other administrative staff. We have three people downstairs in our town office and that's not changing, and we haven't considered changing it." Costigan said this after reading a letter from resident Nancy Fogarty that requests information, through the Maryland Public Information Act, on the rumored new position.In an interview, Town Manager Cheryl Lewis confirmed there are only three employees in the town office: herself, her administrative assistant and the town planner.Fogarty's letter about the secretary position follows a social media posting that questioned whether a new secretary had been hired.The letter formally requests a copy of the job description, the number of candidates considered for the position and confirmation that the hired person is not a relative of or has a personal relationship with Lewis or any other town employee."In addition, I request a copy of the job description of the town manager assistant clerk and planner so I can better understand the responsibilities of each and their assumed support by the newly formed position of secretary," the letter says.Costigan said that because the letter is a PIA request, he would have to pass it on to Oxford Town Attorney Lyndsey Ryan.As of Wednesday evening, Lewis said the town had not yet responded to the PIA request, but will.

no_policy_impact.author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
no_policy_impact.content:
Talbot County 100+ Women Who Care donates $13K at inaugural meeting

 September 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com | Page: A10 | Section: News

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Talbot County 100+ Women Who Care group started off strong at its inaugural meeting Monday evening, which ended on a high note with a $13,000 donation to the Talbot Interfaith Shelter.Living up to the group's name, over 100 women gathered at the Talbot County Free Library to hear quick presentations from three local nonprofits seeking funding.At Monday's meeting, the first three nominees - the Mid-Shore Pancreatic Foundation, Talbot Humane and Talbot Interfaith Shelter - shared presentations and stories on why the $13,000 contribution from group members should be awarded to them and how each would use the funds.Each nonprofit was given five minutes to present, followed by several minutes of questions from attendees looking to make informed decisions.Audience members then filled out voting forms, casting their ballots for the nonprofit they found to be the most compelling.Following a quick tally, Talbot Interfaith Shelter was selected as the first awardee.Founded in 2008, TIS is dedicated to ending homelessness in the Mid-Shore region by providing shelter, stability, support and success to families and individuals in need, said Julie Lowe, the shelter's executive director.But TIS has expanded since then, she added - the shelter now offers education on money management, the root causes of poverty, accessing resources and weaning off those resources."That is when I see the joy in people's faces, when they say 'I don't need that CarePack anymore on the weekends for my kids, I don't need that temporary cash assistance anymore, I have a job and I'm able to provide for my family," Lowe said.However, the cost of childcare remains a significant struggle."The expense of childcare is hard for people with a really good job to manage, much less somebody who's in a homeless shelter trying to find a job, even a minimum wage job, to support their family and be able to get them back into housing," Lowe said.Laura Richeson, TIS' director of development and marketing, said the nonprofit has a $1.3 million operating budget this year, a daunting but fulfilling goal to fundraise for. Finding money to subsidize childcare costs for working parents in the shelter is the "biggest issue." After selecting Monday's awardee, the philanthropic group of women also submitted nominations for the next meeting's presenters.The group's next meeting, slated for sometime in January, will feature presentations from the St. Michaels Fire Department, CarePacks of Talbot County and the Mid-Shore Pancreatic Cancer Foundation, which will be back for a second time.community members who committed to contributing were happy with how the group's inaugural meeting turned out.{p dir="ltr"}Vivian Landau of St. Michaels said she's always been involved with philanthropic events, so the local 100+ Women Who Care group starting up seemed "perfect" for her to join.For Colleen Kennedy of Bozman, making contributions to places she cares about isn't new. She's donated to a scholarship fund at the high school she attended, but the 100+ Women Who Care group in Talbot County has a key difference."I liked that I can actually pick and see where the money goes," she said.The Talbot County group's founding members - Amanda David, Karen Gadson and Michele Lowe - were also pleased with the turnout and excitement for the group's first meeting."It's a very simple and effective way to impact all of the (Talbot County) nonprofits who are in the trenches, making our community a better place," David said of the organization's goal.

Denton shelter offers 42 beds for homeless

 September 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: A1 | Section: News

 DENTON - Local leaders stopped by.Friends and neighbors popped in. And His Hope Ministries Executive Director Stephanie Johnson announced on social media, "To say our shelter warming was a success was an understatement." The Denton-based ministry opened its doors Sept. 1 for the 2023-2024 season, kicking it off with a shelter warming Tuesday, Aug. 29, at 409 Aldersgate Drive.Among the nearly 75 attendees were State Sen.Johnny Mautz, R-37; Del.Jeff Ghrist, R-36-Caroline; Del. Steve Arentz, R-36-QA; Amy Horne, executive director of CASA of Caroline; His Hope Ministries Executive Director Stephanie Johnson; Matt Dahl, president of His Hope Ministries' board of directors; and His Hope Ministries board member and treasurer Andrew Breeding."We are so thankful to each and every person who came to support our event. An extra special thank you to our state Delegates Jeff Ghrist and Steve Arentz, as well as Sen. Johnny Mautz for stopping by," His Hope Ministries posted on its Facebook page."It's really humbling that they take the time out of their busy schedules to come and just see what's happening in their districts," Johnson said.His Hope Ministries is a "Christ-centered ministry committed to ending homelessness in our community through comprehensive services, resources and programs for individuals and families." A handful of residents have moved into the shelter which has 42 beds., but Johnson said His Hope Ministries help provide resources to those "who are facing homelessness and need help staying in their housing." "And if we can't help, we will definitely pass you on to the next person who can," Johnson said.Friends of the of the nonprofit organization donated bags full of "toiletries, hygiene items, cleaning supplies and basic household items," Johnson said. The shelter will be open until about April 30.On display was a preliminary architectural sketch of the one-story shelter the organization hopes to build on a different piece of property.In the meantime, a lot of fundraising is planned, including a designer purse bingo at 2 p.m. Sunday, Oct. 8, at Goldsboro Volunteer Fire Company.For more information about fundraisers, needs and volunteer opportunities, see His Hope Ministries website at hishopeministries.org or visit the Facebook page at www.facebook.com/HisHopeMinistries.

no_policy_impact.author: Laura Tayman
no_policy_impact.content:
Lt. Governor Energizes Democrats at Unity Dinner

 October 18, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 4 | Section: News 
 
 481
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE - In the main hallway of the Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center and Museum in Centreville last weekend, Maryland's Lt. Governor Aruna Miller greeted leaders of the Queen Anne's County Democratic Party for a short meet and greet before speaking to the awaiting audience of supporters."We have our work cut out for us," said Frank Alduino, member of the Democratic Central Committee in QA, when asked how support for the Democrats was faring.The Queen Anne's County Democratic Central Committee held what will now be their annual Unity Dinner, at the Center on Saturday evening, Oct. 14, providing Democrats across the county and state the opportunity to meet.Jordan Himes, political director for the Maryland Democratic Party, attended the event to "make sure we get as unified as we can as Democrats." {p class="p2"}In his introduction of Miller, Himes, whose grandmother is from the Eastern Shore and attended school in the Kennard Center, site of the former Kennard High School, said he was brought up knowing that you can never have the absence of hope."I encourage everyone here to use your voice," said Himes. "One voice can change one person, a person can change the county, the county can change the state, the state can change the country, and the country can change the world." In 2022, Maryland saw the most diverse ticket that's ever won in the history of Maryland. Miller thanked the audience for their support of the Moore/Miller ticket which won by the most votes in Maryland's history, and they were the only two people of color who ever won the office together in the United States.Miller told the audience they didn't vote for the Moore/Miller ticket to be the status quo. "You all wanted us to move boldly, decisively, and deliberately for all Marylanders. You elected us to leave no one left behind." Miller assured the crowd they had heard the voices of rural voters who told them that the only time they saw elected officials was during a campaign year. Because of this, Miller says, Governor Moore has decided to coordinate a tour bus of his entire cabinet to travel to every Maryland county and listen to the concerns of voters.Touting the success of the legislative session, Miller said the administration worked on raising the minimum wage; increasing services to Maryland veterans; providing high school seniors with a year-long, postgrad service option; increasing broadband services in rural areas; and ensuring training for abortion care providers."Things don't just happen, they are made to happen," said Miller. "We are fighting for equity and freedom. Let's all heal the world and make it a better place."

Lt. Governor Aruna Miller joins the Queen Anne's County Democratic Central Committee members from top left, Tom Rider, John Stires, Connie {span}Lee Kratovil-Lavelle{/span}, Miller, Deborah Krueger, {span}Elaine McNeil, Frank {span}Alduino and in front, Lynn Mason with her grandsons.{/span}{/span}

no_policy_impact.title: Easton Mourns All Innocent Lives - Officials Express Support for Israel with Emotional Reading of Proclamation
no_policy_impact.author: Natalie Jones; njones@chespub.com
no_policy_impact.content: Easton - Town officials in Easton voiced public sympathy and support for Israel following the Oct. 7 attacks on the country by Hamas terrorists. Easton Mayor Megan Cook, joined at the podium by Temple B'nai Israel Rabbi Peter Hyman, read a proclamation from the town, her voice full of emotion, at the council's Monday meeting. "The Town of Easton unequivocally condemns Hamas for this deplorable and unprovoked attack on Israel and stands with Israel as it defends itself," she said. "The Town of Easton mourns all innocent lives, regardless of their religious beliefs, that have been and will be lost due to the atrocities," Cook continued, her voice breaking. Speaking tearfully, Cook said the town prays for those whose families have been killed, captured or injured, and calls for swift return of all hostages in hopes for a lasting resolution and peace. After hugging Cook, Hyman took a moment to share his thoughts, thanking the town for its support. "I'm rarely, as some of you know, rarely at a loss for words, but this is difficult," he said. "There are innocent people on both sides who are going to suffer as a result of the terrorism and the horror, and we deeply appreciate your friendship, your support and your acknowledgement." At the start of the meeting, Ward 1 Councilwoman Maureen Curry fervently prayed for refuge and safety for all those affected by the conflict, expressing hope for comfort and security. A moment of silence was observed by all in attendance. Temple B'nai Israel will hold an interfaith community vigil in support of Israel on Thursday, Oct. 19, at 7 p.m. at the temple's location in Easton.

no_policy_impact.title: Housing Secretary Visits His Hope Ministries
no_policy_impact.author: Tom McCall
no_policy_impact.content:
Housing secretary visits His Hope Ministries

 April 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 668
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Maryland Secretary of Housing and Community Development Jake Day, came to His Hope Ministries in Denton Tuesday to learn about the nonprofit's vision for the future.The organization, which provides services and shelter to those experiencing homelessness, wants to develop a new building and move to Market Street.
They toured bunk rooms at 409 Aldersgate Drive, where neat piles of clothes, toothbrushes, laundry detergent and ear buds lie. The shelter welcomes guests from September through the end of April, with accommodations for families, single men and women, and youths.
"They are seeking to grow because the demand is high," Day said. "Part of that is that there just are not enough housing units, particularly affordable housing units in the Mid-Shore. We have underbuilt for the last 15 years. The consequence is that people are unhoused."
Executive Director Stefanie Johnson showed Day some architectural plans for a new facility she would like to build to expand His Hope's services.
"I did show him our design so far. We have an idea in mind for land, but so far, it is not available from the town yet. We have our Senior Haven, which is a three bedroom one bath home. It has three seniors in it. Seniors or disabled — it is transitional so they can stay there for up to three years," said Johnson.
There is a vacant lot next to this senior home where His Hope hopes to build their expanded facility.
One of the barriers to completing the project is its cost. Some of the visit was talking about money.
Day said he believes the best fiscal options for His Hope to complete the project is through the Community Development Block Grant from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. The state has $7.5 million to fund CDBG annually, he said.
"Probably for the Eastern Shore it is CDBG money. It gets to the end user when it is ready to be executed and spent for construction and design. This federal money has to serve the low income population," Day said.
The other option Day mentioned is Sowing Empowerment and Economic Development Inc., a nonprofit organization providing food, education, and training while promoting self-sufficiency and empowerment directly to low-to-moderate-income families.
"I believe both predevelopment and development costs are eligible. SEED is the institutional version of this. For the town, all it has to be is a community development goal that they're interested in. Helping unsheltered homeless be sheltered has positive health outcomes. A hospital and a shelter would go hand and glove," Day said.
Andrew Breeding, treasurer for His Hope Ministries, called their hoped-for property the Market Street Property. The land is owned by the Town of Denton and used to be a Southern States facility.
"The challenge is putting a homeless shelter literally anywhere," said Breeding.
Johnson said some local politicians are hesitant about the idea of building a shelter in town. Day said that representatives from his office, including him, could come and testify to the town council on behalf of His Hope's story.
Day asked some pressing questions about how His Hope Ministries and the community interact.
"What's that look like between you and other organizations in the community?" he asked.
Johnson responded, "It is impeccable. When we closed (for the warmer months), we called and said, 'Hey, do you have room for our families? Talbot Interfaith in Easton, and in Cambridge the Salvation Army, we are all on speed dial. Even the Christian Shelter in Salisbury. This community is so giving."
Day also toured the office and youth drop-in center of His Hope Ministries on 105 Gay Street, housed in a spacious Victorian house with a broad porch. The inside is inviting and colorful. There is room for classes on financial literacy, and there are many positive affirmations on the walls.
Amidst a big black board filled with affirmations, Day was invited to grab some chalk and add his. He wrote, "A mistake will not define you. Get back up and keep going."

no_policy_impact.title: Mixed-Use Residential Development Planned in Easton
no_policy_impact.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
no_policy_impact.content:
Mixed-use residential development planned in Easton

 June 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 492
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Two mixed-use developments will be built on the former Perdue grain facility on Brookletts Avenue. These developments will provide affordable housing opportunities and commercial use for the town of Easton, developers said.The project's developers are Chesapeake Community Development, a subsidiary of The Arc focused on creating equitable, accessible and inclusive committees.
Jonathon Rondeau, president and CEO of The Arc Central Chesapeake Region, said the project will be a thriving neighborhood that will support the various housing needs of the community by offering quality affordable and market-rate rentals.
"When you look at a six-and-a-half-acre site, there's a real opportunity to think more broadly, but also to say, 'how do you really affect the community rather than just building something that's part of the community?'" Rondeau said. "But how can it be a foundation of the community?"
The Arc is a nonprofit organization with a mission to support people with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
About 15 years ago, The Arc decided to create housing opportunities for people with disabilities, which is how Chesapeake Community Development and Chesapeake Neighbors were created.
Though the focus was to establish affordable housing for people with disabilities, the need for affordable housing became so essential that the organization changed its mission to create affordable housing opportunities for all.
Rondeau said they manage about 70 units in Anne Arundel County and the Eastern Shore, including the Primrose and Port Streets Commons. The Arc's subsidiaries seek to create opportunities for people from disadvantaged backgrounds to access services.
Rondeau said mixing affordable and market-rate housing makes development financially viable by allowing subsidies for affordable units through market-rate rents.
He said though Talbot County has a high median income, there are a lot of families that live significantly below the average income. Rondeau said that there is a range of people who have a full time job but make less than $30,000 a year.
workers like baristas and education professionals are people who do important work in the community and should be given the access to live in the area as well, Rondeau said.
Ross Benincasa, a consulting partner and vice president of community development, said the need for affordable housing was great in the area.
"Our vision is to bring a vibrant multi-purpose space to the community that incorporates a wide range of amenities and resources, including much-needed housing," Benincasa said in a press release earlier this month.
Rondeau said they will be hosting a community meeting at the Brookletts Place Senior Center on July 10 at 5 p.m. to hear the concerns and ideas from the local community. He emphasized that community involvement is crucial to addressing any concerns and helping design a development that can meet the people's needs.
"We, The Arc and Chesapeake Neighbors and Chesapeake Community Development want to be part of the community and be part of making Easton an inclusive and equitable community," Rondeau said. "And projects like this allow us to do that, and we hope that the community can help be part of that."

no_policy_impact.title: Choptank Fishing Pier Plans Still TBD
no_policy_impact.author: Maggie Trovato mtrovato@chespub.com
no_policy_impact.content:
Choptank fishing pier plans still TBD

 June 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 737
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Maryland Department of Natural Resources is continuing to determine the best place for a new fishing pier on the Choptank River between Talbot and Dorchester counties.The search for a location began in 2021 with closure of the Bill Burton Fishing Pier.
Gregg Bortz, media relations manager for DNR, said in an email that the department is working with both counties, as well as the City of Cambridge, to find "the best option for access" to the Choptank. He said the department is considering a few sites that are "in the general vicinity of the current pier."
Bortz said after this process is complete, DNR plans to move forward with creating that access.
In late December 2021, the fishing pier was closed due to structural safety concerns. A February 2022 underwater inspection revealed crumbling concrete in multiple areas of the structure below the water's surface.
Although Joe Brooks — who lives a few houses down the road from the Dorchester County side of the fishing pier, on Radiance Drive — was sad to see the fishing pier close, he was happy that it would put an end to the trash in his front yard and illegal parking on the street.
"It was just out of control for many years," he said. "Everyday you get up and walk and pick up trash out in the front yard. ... And it's all kinds of trash."
Brooks helped petition the City of Cambridge to get no parking signs put up on the street, but he said there were people who parked there anyway.
"There's not adequate parking for a fishing pier there," Brooks said about where pier's former location. "I mean, there's a very small parking lot for the use of the pier."
As DNR looks for the best spot for a new fishing pier, Brooks thinks it should go somewhere other than where it currently is. He said the Talbot County side of the river has many acres of land with ample space for parking. Brooks said if the fishing pier must go on the Dorchester County side, the county Visitor Center is on the other side of U.S. Route 50, and would make more sense as the pier's location.
"It's not trying to fit a square peg in a round hole," he said.
Parking and accessibility are primary concerns for DNR when it comes to deciding on a location for a new pier, Bortz said.
Brooks said he doesn't know anyone else in the neighborhood who wants a new fishing pier to be built in its current location.
"Pretty well everyone in my area had issues with parking and sometimes (dis)respectful people on the pier," he said.
American Legion Post 91 Commander-elect and former Maryland Sen. Rich Colburn said he estimates there is room for 12 cars in the parking lot for the closed fishing pier. He said a new fishing pier on the other side of Route 50 or on the Talbot County side would have more room for parking.
The American Legion Post, which is directly across the street from the closed fishing pier on Radiance Drive, has been interested in leasing the fishing pier parking lot from DNR since the pier closed. In a May 24 letter, DNR Secretary Josh Kurtz told Colburn in response to the reuqest that DNR was unable to lease the parking area at that time.
Bortz said the lot is not for sale because it could be part of the department's plans for future park access. Colburn said he understands DNR will need the parking lot when it demolishes the current pier, but until that happens, he believes DNR could easily lease the lot to the American Legion.
Mid-Shore Fishing Club President Tom Wilkison thinks the closed pier should be replaced with a new one in the same location.
"Because the community needs it," he said. "There are so many people that used to use that pier, especially from the Cambridge side."
Wilkison, who has never fished off the pier but has walked on it, said the current location of the pier is accessible. He acknowledged it could use a little more parking on the Dorchester side.
"I just hope that the state puts something back there," he said.
Brooks said when DNR does construct a new fishing pier, it's important that it also maintains and polices the pier.
"That's the best way to keep people — in my mind — respectful, is have a respected place and have a presence of people to enforce that," he said.

no_policy_impact.title: Wittman Community Staple Under Construction
no_policy_impact.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
no_policy_impact.content:
Wittman community staple under construction

 June 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 615
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WITTMAN — The town of Wittman has been without a post office since late May due to a car accident that left the building out of commission.Ted Marshall, owner of the post office building, said a vehicle hit the porch on May 28. Though the post office itself was not damaged, the porch was moved approximately a foot and a half, and the incident dislodged the porch, including the braces.
Marshall said the post office is vital to his family and its legacy. His mother, Betty Marshall, was the postmistress of the establishment, and Marshall said he also spent time working there.
The building was passed down to him after his father died, and he eagerly wants to keep it going.
"My mother and my father always wanted to keep that post office open for the community," Marshall said. "It meant a lot to the community. It was not only a place of business, it was a meeting place, and we wanted to keep it going, and we want to keep it going further."
In 2019 the post office celebrated its 150th anniversary. Since the closing of the Asbury Methodist Church, the Wittman Post Office has been the unofficial gathering spot for the area's communities.
Marshall said the post office not only provided mail to Wittman but also to local towns such as McDaniel and Sherwood.
Since the incident, mail that would have normally gone to the Wittman Post Office has been transferred to the St. Michaels Post Office.
Wittman has a large elderly population, which makes it difficult for many people without licenses or vehicles to make the over-10-minute commute to St. Michaels for their mail.
According to Marshall, even if people can commute to St. Michaels, the summer traffic from tourism creates an additional barrier.
But Wittman lost more than convenient mail access, residents of the town say. Pat Ellison, a Wittman resident, said the post office encompasses a large part of the Wittman community.
"The post office here is more than just a post office. It's a community," Ellison said. "It's a place where people get together and see each other … It's not just the post office. That's one of the reasons losing it hurts so much."
Ellison said people would go to the post office to leave extra produce from their gardens or books that they would want to have a good home to be picked up by other members of the community. It was a center for residents to connect with one another.
Though the post office's closing has caused stress to residents of Wittman, Ellison said she is impressed by the amount of effort the community has made to help Marshall and the efforts by the current postmistress, Chris Henckel, when the accident happened.
That evening after the crash, Henckle, with the help of her mother, went into the post office and hauled out all the mail and packages into big plastic bags to take to St. Michaels.
"I know it all had to be sorted, and they had to find a place for it," Ellison said. "So it must have been a really, really tremendous job."
Marshall said he admires the work that the St. Michaels Post Office has done to accommodate the extra work. He said he has been putting in effort to get the porch rebuilt as soon as possible, but due to the porch's age, more needs to be done to ensure it is up to code.
"There's a good reason for it," Marshall said. "Inspections and all this it's for the safety of the people. Just like bringing back the porch is for the safety of the people, probably a lot better and safer than the one we had since the post office is (over) 150 years old."

no_policy_impact.title: Longtime President and CEO of Delmarva Community Services Retires
no_policy_impact.author: Maggie Trovato
no_policy_impact.content:
Longtime president and CEO of Delmarva Community Services retires

 August 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 633
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Forty-nine years ago, Santo Grande moved from Philadelphia to Maryland's Eastern Shore to take a job with the Dorchester Development Unit, an organization serving adults with developmental disabilities in Dorchester County.At that time, the organization, which had about 15 clients and three full-time staff members, was run out of the basement of a Baptist church on Locust Street in Cambridge.
Nearly five decades later, the organization — now called Delmarva Community Services — has grown to employ hundreds and offer a variety of services from day programs for those with developmental disabilities to senior services, childcare and transportation.
In that time, Grande has stayed with the nonprofit, helping grow it into what it is today. This summer, Grande retired from his long-held position of CEO and president, passing the torch to the former executive director of Upper Shore Aging, Andy Hollis.
Looking back on his career, Grande said he is most proud of how many people Delmarva Community Services has been able to serve.
"We always were serving people," he said. "Children, people with disabilities, seniors. We just continually wanted to provide service. We saw ourselves as a service provider to the community. And by doing that, we really became part of the fabric of the entire community."
Bill Batson, a former president and 16-year member of the organization's board, called Grande a visionary leader, adding that he always had a pulse on what was going on in the community.
"He has left his legacy on Dorchester County through that program," Batson said. "And I pray that it will continue for years and years. But it's all because of the solid foundation that he laid."
The opportunity to grow the organization is what kept Grande with Delmarva Community Services all these years. According to an Aug. 1 news release from Delmarva Community Services, the nonprofit assisted more than 6,000 residents and employed more than 250 people in 2023.
"I've never been one to rest on laurels," Grande said. "I just (felt) like there (were) needs in the community that (were) not being addressed, and we should be in the forefront with services."
When Grande noticed a need in the community, he made sure Delmarva Community Services looked into it.
"We kind of grew the services as the need was out there," he said.
This is how Delmarva Community Services expanded from serving only people with developmental disabilities to serving seniors, Medicaid recipients, children and more.
"So we started to be much more targeted in our services and taking the populations that were not being served as much as they could be served," he said.
Out of this, the organization's transit program, or Delmarva Community Transit, was born.
Grande grew up in Philadelphia, which has an extensive public transportation system he said his family used often. When he got to Dorchester County, there was no public transportation.
"And I thought, we need that here," Grande said. "We needed a public transit program."
Grande said he was able to build the Delmarva transportation program to what it is today: Around 100 vehicles that service residents in Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Talbot and Wicomico counties. He said the program made Delmarva Community Services better-known.
"It was really neat to watch it grow," he said.
As Delmarva Community Services transitions to its new leadership, that focus on continual growth isn't disappearing.
"Delmarva Community Services has a rich history in providing much-needed services to residents in the region," Hollis, the new president, said in an Aug. 1 news release. "Our goal moving forward is to continue to grow these services to meet the challenging times within which we live."
As Grande steps into retirement, he plans spend time with his family, write and possibly teach.
As for the organization that he invested five decades into, Grande has one simple hope.
"I just want them to be a community-oriented agency," he said. "Our goal is to serve the community."

no_policy_impact.title: Rep. Harris, Local Republicans Speak at Denton Rally Supporting Trump
no_policy_impact.author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
no_policy_impact.content:
Rep. Harris, local Republicans speak at Denton rally supporting Trump

 September 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 587
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON – Republican leaders and supporters gathered for a Caroline County rally Saturday in support of presidential candidate Donald Trump and Maryland Republicans running for office this November.The event, which took place at Caroline County 4-H Park, was organized by Caroline County Republican Women. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md., 1st) was the featured speaker Saturday afternoon.
As he runs for his eighth consecutive term in the House of Representatives, he asked voters to support him as well as the entire Republican ticket. He emphasized a tight race in Congressional District 6, where Republican candidate Neil Parrott is vying to potentially join Harris as conservative representation in the House.
"We got a job to do. Because if President Trump is going to succeed, we need to have a House majority, so I'm going to ask for your vote," Harris said.
"Those of you who know people who live out in western Maryland, call them up and tell them to vote for Neil Parrott, because I'm tired of being the only Republican in the House delegation from Maryland, and we got a shot," he said.
Caroline County Republican Women member Joanne Smith helped organize Saturday's event. She said the group held a gathering back in 2020 as well. In her eyes, Trump is a fit for Caroline County voters.
"I think Trump represents our values," Smith said. "We're a very red area. Everybody in Caroline County that's elected is Republican."
"We desperately want to see a change in our government and Trump's our man," she added.
Much of Saturday's discussion centered on ensuring Republicans secure a Senate majority. Harris encouraged attendees to vote for former Gov. Larry Hogan as he runs for Maryland's seat in the Senate against Democratic opponent Angela Alsobrooks.
Harris emphasized that without a Republican majority in the Senate and a Trump victory, conservative judges cannot be placed on the Supreme Court bench.
Adorned in a 'Make America Great Again' baseball cap, Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) also asked voters to toe the party line.
"Vote straight down the ticket, Donald Trump, Larry Hogan, Andy Harris," Mautz said. "Whatever it is, whatever the qualm is, it doesn't matter. We need to get out and we need to vote."
"This is war," he continued. "We're at a national crossroads right now and we need to put all of our cards on the table."
Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Del. Jeff Ghrist (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, Caroline) attended Saturday's rally, as well as Caroline County Sheriff Donnie Baker.
Speaking to eventgoers, Hutchinson predicted that November's general election will play out similar to the 2016 vote, with Trump claiming swing states and the presidency. "We can't wait to see it happen again," he said.
The state delegate said in an interview with the Star Democrat that the economy is the number one reason for residents on the Shore to support Trump.
"We see with our rising food prices, gas prices, housing prices, it's affecting everybody here on the Shore," Hutchinson said. " … I see it within my district, how it's really affecting the middle-income and low-income families."
Smith and Harris both noted an increase in enthusiasm among local Republicans to win back the White House. "We want to get back to the Trump years," Harris said in an interview.
Denton resident Thomas Conneely Jr. attended Saturday's gathering and echoed that sentiment.
"I see that there's more energy," Conneely Jr. said. "But I also see an urgency that it's an emergency. That's what I see. I see people looking at it as, 'We have to.' If we don't, we're in deep trouble."

no_policy_impact.author: Konner Metz kmetz@chespub.com
no_policy_impact.content:
Easton Club East resident requests court to order delay of HOA election

 October 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 368
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A resident of Easton Club East has filed a complaint requesting an injunction against the Easton Club East Community Association's board election after his candidacy was rejected.Jerome Wade, represented by attorney Lyndsey Ryan, filed the complaint on Oct. 21, according to Talbot County Circuit Court records. It outlines why he is "challenging the unlawful rejection of his nomination" and his claims that the association exceeded its authority and violated its bylaws.
Easton Club East, a single-family home neighborhood located off of Dutchmans Lane, is home to more than 800 residents, according to its website. Its Board of Directors, made up of three to seven members, sought nomination forms for three expiring positions on Sept. 16, according to the complaint.
Election voting takes place from Oct. 23 to Nov. 6. Wade is requesting the Circuit Court issue an injunction to prevent Easton Club East from holding its election until the court issues a judgment.
In Wade's filing, which also requests a declaratory judgment and temporary restraining order, he stated that residents wanting to be board candidates were "asked" to answer a list of questions in 100 words or less for each question.
After submitting the candidate nomination form on Sept. 30 — the deadline day — to Easton Club East Community Manager Rhonda Bennett, Wade says he was asked shorten his answers to be within the 100-word limit and given until the next morning to do so.
The complaint states that Wade sent a revised form on Oct. 1. Later that day, the association's nominating committee informed Wade his nomination submission was rejected "due to noncompliance" with Easton Club East guidelines.
Four other candidates submitted nomination forms that were accepted, three of which included responses more than 100 words, the complaint states.
"The unequal treatment of the Plaintiff led to the denial of his nomination and preclusion from participating in what should be a democratic process," the complaint reads.
The association's bylaws prescribe a nominating committee to collect written candidacy submissions "within the timeframe and in the format established by the Board of Directors."
Bennett declined to provide comment when reached by the Star Democrat Wednesday.
A hearing for the injunction originally scheduled for Wednesday was postponed. As of Wednesday, no replacement date had been set.

no_policy_impact.title: Trappe's Post Office reopens after 2-year closure
no_policy_impact.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
no_policy_impact.content:
Trappe's Post Office reopens after 2-year closure

 November 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 375
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — Residents of Trappe celebrated the reopening of the town's post office this week after it had been under construction for two years.In Oct. 2022, the Trappe Post Office was forced to close due to a burst pipe. Mark Wahl, strategic communications specialist for the U.S. Postal Service, said construction had to be extended due to complications with the removal of asbestos.
According to Trappe Town Council President Brian Schmidt, the closure of the post office caused significant inconvenience to residents of the town.
Schmidt noted many residents had to travel to Cambridge to pick up their mail since there were many homes in Trappe that could not have mail delivered directly.
"All those people, including the town hall, had to drive to Cambridge every day to pick up mail," Schmidt said. "So the fact that we can now get our mail a lot closer is nice. And the services that (the post office) offers, not just for the town, but for the people outside of the town as well."
According to Schmidt the construction process was slow and disorganized and lacked good communication with town leadership. Schmidt said the town had a hard time communicating with anybody who knew anything about the post office and its ongoing progress.
Schmidt said many of Trappe's residents were pushed to be creative when it came to obtaining their mail. Older constituents of the town could not easily drive to the post office in Cambridge.
Schmidt said he knew of one resident who changed her address to one of her neighbor's. According to Schmidt, the resident was also caring for her husband whose health was failing, and the closure of the post office created another burden for her.
Ann Frock, a resident of Trappe, said before the closing of the post office she had maintained the same P.O. Box for 28 years. She had to find new arrangements to get mail after the office's closure. Frock said she would drive to Cambridge to retrieve her mail and her friend's mail.
"We're really glad that it reopened, and we're sorry that it took so long," Frock said. "And the whole community wishes that we would have been more informed about what was going on. But we're just really glad to have it back open again."

no_policy_impact.title: Veterans Affairs Committee Visits Disabled Veterans
no_policy_impact.author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
no_policy_impact.content:
Veterans Affairs Committee visits disabled veterans

 November 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 455
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — On Oct. 30, Michael Feehley, chairman of the Veteran Affairs Committee, spent his morning bringing pastries, coffee and plenty of fun stories to veterans living in Pleasant Day Medical Adult Day Care.In an effort to provide appreciation and socialization to disabled veterans on the Eastern Shore, members of the Veteran Affairs Committee of Easton took time to provide enrichment to those who have served.
Over a dozen veterans from a variety of ages gathered together in the common room and spoke of their time in service, their favorite rock n' roll artists and the girls they flirted with while overseas.
According to Feehley, spending even an hour with veterans could provide essential socialization to the many men and women who spent their time serving the country.
"Socialization is just a great part of life, and they don't get an opportunity to socialize too much," Feehley said. "So I give an hour a day every now and then. For me it's giving back. It's giving back for what they gave to me and to you and everybody else."
The members of the Veteran Affairs Committee shared their different reasons for joining the military, and as they opened up, more veterans began sharing their experiences.
For one of the veterans in the facility, the Air Force provided him the opportunity to go to college. As the eldest of six, economically it would not have been possible otherwise, but through signing up for the service he said he was able to grow into the man he became.
Another man said he was one of the first Black men to be invited to the Gold Naval Academy in Annapolis. He said it was a sign of progress, since months before Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee.
Chivy Wieland, a member of the Veteran Affairs Committee, shared stories of his time in basic training and the hardships he and other recruits endured.
Wieland said, drill sergeants that molded the new recruits did so with purpose.
"They will tear you down, so they can build you back up, and then you'll be ready to fight and you'll be somebody that you're supposed to be," Wieland said.
Mike Hare, a Navy veteran, said he spent time in Spain while in service. During his time there, he tried Ouzo, a spirit made from grape must, for the first time and proudly bought his first leather jacket to impress local women.
Over the course of the morning, the veterans laughed, shared stories, jokes and concerns for the future of the military as it continues to change. Feehley said these social actions allow veterans to feel personally enriched and it is good to recognize the sacrifices made by veterans.
"We have a good time because it's veterans helping veterans," he said.

no_policy_impact.title: Hundreds Protest Rep. Harris, Trump Outside Tidewater Inn in Easton
no_policy_impact.author: Konner Metz
no_policy_impact.content:
Hundreds protest Rep. Harris, Trump outside Tidewater Inn in Easton

 March 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 437
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Hundreds lined Dover and Harrison streets Thursday evening, protesting Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md., 1st) and the Trump administration outside a fundraiser hosted by Harris at the Tidewater Inn.By 5 p.m., a large crowd gathered outside the Talbot County Democratic Party headquarters and began walking down sidewalks and past the Tidewater.
They repeated chants of "Andy Harris has got to go" and "fire Andy Harris." Some called for the congressman, who represents the Eastern Shore of Maryland, to host a town hall.
Phil Jackson, chair of the Talbot Democratic Central Committee, said Harris is "absolutely failing to represent Talbot County."
"Andy Harris has historically done very little for the Eastern Shore," Jackson said. "... I think this is indicative of a very strong desire for new leadership."
By 6:30 p.m., Harris' event inside the inn continued and most of the crowd had dispersed. The large crowd did not appear to encounter Harris at any point Thursday evening.
Following his event, Harris told The Star Democrat that the Eastern Shore elected him and President Donald Trump, and that he's "delivering on President Trump's agenda."
Among the president's agenda items raised by protesters Thursday was the Department of Government Efficiency, Elon Musk and mass firings of federal workers. Many of the more than 300 protesters held signs opposing DOGE.
"I think folks have had enough with the current administration and the overreach and behavior we're seeing right now," Jackson said.
Harris, meanwhile, said the cuts are necessary due to a federal deficit nearing $2 trillion.
"If they want to help us with some way to make the government more efficient — other than actually letting go of people whose jobs are probably not contributing to government efficiency — I'm all ears," Harris said of those who oppose the firings. "But they're not offering solutions."
"I feel bad for anyone who's losing a job, but I'm hoping with the economic growth we have, we're going to provide plenty of private sector jobs for those leaving the federal government," he added.
Harris, who chairs the House Freedom Caucus, met with Trump at the White House Wednesday. He said people at his fundraiser Thursday were excited to hear about what's going on in Washington, D.C.
"I told them some of what it's like to be sitting next to the leader of the free world," Harris said.
Outside the Tidewater, the tenor from protesters was much different. The crowd of hundreds loudly cheered as cars drove by and honked in support of the protest.
Jackson was pleased with the large turnout and says the protest was a "tipping point."
"It's really reached an egregious point," Jackson said. "And I think people are really upset about it."

no_policy_impact.title: 'You are all God's gift': Volunteers Honored for Dedication, Service to Seniors
no_policy_impact.author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
no_policy_impact.content:
'You are all God's gift': Volunteers honored for dedication, service to seniors

 April 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Seniors 
 
 550
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Susan Higgs of Upper Shore Aging Inc. showed appreciation for the many volunteers dedicated to serving the Retired and Senior Volunteer Program, RSVP, of which she is project director."We're a team and I can't say enough. You are all God's gift and I thank you," Higgs said at their annual recognition event on Friday at the Amy Lynn Ferris Adult Activity Center on 200 Schauber Rd.
Upper Shore Aging, Inc., a non-profit organization, is a designated Area Agency on Aging by the State of Maryland, serving over 31,000 seniors in Caroline, Kent and Talbot counties. Over a catered dinner from Out of the Ordinary Catering, run by Robert Yalley, Upper Shore celebrated 50 years of service.
Higgs, using a PowerPoint presentation, showed that when they first began the Retired and Senior Volunteer Program there were only a few cells of busy bees.
But over the years, Kent County has produced more than 100 volunteers, who this year already put in more than 7,000 hours.
Each volunteer agency is called a station with a station manager. The Kent Association of Riding Therapy's (KART) station manager is Sue Caswell. Her volunteering duties involve walking with the horses and helping children with disabilities with them. She said it is an extremely rewarding experience.
Another station is the Museums of Kent, and with 11 museums, it can be a busy one, run by station manager Carolyn Sorge.
The list of Program stations is long in the county and getting longer, Higgs pointed out. Their goal as stations, volunteers or busy bees, is to produce honey, a sweetness to the community — to establish and build connections creating a better quality of life for everyone.
As they do this this year, they face some challenges.
Upper Shore Executive Director Herb Cain pointed out their funding comes from the Maryland Department of Aging, which may be facing federal and state cuts. Cuts to that department means potential cuts to Upper Shore, which may fall to county government to support some programs in their jurisdiction.
Cain has already visited the Kent County Commissioners and expressed his concerns, and so far, all the counties have been supportive, he noted.
But there is a level of uncertainty, he acknowledged, especially in the federal funding.
In this financially unstable environment, Higgs said, volunteers are needed more than ever. Having professional, knowledgeable seniors active and involved benefits the community. Placing older adults in these high-quality positions improves their quality of life as well.
Higgs said with 10,000 baby boomers retiring since COVID-19, isolation and loneliness can set in. Volunteering provides purpose, decreases loneliness and adds a sense of fulfillment.
Higgs' positive energy and optimism is an example of the benefits of volunteering, and she encouraged residents to reach out to them if interested at shiggs@uppershoreaging.org.
Upper Shore Aging's website for the Retired Seniors Volunteer Program, volunteersontheshore.org, is a centralized place for anyone seeking a volunteer opportunity in Kent, Caroline or Talbot counties. The site includes information on the enrollment process and a listing under each county of volunteer opportunities.
In Kent County, a handful of these organizations include the Chester River Hospital Center Auxiliary, Amy Lynn Ferris Adult Activity Center, Meals on Wheels, Kent Association of Riding Therapy (KART) and many more.
"To me this is a very special program. We're still here and making things happen and living life. Look at us now!" Higgs said.

no_policy_impact.title: Cambridge Indivisible Aims to Teach Members About Civics, Cofounder Says
no_policy_impact.author: Maggie Trovato
no_policy_impact.content:
Cambridge Indivisible aims to teach members about civics, cofounder says

 May 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 645
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — For Cambridge Indivisible cofounder and Cochair Michelle Fowle, it's about understanding the power you have."I think the really important thing is for people to understand the power that they actually hold," she said. "So that's kind of my focus. And I'm doing that here."
When Fowle moved to Cambridge from California with her husband, Andy, in September, the two hit the ground running to form Cambridge Indivisible, which is a chapter of a national organization that aims to elect progressive leaders.
Fowle said the overarching goal of the group is to give people a place to build community and learn about civics. She said everyone is welcome.
"We have Republicans who are showing up now at our protests, asking how they can help," she said. "And I embrace them."
Mentioning health care and housing, Fowle said there are issues that people on both sides of the aisle can unite on. She said that for her, the organization isn't about identity politics.
"We don't have to agree," she said. "In fact, we shouldn't agree. And it's healthy to have that conversation. I'm not trying to make you be me."
There was a time when Fowle knew very little about politics.
"They say that there's two days that are critical in your life," she said. "It's the day you're born and the day you find out why. And in November 2016, I found out why."
Fowle said the 2016 general election results thrust her into a world of activism after not paying close attention to politics for many years. While living in California, Fowle learned from other organizers, helped put on rallies and marches, and built relationships with elected officials.
"For somebody who didn't know anything, I can teach it now," she said.
MAKING WAVES
In recent months, Cambridge Indivisible has garnered attention over events it has hosted around town. During one event in March, the chapter hosted Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) for a town hall.
The chapter also has hosted multiple rallies to criticize elected federal leadership. That criticism has been largely directed toward Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.) for not holding in-person town halls for his constituents. Harris hosted multiple virtual town halls in the past two months.
Fowle said the Cambridge chapter of Indivisible has more than 1,000 members from across the Eastern Shore. She said there is no formal registration process to be a member.
Cambridge Indivisible Treasurer Ilia Johnson said she joined the chapter this year to get more representation for the Hispanic community in the area and to support her neighbors. She said she likes that Cambridge Indivisible is a group "for everybody."
"All we want to do is what's best for everybody," she said.
During a Cambridge Indivisible rally held along U.S. Route 50 in Cambridge on April 19, Gloria McVeigh said she joined the chapter after Harris was elected in November. She said it's a nice group that holds the same values as herself.
Although there have been disapproving shouts from people driving their cars past Cambridge Indivisible rallies these past few months, Fowle said the chapter hasn't faced much opposition other than from Harris.
In the past, Harris has shared his criticisms of and concerns with the Indivisible organization as a whole.
Following a Cambridge Indivisible rally held March 13 that called on Harris to hold an in-person town hall and questioned his allegiance to his constituents, Harris alleged those at the rally were "brought in by buses" and not his constituents. He said he heard from a Washington, D.C., organization's leader "who knows what's goingon" that people at the rally were getting paid to be there.
"This is AstroTurf," Harris said about the organization in March. "This is not grassroots."
Fowle said the chapter does get internet trolls on its public page, and she deletes their comments and blocks them.
"It's like listen, when this hits you — and it will — I'll be there for you if you want," she said about the internet trolls.

Greensboro Historical Society building decision to be made June 5

 May 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News

 GREENSBORO — At the Greensboro Town Council Meeting Thursday, the council decided that on June 5, they will make a decision on whether or not the historical society would keep its space.Town officials began discussing potentially moving the Greensboro Historical Society out of the Weaver Building in March. The move would free up space for other organizations and town agencies, but it would leave the historical society without a permanent home.
Though no decision was made Thursday, Councilman Joe Noon made it clear he feels the council and the town should make a decision very soon because the town needs the building.
"Mayor, council, this was already discussed," Noon said. "We said that we were going to ask them to leave at one meeting, then we come back, then we say, 'we don't know if we want them to leave or not.' We need our building back.
"Let's stop playing with the historic society, please. You already know that we all need the building back. Let's just come up with the date."
The council members elected to hold a public hearing at the June 5 meeting, then make a decision on the historical society after the public hearing.
Councilwoman Christina Robinson and Councilman Pete Brelia said they had met with Greensboro Historical Society President Charles Dean and discussed multiple relocation options for the historical society.
While Dean couldn't make it in person to Thursday's meeting, he told the Star Democrat that the he had a "pleasant exchange" with the council members.
"We had a pleasant exchange of ideas when we did meet," Dean said. "It was not adversarial at all, nor did I think it would be, so I just look forward to the June 5 hearing and hope that the public would turn out to support the Greensboro Historical Society."
Robinson and Brelia made points on different locations, but no location has been solidified and no final decision was made. The council members say they plan to continue to work towards a solution that would be best for both parties.
"We all value the historical society," Robinson said. "We are trying to keep it within the town limits. No final decision has been made, but we're all aware that something needs to be done, and we are working to try and work out a solution that works out for everybody."
Dean assures residents that the Greensboro Historical Society will not be dissolved and will work to find a location if moved.
"If they vote to remove us from the Weaver building, they're not dissolving the historical society," Dean said. "The Greensboro Historical Society will continue to exist. We will find a place for the collection even if the museum has to go dormant for some time, things will be in storage and eventually we'll find a better place and we will to continue to celebrate Greensboro's history at that point."
