no_policy_impact.title: Memorial Day Parade Remembers Vets, America's 'Forgotten War'
no_policy_impact.author: WILL BONTRAGER
no_policy_impact.content:
Memorial Day parade remembers vets, America's 'forgotten war'

 May 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER | Section: Life 
 
 560
 Words 

 Read News Document

 High Street in Chestertown was clear Memorial Day of many tourists following a successful Tea Party weekend, but the streets remained filled with locals honoring veterans during an annual parade, a longstanding tradition in the area.First responders from all Kent municipalities, local businesses, organizations, vintage vehicles and marching bands, symbolized the community's appreciation to the fallen. A crowd of approximately 500 lined the sunny streets, shouting well-wishes and flag waving.
After the festive Memorial Day parade, keynote speaker, veteran and board member of Sumner Hall, Aubrey Sarvis, spoke about his time serving during the Korean War, a conflict that started on June 25, 1950 — July 27, 1953.
Sarvis' message was simple yet strong — to never forget.
As a member of the U.S. Army 32nd Infantry Regiment, 7th Infantry Division from 1961-1962, he talked about that war, dubbed the "forgotten war" because it was overshadowed from World War II and Vietnam.
But for those who experienced the conflict, there was no way of forgetting it.
Sarvis said while on guard duty in the 38th parallel, separating North Korea and South Korea, he knew two things about his fellow soldiers: they were afraid and they did not want to die.
Surrounded by veterans, he provided sobering statistics of those who were killed in action or severely wounded, starting from World War I to the wars in the Middle East following Sept. 11, 2001.
He talked about those who died on the Western Front, France and Belgium, buried under poppy fields. He spoke of those 23,613 killed in action in Korea and the 58,220 who deployed in Vietnam and came home in a fresh casket with brand new American flags.
Thinking about his fallen comrades in every conflict, he recited the poem: "In Flanders Fields," by John McCrae, written in World War I. The poem beckons the hearers to remember the dead buried under poppy fields or those living would never be free.
President of Sumner Hall, Vanessa Isaacs Ringgold also remembers the sacrifices of these soldiers and stated how Sumner Hall is one of two existing African American Grand Army of the Republic (GAR) buildings still standing in the country.
She said that in 1868, founder of the Grand Army of the Republic Colonel John A. Logan issued a general order to 7,000 post members to decorate the graves of fallen comrades.
Sumner Hall aims to carry on that tradition of honoring and remembering. She said fraternity, charity and loyalty, is what they strive for, and will continue the legacy of the Parker White American Legion #143, formerly led by by the late Calvin Frasier. It was founded in 1919 and was the first Post in Kent County Maryland started by African Americans.
After the speakers, veterans gathered around the memorial and held a moment of silence for the lost, followed by "Taps" played by trumpeter Brad Holloman.
Ringgold said she was honored to be a part of this ceremony. She added whereas in former years, Sumner Hall has done something separate for Memorial Day, this year, two groups came together, and she hopes they will continue planning the Memorial Day Parade together.
She thanked Katy Weddell, Ellen Uzelac and everyone on the planning commission for their hard work, starting around February.
Sumner Hall encourages veterans to reach out to them, young and old. They hosts monthly events and meetings and is open to the community as an event venue. For information, visit sumnerhall.org.

no_policy_impact.author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
no_policy_impact.content:
Federalsburg Activities Center hopes to bring joy to the whole community

 August 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 631
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — An idea for a space where children could have fun in Federalsburg turned into a place where everyone could have fun.The Federalsburg Activities Center began with a conversation between the Rev. Pam Bockart and the Rev. Stanford Ricks at a meeting in 2019.
Bockart was the Pastor at Christ Church, and she recalled "kids outside just walking the streets having nowhere to go."
She decided to call a meeting about finding something for the children to do. After the meeting, Bockart and Ricks selected a location for a community center project at the old Dollar General building on Morris Avenue in Federalsburg.
Ricks is the vice president of Men for Change, an organization the specializes in "changing our community through service" by mentoring youth in Federalsburg. The group wanted a central location.
A partnership was formed. For the next five years, Bockart, Ricks and a board of stakeholders overcame financial and logistical obstacles to open the Federalsburg Activities Center.
"We started on a journey. We had nothing, no money, just a vision to open up this building," Ricks said, looking around the center, which opened in the former Dollar General building earlier this year.
The group gained ownership of the building with help from its former owner and a loan. But even after the building's ownership was squared away, multiple renovations needed to be done to make the space functional.
After multiple grants, donations from local businesses and an anonymous $400,000 private donation, the Activities Center was renovated and ready for the community.
"Over the five years, we never got frustrated," Ricks said. "That was the great thing to me. The the board that we had, we met every week, we came here, we enjoyed each other, we talked positive and never got frustrated. I think we kind of knew it was going to be a long journey.
"... So now we went from phase one, which was to get the building open. Now were going into phase two of the project, getting the programs up and running in the building."
The current programs at the Activities Center are Men For Change on Friday, bible study on Saturday, senior lunches on Friday, garden club once a month and Make Federalsburg Beautiful meetings once a month. Men For Change sees 30 to 50 kids on Fridays, and the senior lunches see 20 to 40 seniors.
Part of the next phase for the center will be partnering youth with older community members. Board members said older community members tend to feel left out, with a lack of activities catered toward them. The board hopes this partnership will increase seniors' drive and provide mentorship opportunities for local youth.
"We would like to bring the young ones, who are starting their vision, and the old ones, who have their vision, and we want them to kind of get together so that the seniors can tell the younger ones about their story and how to get there themselves that they may have a good life," Ricks said.
Another part of the next phase is adding new programs within the activities center. The board has plans to add a science, technology, engineering and mathematics program; arts and crafts; a coffee club; and a running club. Board members said negotiations for Boys and Girls Club and 4-H partnerships are ongoing.
The board is most excited about the potential of what the activities center can do for the town of Federalsburg.
"There is something in all of us when we give to others," said Wendy Garner, secretary for the board. "We get back as much if not more, and that's what I think all these skills, all these learning curves, whether it's for the kids, the adults, or the seniors — this is a community center."
The board encourages all community members who want volunteer or who have ideas to email fac2024@aol.com.

no_policy_impact.title: In Claiborne, Many Depend on Volunteer Efforts of a 'Water Czar'
no_policy_impact.author: Konner Metz
no_policy_impact.content:
In Claiborne, many depend on volunteer efforts of a 'water czar'

 September 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Headlines 
 
 184
 Words 

 Read News Document

 To some, Renny Johnson is known as Claiborne's "water czar."The 77-year-old graphic artist and sign painter moved to Tilghman Island in 1976, then bought a house in the Claiborne village in the summer of 1979, where he's lived since.
For nearly all of those 46 years, Johnson has run Claiborne's main water supply. He tracks billing (annual fees are just $200 for residents), tests the well system, coordinates with state regulators and answers phone calls from neighbors with concerns or questions.
But the task has become more and more difficult for Johnson and his counterparts in recent years. They say the Maryland Department of the Environment has become more intentional in asking the residents to secure a licensed operator, since the water system serves 30 properties, over the limit of 15 for a community water supply.
And the small, waterfront community is "aging out," Johnson said. Volunteers aren't as easy to find.
Johnson and three other residents talked with county officials at a workshop on Tuesday to discuss potential solutions to the unique, volunteer-run well in Claiborne.
To learn more, read our story below.
Thanks for reading.

no_policy_impact.title: Claiborne Residents, Operating Their Own Well, Look for Water Supply Solution
no_policy_impact.author: Konner Metz
no_policy_impact.content:
Claiborne residents, operating their own well, look for water supply solution

 September 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 819
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CLAIBORNE — When Rob Todd moved to Claiborne in 2013, he didn't expect to be partially responsible for the village's water services. But it's a role he and others have assumed.From 2015 to 2019, Todd was one of four volunteers for the resident-led Claiborne Water Company, a group that oversees a water system serving about 30 properties.
"I, for one, didn't envision my retirement years being a well operator," Todd said while taking a walk to the community's well on Thursday afternoon.
Todd, 77, volunteered for a relatively short stint. He credits longtime Claiborne resident Renny Johnson — the "water czar" — with the decades-long heavy lifting of maintaining Claiborne's water. Johnson handles the billing, fields questions from residents and arranges testing of the well system.
Johnson moved to his Claiborne house in 1979 and was handed the water company books just a few years later by the outgoing man in charge.
"We had a water company meeting where we invited the people that were on the system to talk about (it), and no one else would take it over," Johnson recalled. "So I said I would, not thinking that I would be doing it for this long."
Johnson, 77, and others are hoping to pass the duties off and find a long-term solution to what's become a multifaceted problem keeping the water system in line with state regulations.
As Claiborne's population ages, attracting volunteers is difficult, Johnson and Todd said. And now more than ever, the Maryland Department of the Environment is pushing Claiborne to meet standards for what the state considers "community water systems."
Community water systems aren't served by a municipal company. They are smaller-scale, like the Claiborne water well. However, MDE requires systems with over 15 properties hooked up to have a licensed operator, according to residents and county officials.
Four Claiborne residents — Johnson, Todd, Jim Richardson and Kirke Harper — explained the issue at a Talbot County Council work session on Sept. 9. While the county doesn't maintain the water system, County Engineer Ray Clarke is willing to help where he can.
"We're grateful that the county was willing to listen to our problem," Todd said.
'WE'RE AGING OUT'
Claiborne, an unincorporated village on the Chesapeake Bay, is a short detour on the drive from St. Michaels to Tilghman Island.
According to residents, a 19th-century railroad company drilled Claiborne's old water well, which was then turned over to the residents when the railroad closed in 1928.
Johnson and Richardson took over in the early 1980s, back when each household paid $18 annually to hook up and just before the railroad's well was replaced. Now, the yearly fee is $200. A second, separate water system serves 14 properties closer to the Bay and past the main Claiborne Road strip. It's not subject to all of the same MDE rules.
Claiborne Water Company's current building is a white structure housing a pressure tank and chlorine pump. It sits a handful of paces away from the well cap a few feet above ground level.
Residents say efforts to find a licensed operator in recent years have come up empty, which is why they're seeking county assistance.
MDE spokesman Jay Apperson said in an email that the state's increased rules on water system operators were implemented in 2001.
"Maryland regulations include requirements for certification, such as passing examinations and continuing education," Apperson wrote.
Claiborne's water company volunteers aren't overly concerned about water quality. MDE's most recent review of the Claiborne water system indicated that it meets state and federal requirements. Low levels of arsenic, while in compliance, was the leading worry.
MDE inspects the water system at least every three years, Apperson said.
Residents' core concern, instead, boils down to meeting MDE's certification requirements, which likely means passing the buck off to a qualified operator.
And for Johnson, who beat cancer a few years ago, juggling the billing, testing and upkeep responsibilities continues to take a toll. "I'm older now, and I don't have as much strength or wherewithal to carry on," he said.
"We're aging out," Johnson added. "Nobody who's retired wants to take on the responsibility of running the water company."
SOLUTIONS
At the county work session, officials agreed to explore options for the Claiborne Water Company through a preliminary engineering report, or feasibility study, which could be authorized at the council's next meeting on Sept. 23.
Clarke, the county engineer, explained that homeowners connected to the community system mostly can't drill individual wells because of necessary setbacks from private septic systems.
Extending sewer services down to the Claiborne village could be a longer-term solution to make private wells a possibility, officials said. But in the short-term, the residents are still seeking a fix.
County Council Vice President Pete Lesher, acting as a liaison to the Public Works Advisory Board, said he understands Claiborne residents have been "clamoring for some assistance" for a long time.
"I'm well aware that, in (this) process, you've already actually explored a lot of options and are coming to us because you've come up empty," Lesher said.

no_policy_impact.title: On Constitution Day, U.S. district judge speaks on checks and balances in Oxford
no_policy_impact.author: Lily Tierney
no_policy_impact.content:
On Constitution Day, U.S. district judge speaks on checks and balances in Oxford

 September 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 578
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Part-time Oxford resident and U.S. District of Maryland Judge James Breder spoke about judicial independence and the constitutional system of government at the Oxford Community Center on Constitution Day, Sept. 17.Breder explained the U.S. Constitution's division of federal government power among the three branches — legislative, executive and judicial — and the importance of checks and balances.
"This division of power was a central feature of the framers' plan for a representative and democratic government," he said. "Now, when I refer to the framers, I'm referencing the men, and they were all men, who met and conceived the Constitution and the Bill of Rights."
The framers wanted to prevent the concentration of power and subsequent tyranny they experienced under the British king, as noted by the founders in the Declaration of Independence.
They divided power as an intentional design to prevent any single person or group from amassing too much power. When describing this system of checks and balances, Breder quoted James Madison, who called it "essential to the preservation of liberty."
For Breder, friction between the branches of government is a predictable consequence and a sign that the system is working as intended, ensuring the government can control itself.
That's Breder's job as a U.S. district court judge. It is the judiciary's job and power to check the other branches, a process known as judicial review. Though this concept is not explicitly stated in the Constitution, Breder said the principle has been in practice since the early days of the country and was formally established through the benchmark case Marbury v. Madison.
"The Marbury decision established this power of judicial review as a part of our constitutional government, and it has endured for more than 200 years," Breder said.
In order for Breder to properly do his job, he said he must be independent from political influence.
"They must be free to decide cases according to the law. A judge under the control of the government will be reluctant to rule against the government even when the government acts improperly and even when citizens' constitutional rights are at stake," he said.
Breder cited the French Revolution "reign of terror" as a historic example of where the lack of an independent judiciary rendered a declaration of rights ineffective, leading to the imprisonment of 300,000 people and nearly 20,000 executions by guillotine through a revolutionary tribunal that denied rights like counsel and appeal.
Breder then outlined the constitutional grounds for impeaching a judge. "The Constitution provides that, 'the President, Vice President, and all civil officers of the United States shall be removed from office on impeachment for a conviction of treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors.'"
The term "maladministration" was removed from early drafts of the Constitution to prevent impeachment based on political disagreement with a judge's rulings. The word was deemed too vague.
"Several thousand (individuals) have served as federal judges during the course of U.S. history, and yet, only 15 have been impeached by the House, and only eight of those have been convicted by the Senate," Breder said.
All eight impeachments were for reasons outside of the judges' rulings, such as habitual drunkenness, improper business relationships with litigants, perjury, bribery, and one Civil-War-era judge who was impeached for waging war against the United States.
In his closing remarks, Breder reiterated the importance of checks and balances within government.
"The framers did not make impeachment available for maladministration, and it should not be used to remove judges who make decisions viewed as erroneous or unpopular," Breder said.

no_policy_impact.title: 'The end of an era': St. Paul's Church gets deconsecrated
no_policy_impact.author: Lily Tierney
no_policy_impact.content:
'The end of an era': St. Paul's Church gets deconsecrated

 October 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: News 
 
 515
 Words 

 Read News Document

 VIENNA — On Sundays, when the pews should have been packed, the Rev. Dennis Morgan would walk into St. Paul's Episcopal Church in Vienna and, at most, see two parishioners prepared for sermon.That is until Sept. 21, when the parish had its final service and St. Paul's closed its doors for good. The church's closure was not the town's first this year.
St. Paul's was deconsecrated just months after Vienna United Methodist Church, located directly across the street, stopped its services, Morgan said.
"It's a very, very bittersweet time," he said. "You know, realizing that it must be done, but, at the same time, you know, it's heartbreaking."
The church closures are the consequence of attendance trends seen in Vienna and across the country.
About 33% of adults in the United States attend religious services in person as of February 2025. This is a dramatic decline from 2007, when 50% of adults attended religious services in person, according to a recent Pew Research Center study.
"There have been really low numbers at St. Paul's for several years, and it just wasn't sustainable," said Administrative Assistant to the Bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of Easton Lynn Anstatt.
In 2020, there were 18 parishioners on the books at St. Paul's, with roughly eight members attending services weekly. This dropped to 11 members on the books with around two attending weekly services by 2025, Morgan said.
He said the pandemic and static population of Vienna largely contributed to decreased attendance of all the churches in the area. Only a handful still hold weekly services.
Keeping St. Paul's open and active had become an existential question for Morgan.
"We could have kept the property going probably for quite a while, but we had no mission, no outreach and we questioned the 'why' of it more than the 'how' of it," the pastor said.
Morgan was in conversation with the Bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of Easton for around three years in an attempt to keep the church open. But after seeing minimal improvement, he could no longer justify keeping the parish going.
"The church is still available to use although it has been deconsecrated, so we do have access to the church. But in terms of services and everything, that does come to an end," Morgan said.
The decommissioning of St. Paul's comes after more than 300 years of active service in Vienna.
There are now no Episcopal Churches in Vienna, but because attendance was so low and the church was not involved in the community, Morgan doesn't think the deconsecration will have much negative impact on the larger Vienna community.
Many community members have family buried in the cemetery on the property and have inquired with Morgan about the cemetery's future.
"The difficult decision to close the church, despite such a vast legacy, was driven by factors such as declining membership and the increasing costs of maintaining historic structures," former parishioner of St. Paul's and Vienna resident Susan Donaghue wrote in an email to the Star Democrat. "The conclusion of ministry at St. Paul's marks the end of an era for the town of Vienna and the community it so faithfully served."

wrong_jurisdiction.author: Kiersten Hacker; Capital News Service
wrong_jurisdiction.content:
I don't come from political lineage

 September 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Kiersten Hacker; Capital News Service | Page: A4 | Section: News 
 
 600
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON - Gov. Wes Moore fended off questions Tuesday on whether he'll run in the 2024 Democratic presidential primary during an interview with global news organization Semafor, saying he had no interest in higher office and turning the subject to his nontraditional political background."I think it's really important for people to remember that I am probably the most improbable governor in this country," Moore said in answer to the first question from Semafor cofounder and Editor-at-large Steve Clemons. "I'm a person who has never come from a political lineage." Moore, an author, nonprofit executive and former Army officer, had not held political office before winning the governor's election in 2022.Moore turned his focus to Maryland, discussing plans to revive the state's economy through targeted investments in its assets and better serve constituents with a data-driven approach to policy changes.Moore often defines Maryland as "asset-rich and strategy-poor," and cites the contrast presented by the state's high concentration of prominent institutions of higher education, military facilities and government agencies, such as the National Security Agency, with its sluggish economic growth rate of.2% in the past 4 years. The current economic strategy of spreading funding across numerous projects "doesn't make sense," he said, explaining he'll use a more focused approach.In June, Moore established the Maryland Economic Council, charging it with creating economic recommendations by the next legislative session in January. After the General Assembly passed numerous measures to affect systemic budgetary changes during the last session, a report from the Department of Legislative Services predicted a $418 million structural deficit for fiscal year 2025.Moore said his administration will use data to drive policy decisions, especially when looking to minimize socioeconomic disparities, and he used environmental injustice in Baltimore as an example."You can't understand what these disparities look like if we aren't able to fully appreciate the measure of intentionality that very much existed in the creation of that and the lack of intentionality when it comes to how we're going to address it." The administration must consider the root causes of poverty, investing in transit, the public education system and programs to combat the teacher shortage, Moore said, to jumpstart economic growth.Creating new opportunities for young people to succeed in different areas will help fight juvenile crime and keep violence out of communities, Moore said. Using data and technology in innovative ways can also help ensure that solutions to crime are predictive rather than reactive.Increasing public safety is his top priority, Moore said, highlighting the need for "appropriate intensity, absolute integrity, and full accountability" in the policing system as well as a need for crisis intervention teams to shift the response of mental health calls away from police officers. Over $100 million was invested directly in behavioral health, Moore said.Moore noted that police officers respond to all situations, and many times they are met with circumstances they cannot fix.He called for change, saying that public safety is in part a matter of creating a better livelihood for people.Moore said his administration invested $122 million in local law enforcement, $17.5 million of which went to Baltimore City, where the police department has been under a federal agreement to make reforms since 2016.Moore also invested in intelligence sharing through the Maryland Coordination and Analysis Center and organized crime units.In Baltimore, other reform means combating gun trafficking, filling the police shortage with well-trained officers, and developing more intentional solutions, said Moore, who places special importance on these issues as a Baltimore native."I love my state, all 24 jurisdictions. But I'm a Baltimorean," Moore said."That's who I am. Can't understand me if you don't understand Baltimore."

Beach town bans smoking, eating cannabis - Pot now prohibited on public property and in meeting places in Chesapeake Beach

 With no comment from the public during a hearing or remarks from the town council during an Oct. 19 monthly meeting, the town ofChes-apeake Beach unanimously passed an ordinance addressing legal cannabis.The new law prohibits the smoking or ingesting of cannabis in several public areas, including town hall, Veterans Park, Bayfront Park, Kellam's Field, boardwalk and town pocket parks. Additionally, the ban includes public areas at local businesses.The ordinance was discussed during the mayor and council's September work session, with it then being introduced during that month's council meeting.Acting upon Maryland voters' approval by referendum of the legalization of recreational marijuana for adults 21 or older, the Maryland General Assembly passed the accompanying Cannabis Reform Act earlier this year."Because I'm a nerd, I probably read that 100-page bill 20 or 30 times," Chesapeake Beach Mayor Patrick "Irish" Mahoney declared during the September work session.After familiarizing himself with the new law, Mahoney told the council he has testified before a state Senate committee and worked with other mayors through the Maryland Municipal League to find ways to comply without ceding total control."Just common sense," Councilwoman Valerie Beaudin said of the ordinance draft. "It falls along the lines ofwhat's already in place" for smoking and vaping tobacco and drinking alcohol.Councilman Charlie Fink said he wanted assurances the ordinance wouldn't result in people "being stopped and frisked.""If you have it in your pocket, that's fine,"Todd Pounds, town attorney, stated.During that same work session the mayor and council discussed a second cannabis-related ordinance affecting the legal sale of the substance within the town limits.Mahoney noted that unlike many other states, Maryland lawmakers declined to consider a "local opt out" for state jurisdictions that don't wish to have cannabis sales within their confines."You're trying to create a wholesome environment," Mahoney said of a prohibition on cannabis sales.The mayor added that the way the state is planning to tax the newly legalized product and distribute receipts to jurisdictions would mean the town would receive "basically nothing."A public hearing on the latter ordinance proposal did not happen at the October meeting.When asked late last week why there was no hearing for the other proposed ordinance, Mahoney told Southern Maryland News that he learned at a Maryland Municipal League meeting recently that the state legislature is planning to revisit the law next session to clear up some of its ambiguous aspects.

Elections Board audit finds ineligible voters, security issues

 November 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tommy Tucker; Capital News Service | Page: 11 | Section: News 
 
 398
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS - An audit released Friday found that the Maryland Board of Elections did not report for more than a year its findings that people voted or tried to vote more than once in the 2020 general election - well after the results were certified, according to The Office of Legislative Audits.The state elections board identified 134 voters who voted more than once and 1,371 voters who attempted to vote multiple times in the 2020 general election, but it did not report these individuals to the The Office of State Prosecutor until April 2022, the audit said. The audit is part of a routine physical compliance audit of the SBE conducted every three to four years."Definitely the (reports) for the 2020 general election were significantly late and I think they indicated that was due to staff turnover within their office," said Matthew Streett, an assistant director for the Compliance and Performance Audit Division of the OLA. "They reported them after the election results were certified." In the July 2022 primary election, the audit found, the elections board identified four individuals who successfully voted multiple times and 263 voters who attempted to vote multiple times, referring the information to the state prosecutors office in a "timely" manner.Election integrity has become a high-profile issue with former President Donald Trump and his supporters repeatedly challenging the outcome of the 2020 presidential election.The audit also noted that the elections board could enhance its procedures to fully identify deceased or duplicate voters. The audit identified 2,426 "potentially deceased individuals" whose voter registrations were active and 327 individuals with potential duplicate voter registrations."We're just pointing out areas where they can improve," said Streett. "The information they're getting from the Maryland Department of Health was not fully complete and accurate, so they were missing out on a certain pocket of deceased individuals." The Health Department could not be reached for comment on Friday.The audit also found deficiencies with the state elections board's security and control over its information systems, but did not go into detail for security reasons. The department's response to those concerns also was redacted from the report.The elections board did agree to implement the recommendations, but disagreed with several findings.The State Board of Elections could not be reached for comment on Friday.The current Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis took the helm in June 2023 after longtime administrator Linda Lamone retired.

wrong_jurisdiction.author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
wrong_jurisdiction.content:
Local state legislators discuss predicted state revenue shortfall

 December 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 759

 CAMBRIDGE - Local state legislators gathered at the Chesapeake Grove Intergenerational Center Tuesday afternoon to share their expectations for the 2024 Legislative Session with constituents.At the event, hosted by the Dorchester Chamber of Commerce, attendees were served lunch before getting the opportunity to ask questions to District 37 legislators Sen. Johnny Mautz (R, Talbot County), Del. Chris Adams (R, Wicomico) Del. Tom Hutchinson (R, Dorchester) and Speaker Pro Tem Sheree Sample-Hughes (D, Wicomico) regarding the 446th session of the Maryland General Assembly that will commence in Annapolis on Jan. 10.The legislators answered questions on topics ranging from the Blueprint for Maryland's Future to economic development to juvenile crime.Matthew Teffeau, manager of government affairs and economic development at Choptank Electric Cooperative, asked the first question of the event. He asked for ways in which the estimated state revenue shortfall of more than $460 million could be addressed.Sample-Hughes, who spoke first, said that this situation with the budget is challenging."There have been many task forces that have taken place this interim to address issues," she said about the shortfall.When it comes to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, for example, Sample-Hughes said the state won't have enough money in the budget to cover what has been proposed until 2027.Sample-Hughes also brought up fuel tax funds, which have decreased in the state due to the increase in electronic vehicles."That requires a whole other level of structure and planning to see what that looks like for the state," she said. "Do we put in fees for these electric vehicles and hybrid vehicles so we can come out into somewhat of a balanced budget?" New legislation regarding this could come out of the upcoming General Assembly session, she said.Adams followed Sample-Hughes in answering the question. He said the budget will be the "number one topic" of discussion going into Legislative Session this year.He said that COVID-19 emergency funding has helped the state's budget in the past couple years, but said he has noticed many municipalities and county governments using these funds for programs that move into the future, not just one-time appropriations."Many of the budget problems that we're going to have are going to come down to this: Ongoing spending of dollars for social programs for which there are no tax revenue sources to derive those from," he said.Adams said this could lead to fee and tax increases as well as cuts to spending "in places where we should not be cutting."Adams concluded his answer by saying that the state's budget deficit could reach $1.8 billion by 2027."So we're talking $400 million next year," he said, "In a couple years, if we don't right this ship, we're talking about multiple billions of dollars of revenue shortfall.That's going to hit hard."Mautz spoke next, saying that there is no simple answer to fixing the predicted budget shortfall."I think everything is going to be on the table this session," he said. "There's going to be all kinds of maneuvering."Mautz said that it's important to make sure that the burden of the budget shortage isn't left on local governments. He said that the best solution to the problem is to drive investment."The budget depends on revenues, and the way you do that is you try to get capital investment and you try to fuel small business," he said. "And that's the backbone of the Eastern Shore."Mautz said that lessening the economic burden on independent businesses and constituents at a statewide level is important to drive economic activity."Anything we can do statewide to loosen that burden, to drive economic activity, I think will be a fundamental policy that will help change that budget imbalance," he said.Hutchinson answered the question last, saying that government can only make money by raising taxes, raising fees or cutting spending."I'm sure - based on what I've heard from the chairman of appropriations - we'll see a number of bills about taxes and fee increases," he said.Hutchinson brought up the recent announcement from the Maryland Department of Transportation that it will be reducing funding for its six year capital budget for transportation projects."We'll probably start seeing that across the other departments as well," he said. "But there's a lot of projects that, if they're not announced by the end of January, won't be seeing the light of day next year."

 ANNAPOLIS - Gov. Wes Moore's administration is proposing roughly $3.3 billion in wide-ranging cuts for the state's six-year transportation spending plan, which is facing inflationary pressures as traditional revenue sources haven't kept up with costs, the state's transportation secretary said Tuesday.The proposal, which could be adjusted by the General Assembly next year, will have an impact on highways and transit service, as well as other transportation spending.The approach includes about $1 billion in reductions in the transportation department's operating budget, $2 billion from the capital program and about $400 million in grant reductions to local governments, the department said in a news release Tuesday."We're trying to pull as many levers as we can to make this as painless as we can," Paul Wiedefeld, Maryland's transportation secretary, told The Associated Press in an interview.The proposal is part of a larger budget challenge the state is facing. Moore, a Democrat, and the legislature, which is controlled by Democrats, are grappling with projected future budget deficits in the state's operating budget, which is separate from the transportation spending plan.Moore put officials on notice in August that tough budget decisions were coming, during a speech at the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference.When state lawmakers convene for their annual legislative session in January, they will be working to balance the budget for the next fiscal year with an estimated shortfall of about $400 million.They also are facing rising budget gapsin future years, as the state continues to implement an education funding reform law with phased-in funding.One of the biggest cuts in the transportation funding plan would be to major highway and transit expansion projects that are not advertised by Jan. 1. Those construction dollars would be moved out beyond fiscal year 2029, Wiedefeld said.The plan also would cut funds for maintenance projects by 30%. For highways, that reduction would affect day-to-day operations such as mowing lawns, picking up litter and fixing potholes."They're still going to be doing them, but not at the degree that we would prefer," Wiedefeld said.The plan also calls for saving roughly $40 million a year by shutting down smaller branch offices for the MVA and reducing office hours. The plan also includes increasing airport parking fees.Wiedefeld said the state will maintain matching money to receive federal funding. The transportation department said federal investments add up to about $7 billion."We're not going to leave any money on the table because you're getting roughly 80 cents on the dollar," Wiedefeld said.U.S. Rep. David Trone, a Democrat who represents western Maryland and parts of Montgomery County in the suburbs of the nation's capital, criticized the plan for using funds in the federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to backfill the department's budget. In a letter to Wiedefeld, Trone wrote that the plan would re-allocate funds from 12 of 33 approved priority roadway projects, reduce transit services and cut maintenance projects."These projects were a huge win and Marylanders were excited to see these long-awaited investments being made in their communities, as well as the thousands of good-paying jobs that would come with them," Trone wrote.The proposal retains project development funds for Baltimore's Red Line, Southern Maryland Rapid Transit, the Frederick Douglass Tunnel Project, the replacement American Legion Bridge and other key projects, the transportation department said in a news release Tuesday afternoon.The secretary, a former general manager and CEO of Metro, said Maryland won't back away from investments needed to support the subway system linking Maryland and Virginia with the District of Columbia.The funding crunch comes as revenue sources have not kept up with operating costs, Wiedefeld said. Operating costs have risen roughly 7% annually, while revenues have gone up only about 1%, he said.The state's vehicle titling tax isn't keeping up with costs, as more people keep their vehicles longer, and the gas tax also doesn't keep pace because of increasing efficiency and electric car use. Wiedefeld also noted that transit ridership has not bounced back to what it was before the COVID-19 pandemic.The secretary also pointed out that the state has hit a debt-limit cap, creating another challenge for capital needs.

Moore's administration is proposing about $3.3 billion in wide-ranging budget cuts for the state's six-year transportation spending plan, which is facing challenges from inflation as traditional revenue sources haven't kept up with costs, Wiedefeld said Tuesday, Dec. 5, 2023.

NEWS Rural council reflects on 2024 challenges - 'Pathways to Prosperity' Summit caps another successful year

 December 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CONTRIBUTED | Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 726
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS. When more than 200 rural community leaders and other stakeholders came together for the Rural Maryland Council's recent Pathways to Prosperity summit, there was one clear message. rural communities have an inherent ability to pivot, respond and recover during hard times.The breakout sessions focused on this ability to dig deep and come up with creative solutions, a quality that rural communities can share with its suburban and urban counterparts so that all of Maryland can tackle the tough issues and come out the other end more resilient and sustainable, the council said in a press release.
"Housing is an economic development issue," said Andy Bauer, vice president and Baltimore Branch of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, during the lunch plenary. "The housing issue is something that's going to be with us for a while. It's going to take a lot of innovation in order to provide or make it easier for more supply to come online in either the form of greater density and more single family units." "It's going to have to be intentional," he added. "At the end of the day everybody in those communities are going to have to be onboard." Finding balance and leveraging challenges for the better was the message that Maryland Secretary of Agriculture Kevin Atticks delivered to summit attendees.
"Agriculture has to be profitable," he said. "Our farmers and our agricultural land are under so much pressure from development and from our clean energy goals." He didn't stop there, adding a message about resource conservation.
"We are farming in the context of the Bay. That's a pressure. We need to protect the land, preserve the land, and make sure the land is working for the Bay, not just being profitable," he said.
The summit closed with a message of hope and encouragement to tackle the challenges that lie ahead and to continue to break barriers from Maryland's first woman comptroller Brooke Lierman.
"We are focused on a new vision under our new leadership, and that is to be a partner in creating a state that is more equitable, more resilient and more prosperous so that every Marylander can reach their full potential," Lierman said. "There are still barriers to break, but by working together we can keep breaking them." The summit was just one of the key accomplishments for the Rural Maryland Council this year, the press release said. The Council received historic funding of the Rural Maryland Prosperity Investment Fund in the amount $9,050,000, along with the Maryland Agricultural Education and Rural Development Assistance Fund (MAERDAF), which received an additional $118,485. The funding enabled RMC to provide grants to the state's five rural regional councils as well as 84 RMPIF grants totaling $8,369,629 and 47 MAERDAF grants totaling $1,153,203.
Other 2023 RMC achievements include monitoring 135 bills, writing 60 position statements, passing three bills and hosting seven legislative committee meetings as well as co-hosting the 2023 Regional Rural Broadband Forum with the USDA Rural Development on June 21.
Looking to the coming year's legislative session, RMC has established several key priorities including: ¡ Level funding of $9 million in the fiscal year 2025 operating budget for Rural Maryland Prosperity Investment Fund.
¡ Efforts to address affordable housing issues such as efforts to repair and weatherize homes to keep seniors aging in their homes as well as the creation of additional workforce housing units to serve public service and moderate income workers.
¡ $1,000,000 for the Wood Products Industry Equity Investment Fund to reach renewable energy goals and support upgrades in electric infrastructure.
¡ Establishing programs and policies to sustain and enhance agricultural production and agri-tourism and efforts to address food security.
"As we close this year, we'll take a moment to appreciate our successes, and then quickly roll up our sleeves as we know that the challenges facing our rural communities continue to be numerous and complex," RMC Chair Susan O'Neill said. "We encourage all our stakeholders to join us and draw on their resilience and ability to innovate so together we can build a stronger future for all Marylanders." Founded in 1994, the Rural Maryland Council operates under the direction of a 40-member executive board in a nonpartisan and nondiscriminatory manner.
For more information on the Rural Maryland Council or to get involved, visit rural. maryland.gov or contact RMC at 410-841-5772 or rmc.mda@maryland.gov.

Maryland lawmakers return to Annapolis for 446th General Assembly

 January 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: General Assembly 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Despite flooding in downtown Annapolis and a maze of construction surrounding the State House, Maryland lawmakers were eager to get back to work as the 446th General Assembly kicked off Wednesday.Over 500 bills were prefiled ahead of the session's Wednesday start, with conversations about public safety, budgetary concerns, health care, climate change and housing expected to dominate the 90-day legislative session.
Although national change is on the horizon with primary and general elections, the General Assembly is returning to normalcy after the past few sessions saddled lawmakers with a number of challenges and adjustments, including the pandemic, redistricting and a new Democratic administration.
Senate President Bill Ferguson, a Baltimore Democrat heading into his fifth year at the helm of the Senate, acknowledged the settling pace in his address to state senators.
"The good news is we're back to governing," Ferguson said. "We are in a place where we are normalizing the world; we're back to where we've always been, and we got to focus on the things that matter the most."
To Ferguson, the top priority is balancing the state budget, he said, but making investments in education, health care, public safety and the environment are also key to making Maryland safer and stronger.
Gov. Wes Moore (D) must submit his budget proposal to the legislature by next week.
Ferguson and President Pro Tem Malcolm Augustine, a Democrat from Prince George's County, were unanimously nominated to reassume their positions, maintaining consistency in the Senate's leadership.
Similar priorities were echoed in the House of Delegates by House Speaker Adrienne Jones, a Democrat from Baltimore County who was nominated to lead the House as speaker for a fifth full session. She first assumed the role in May 2019.
In spite of the alignment in priorities, a significant change was seen in the chamber as Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico) was ousted as the House speaker pro tem.
Del. Dana Stein, a Baltimore County Democrat, was Jones' choice as the next speaker pro tem — a nomination that was echoed and affirmed across the chamber.
Though Jones did not speak to the change in leadership on the floor Wednesday, she acknowledged the significant challenges the state is facing: difficult fiscal realities, an "untenable situation" around juvenile crime and efforts to maintain the state's transportation system, among others.
Numerous bills tackling juvenile justice reforms were filed prior to the session.
This year, the legislature will fund the state trauma system, increase the availability of workforce housing and keep its commitment to the Blueprint, Jones said.
The speaker also plans to promote a set of bills she called "the decency agenda" — legislation to put safeguards and best practices in place to prevent intolerance and hate from taking root in the state.
But overall, Jones wants lawmakers to remember that shared values are more powerful than what divides them.
"We will do this work with civility and with expediency, we will talk and then listen to each other. We'll keep an open mind to and opinions that differ from our own," she said. "We'll do this work together, united as public servants working for the people of Maryland."

Sample-Hughes ousted as House speaker pro tem

 January 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: General Assembly 
 
 250
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes, a Democrat representing Dorchester and Wicomico counties, was ousted as the House of Delegates' Speaker pro tem at the start of the General Assembly Wednesday.Sample-Hughes had served as the House speaker pro tem since 2019. She has served in the House since 2015.
The decision was one Sample-Hughes and other lawmakers saw coming.
Last May, House Speaker Adrienne Jones, a Baltimore County Democrat, announced that Del. Dana Stein was her choice as the next speaker pro tem.
Stein, also a Baltimore County Democrat, was formally nominated to the position Wednesday. The nomination was affirmed across the chamber.
Jones' preference for Stein to take the position over Sample-Hughes came after Sample-Hughes voted differently on several pieces of legislation during last year's session.
The Eastern Shore Coalition of NAACP Branches vehemently opposed the speaker's request last June, saying Sample-Hughes was critical to providing the region with a voice in legislative leadership.
With the House now lacking that local representative voice, Sample-Hughes said all of the Eastern Shore counties will have to step up and be present in Annapolis.
"Each county has to come through. (They) have to be that noise," she said.
The Shore's rural communities have different needs, Sample-Hughes said, citing health care, infrastructure and struggles to fund the Blueprint — a set of policies and spending for education in the state's public schools — as examples.
"But I hope that this leadership — I hope they recognize and know that the Eastern Shore is still part of the state of Maryland," she said.

wrong_jurisdiction.title: Harris: No Offshore Wind Turbines
wrong_jurisdiction.author: Connie Connolly
wrong_jurisdiction.content:
Harris: No Offshore Wind Turbines

 January 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 1914
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OCEAN CITY — Outside the doors of the Roland E. Powell Convention Center in Ocean City, two masked protestors stood quietly with posters criticizing U.S. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.).Just inside, two volunteers handed out postcards stating, "Stop Offshore Wind" and "Join Facebook group 'Protect Ocean City.'"
In the auditorium, Worcester County residents slowly filed in. At least 300 people came out in below freezing temperatures Saturday afternoon, Jan. 20, for a congressional hearing held on their sandy turf.
Warning of dire consequences if offshore wind industrialization is allowed off Maryland's Atlantic coast, three legislators called on experts to bolster their call to halt construction of wind turbines off the mid-Atlantic coast. Harris was joined by New Jersey Congressmen Jeff Van Drew (R) and Chris Smith (R).
EXPERTS WARN OF DANGERS
Six experts testified and answered questions from the legislators. whose districts "are directly impacted" by "offshore wind industrialization," according to news releases issued by the congressmen's offices.
The panel of experts focused on the negative impacts of offshore wind energy to the fishing industry, environment and energy policy, national security, tourism, the local economy — including the Mid-Shore counties — and even the medical value of horseshoe crabs.
While the general economic impact of offshore wind development was explored, Harris told The Star Democrat following the hearing that allowing wind turbines off the coast of Ocean City to generate power would increase energy costs for all Eastern Shore residents.
Harris doubted that "the average person would be willing to pay the extra taxes and extra rates in order to develop a source of energy that … is roughly four times as expensive as what your current source of energy is," he said. "That impacts everyone whether or not you live on the Shore."
Harris lives in Dorchester County.
"Most people I know who open their electric bills this year say, 'Wow, I can't believe it's that much higher than it was last year," Harris said. "It will get even higher if we insist on producing very high-cost sources of energy."
"We might be willing to bear the costs, but are we ready to industrialize the ocean floor?" he said.
One of those costs is the increase in deaths of whales and dolphins, which the legislators attributed to the construction of wind turbines. Smith called them the "canaries in the coalmine" and blamed the Biden administration and New Jersey Gov. Phil Murphy for their "(refusal) to even listen to the numerous warnings from local leaders, mayors and state senators" and "continuing with false promises."
Smith said the construction of 3,400 offshore wind turbines across 2.4 million acres was being "fast-tracked."
Lisa Linowes is executive director of WindAction Group, which studies and provides information on "the potential harmful impacts of large-scale wind energy facilities on wildlife and the natural environment."
Although Linowes has been concerned about the dangers posed to marine life, She expressed concerns about maritime safety, and the Biden Administration's relaxing of regulations designed to protect baleen, right and humpback whales, sentiments echoed by others on the panel.
For instance, radar interference, physical obstacles and turbulence caused by wind turbines pose dangers to aircraft, according to the Coast Guard and Air Force, she said, and no "comprehensive assessment" has been conducted.
Other panelists agreed with Linowes' assessment of the dangers, and Harris said radar interference constituted a national security concern.
Meghan Lapp of Seafreeze, a Rhode Island commercial fishing company, said offshore wind turbines would interfere with "all classes of U.S. radar."
In December 2023, a new series of leases were proposed farther off the Maryland coast, Harris said, but were "withdrawn from consideration by the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management because of protests from the Department of Defense and from NASA, who said that those leasing areas would adversely affect our ability to maintain national security and, in the case of NASA, … interfere with the Wallops Flight Center."
In addition to maritime safety concerns, Linowes said the "discrepancy between federal treatment of ocean industries is staggering," citing federal agencies' downplaying correlations between "last year's surge of large baleen whale deaths on the East Coast coinciding with unprecedented offshore wind seismic surveys."
"Had the whale deaths coincided with oil and gas surveys instead of offshore wind surveys, the pause and investigation requested by the congressmen would have been standard procedure," she said.
Robert Rand of Rand Acoustics LLC in Brunswick, Maine, said underwater testing and sonar surveys by offshore wind development was damaging the hearing of marine mammals, which is vital to their survival.
"I know how to measure sound," Rand said. "More than that, I care about whales."
His independent surveys of whale populations off the coasts of Hawaii and Cape Cod revealed stark contrasts in their communication patterns, suggesting that, even with NOAA's noise mitigation requirements, whales were adversely affected by high decibel sounds associated with offshore wind development, he said.
Panelist Travis Fisher is the director of energy and environmental policy studies at the Cato Institute. With wind turbine power, he said Marylanders would end up paying more for wind, in addition to a backup source of power, hitting lower income residents harder.
Observing the results of California and Germany's green energy policies has been instructive, he said.
"Both places have chosen to embrace intermittent energy at the expense of reliable energy," he said. "Germany's energy transition has caused its residents to pay three times more for electricity than we pay in the United States. California has higher electricity prices than any other state in the lower 48."
"It's not too late to recognize the folly of a forced energy transition," Fisher said. "There is no justification for an off-shore wind mandate."
Also testifying was Bonnie Brady of the Long Island Commercial Fishing Association.
LOCAL LEADERS UNIFY
Although Danish company Ørsted canceled two off-shore wind projects in fall 2023, it was continuing to develop Skipjack Wind 20 miles off the Maryland coast.
However, on Jan. 25, Ørsted announced it had "withdrawn from the Maryland Public Service Commission orders approving the Skipjack 1 and 2 projects" following "consultation with the State of Maryland" and "an extensive review of the orders." It cited "challenging market conditions, including inflation, high interest rates and supply chain constraints" as reasons for the decision.
The company "intends to continue advancing development and permitting for the combined project, including submission of its updated Construction and Operations Plan to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management," according to a press release.
Harris said another company besides Ørsted holds a Maryland offshore lease, a "cleverly named U.S. Wind, which is a wholly owned subsidiary of an Italian company."
The project doesn't sit well with Worcester County and Ocean City's leaders, four of whom spoke during the hearing.
"The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management's own environmental impact statement study further convinced me that the potential negative impacts of offshore wind industrialization off Maryland's Coast outweighs the many promised benefits by European-based offshore wind developers," said state Sen. Mary Beth Carozza (R-Somerset, Wicomico, Worcester).
"With my prior work experience at the Pentagon and the U.S. Senate Homeland Security Committee, I especially am sensitive to the security and safety concerns raised by the Department of Defense, including the detrimental effect of wind turbines on existing radar systems by false alarms and missed detection of real targets," Carozza said.
Mainly concerned with tourism, they warned of potential hazards caused by strong storms, and even the health of the horseshoe crab population.
Del. Wayne Hartman (R-Wicomico, Worcester) said the "vast majority" of constituents who had contacted him were "adamantly opposed to the implementation of offshore wind projects."
"According to a study from North Carolina State University, 55% of vacation renters would not return to the vacation destination if turbines were visible," he said. "This is very concerning for the future of economic development in Ocean City as tourism accounts for the largest percentage of the local economy."
"We have a horseshoe crab harvest here critical for the safety of injectable medications, yet there were plans to put turbines right in horseshoe sanctuary areas," Pat Shrawder of said. She is district representative for state Sen. Mary Beth Carozza (R-Somerset, Wicomico, Worcester).
"My understanding is that the horseshoe crab industry is centered in the mid-Atlantic here," Harris said. "As a physician I'll tell you, a lot of people don't know when you get an intravenous medication of any kind — something that comes out of a sterile intravenous vial — that batch has been tested against a derivative of horseshoe crabs to make sure it doesn't have bacterial endotoxin — something that would kill you."
Electromagnetic fields and underwater cables would also interfere with horseshoe crabs' migration paths.
The effect of strong storms on wind turbines has not been adequately studied, Harris said.
"Our residents are fearful of the effect of hurricane force winds on wind turbulence," Schrawder said. "Ocean City is subject to strong northeasters or hurricanes. Even the EIS (Enterprise Infrastructure Solutions of the U.S. General Services Administration) report states that a hurricane could result in the loss of a blade and or turbine collapse. We worry about a football field-sized blade hurtling (sic) through the air."
Ocean City Mayor Rick Meehan, a Republican who has served as mayor since 2006, galvanized the mostly local audience. He said he represented 26,000 property owners, residents and a million visitors who stand in "total opposition to the proposed U.S. Wind project."
"The discussion on wind turbines off the coast of Ocean City goes back as far as 2010," Meehan said. "Yet this is the first time a committee from the federal government has actually held a hearing here in Ocean City."
Meehan said the wind turbines would mar the resort's vista. "The sunrise over the Atlantic would look like a backdrop from Star Wars," he said.
"The first time I saw the renderings of what U.S. Wind was proposing — and at the time, those were four megawatt or possibly six megawatt turbines approximately 450 feet tall — I had stated our opposition to the size and locations of those turbines at that time seven years ago. Our concerns fell on deaf ears," Meehan said. "Today, those same turbines are now 18 megawatt turbines at … maybe 1,065 feet in height, and they're proposing the same locations. Our concerns continue to fall on deaf ears."
"What has also been ignored is the revenue that Ocean City sends: Millions of dollars to both the state and the federal government each year," Meehan said. "We only have one industry in Ocean City, and that's tourism. Why would the state or the federal government want to unnecessarily jeopardize our future?"
"What I can assure you is that the Town of Ocean City will not back down from our opposition to these projects and to our future here in Ocean City," Meehan said as the audience applauded and cheered.
FIGHT CONTINUES
U.S. Wind, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration were invited to attend the hearing. U.S. Wind did not respond and the federal agencies "declined to attend," Harris said.
Smith said "calls for an honest review of offshore wind industrialization has left unaddressed and unanswered so many questions; so much so, that in March of last year, Andy Harris, Jeff Van Drew and I offered an amendment that passed 244 to 189 to have the watchdog of Congress, the Government Accountability Office, investigate the impacts of wind turbines, and their audit will be coming out very soon."
The bottom line for Harris: "I believe it's time to reconsider whether offshore wind is the right approach for Maryland."
Van Drew was more pointed. "We have a war to win," he said. "Do not succumb, do not be weak, and we will prevail."
To watch the entire hearing, go to www.youtube.com/watch?v=1ThWS1FT1Qo

wrong_jurisdiction.title: Local Lightning Rods: Social media, national partisan divisions, culture wars have changed tone and tenor of local politics
wrong_jurisdiction.author: Mike Sunnucks APG National Enterprise Editor
wrong_jurisdiction.content:
Local Lightning Rods: Social media, national partisan divisions, culture wars have changed tone and tenor of local politics

 March 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Sunnucks APG National Enterprise Editor | Section: News 
 
 1445
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Megan Cook, Russ Nelson and Ann Groves Lloyd are mayors of small towns in Maryland, Montana and Wisconsin.Nelson has been the mayor of Belgrade, Montana, for 20 years.
Karen Rose has been with Sarasota County Schools in Florida for more than three decades serving as a special education teacher, middle school principal and since 2020 on the local school board.
Over their tenures, the quartet and local officials across the country have seen the exponential growth of social media and its impacts on civil discourse, as well as the increasing intersections between divisive national politics and what's happening at the community level.
Rose, who became chair of the Sarasota County School Board in November, said she's worked for and with multiple superintendents — and times have definitely changed.
"We took great pride in no one knowing our political affiliation. We kept each other in check. It was a matter of pride," Rose said.
Now, Florida conservatives (including Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis) and progressives (including some outspoken teacher unions and Democratic-leaning school boards) clash locally over COVID and vaccine rules, controversial books in libraries, the state's so-called "Don't Say Gay" law restricting elementary school teachers from talking to young students about gender identity and sexual orientation and how to teach America's racial history.
Rose said she saw some previous superintendents let politics take away from the focus on academic achievement.
"Cultural wars were being let in and taking hold," she said.
Rose, a Republican, said the current superintendent, Terry Connor, (who was hired last year) has shown a focus on academic achievement and data-driven solutions.
But that's not stopping the politics at board meetings, she said.
"There is clearly an organized agenda that is political in the boardroom during public comment," Rose said. "It's very organized."
Rose said Democratic advocates will speak during the comment period, noting a recent hearing where 67 people spoke, with only three focused on academics.
Some of the recent comments have been geared toward Bridget Ziegler, who has served on the Sarasota school board since 2014 and was a co-founder of the lightning rod conservative education group Moms for Liberty, which has become a GOP political force.
Liberal activists and other critics have called for Ziegler to resign her post amid a police investigation of her husband, former Florida Republican Party Chairman Christian Ziegler, over an alleged sexual encounter with his wife and another woman. Christian Ziegler could face video voyeurism charges for allegedly videotaping the encounter. Bridget Ziegler has never faced any legal allegations in the episode. She did not respond to an interview request.
Rose said political advocates, as well as some media outlets, have focused on Florida controversies, including debates over controversial and mature content at libraries. Those debates, along with fights over drag shows at libraries, other public venues and local businesses, have been happening across the country.
"They continue to talk about book banning. This board has not banned one single book," she said.
Conservative and progressive advocates increasingly view local councils and school boards as venues to mobilize supporters and address issues of concern.
Carlos Guillermo Smith, senior policy adviser for Equality Florida (an LGBTQ rights group), said the group has "a long history" of mobilizing parents and community members to attend school board and council meetings when issues of concern arise.
"We have also had a regular presence at the Sarasota school board meetings, especially in the wake of recent Moms For Liberty/Ziegler scandals," he said.
Anti-war and pro-Palestinian activists have pushed liberal jurisdictions, including San Francisco, to approve resolutions condemning Israel's war in Gaza after the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks and calling for a ceasefire. Other progressives advocated for spending cuts and shifting money away from police after the death of George Floyd in 2020.
Among conservatives, Mark Lee Dixson, a Christian pastor and anti-abortion rights advocate from Texas, has gotten 65 cities and seven counties in Texas, Nebraska, New Mexico and other states to pass Sanctuary Cities for the Unborn Initiatives. The measures aim to signal communities' oppositionto abortion rights and resistance to having abortion clinics in their jurisdictions.
'THAT'S MY TECHNOLOGY'
Frustrations with and more cautious approaches related to social media are common refrains from local officials wary of viral controversies and local rumor mills.
In small-town Montana, where Belgrade has a population approaching 13,000 people, Nelson avoids social media and its penchant for unpleasant and contentious discourse.
"I'm not on Facebook. I'm not on social media," said Nelson, who has been in office since 2003 and won reelection in November for a final term before his expected retirement. "You can call me, or if you need me, you can text me. That's my technology."
The more contentious nature of local politics — whether it comes from social media criticism or its mirroring of national fights over hot-button issues or former President Donald Trump — also can discourage potential candidates for local office and can lead to shorter tenures for some city, county and school district staff, Nelson said.
"Good people see how challenging it is and don't enter the game," he said.
Ann Groves Lloyd is the mayor of Lodi, Wisconsin, a town of just over 3,200 residents near Madison. Groves Lloyd describes herself as a "progressive feminist" and "small-town mayor" on her social media profile on X (formerly Twitter).
The progressive mayor is a vehement critic of former President Trump, is no fan of U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., and is not sure she can find compromise or common ground with conservative adherents of alt-right media such as Alex Jones or those getting worked up about drag shows.
Groves Lloyd also said she saw already rough civil discourse get even rougher during the debates over COVID mask mandates, vaccines and shutdowns.
"It was pretty toxic," she said. "For me, personally, I took a giant step back from social media. I used to post a lot of mostly progressive things on Facebook."
Now, the Wisconsin mayor keeps her ideological posts to X, which has a national and international focus.
She also worries about social media rumor mills and rabbit holes leading constituents astray.
"From a city perspective, we just wish people would pick up the phone and call us. We are constantly fighting the rumor mill," she said.
Some activists counter that local governments and school boards are not always forthcoming with information or friendly with constituents who are less connected or come from opposing political camps.
Still, social media and live and replayed online broadcasts of meetings allow more residents and local businesses to engage with and keep tabs on local matters.
"The more information that we share with the public about what's happening in town, the better. We also have a live feed for all of our council, board and commission meetings. If residents aren't able to make it, they can always watch the recordings from our website," said Cook, mayor of Easton, on Maryland's Eastern Shore.
"The town is using social media as another way of sharing information with the community. It's a quick, easy and efficient way to share information," she said.
Even Nelson said social media helps drive interest and council meeting attendance on hot-button issues such as "dogs, fireworks and marijuana,"referring to city regulations and decisions on dispensaries after Montana voters legalized cannabis for recreational use in 2020.
PUTTING THE PARTISAN IN NONPARTISAN
While many local elected offices are nonpartisan, partisan politics has increasingly become part of local elections and governance.
In Montana, Nelson, a self-described moderate Republican, voiced frustration with the "far right" conservative agenda from the state legislature impacting and dictating policy paths to local entities.
Conservative state lawmakers have passed laws requiring local school districts to open their enrollments to out-of-district students, and looked to put limits on some municipal zoning powers, including efforts to develop more affordable and multifamily units statewide.
Back East, Easton, which has a population of close to 17,500, is part of Talbot County, which saw a contentious fight that drew national political and media attention over a Confederate statue in front of the county courthouse.
The Talbot Boys statue, erected in 1916, was relocated to a private memorial park in Virginia in 2022 after a vote by the county council. Cook said Easton has been able to avoid some of the wave of national divisiveness, but she has definitely seen a greater interest from Democratic and Republican groups in local races, as well as more questions from voters about her own party affiliation.
"In town elections, we don't run on a party system, which I love. It shouldn't matter what you're registered as, if you need assistance from the town we're going to be there," said Cook, a Democrat, who was elected mayor last year after serving as Town Council president.
"That being said, I was asked more during my last campaign what I was registered as than I have before and both Central Committees seemed to want to be involved."
