wrong_jurisdiction.title: Data Center Pause Underscores Local Concerns About Widespread Impacts
wrong_jurisdiction.author: Peter Riccio and Holliday Woodard Capital News Service
wrong_jurisdiction.content:
Data center pause underscores local concerns about widespread impacts

 September 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Peter Riccio and Holliday Woodard Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 958
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON — A proposed data center project in Prince George's County, Maryland, was paused on Sept. 16 to give a task force time to evaluate potential impacts on public health, the environment and energy demand.The Prince George's project is controversial, underscoring growing public concerns over the proliferation of data centers nationwide.
Data centers can range from massive warehouse-sized facilities to office buildings and are the physical backbone of everything digital.
The growth of these centers has surged, with 44 operational or planned data centers in Maryland, according to Data Center Map. Prince George's County is one of the latest battlegrounds where local opposition has slowed what data center supporters insist would be a major boom to the economy.
"The only reason the county is considering data centers is for money," Prince George's County Council Member Wala Blegay said in an interview with Capital News Service. "The reality is that our commercial tax base is very low. We're mostly relying on residential (taxes) because our residents are not able to get relief on the high property taxes that we have here. That is why we are looking at data centers."
Blegay's District 6 borders the District of Columbia and is mostly inside the Capital Beltway, encompassing communities including Suitland, District Heights, Marlow Heights, Camp Springs and Forestville.
The county council created the Qualified Data Center Task Force in April 2025. The council faced local protests at their three meetings in July from residents concerned about energy consumption, electric bills and environmental factors.
On Sept. 16, the council approved a resolution pausing the development of current and future data center projects until the task force has completed its work. The task force is expected to release its findings in November.
"There is no point in having a task force if all of these projects can move forward," Blegay said. "We're studying all of these infrastructure issues. So we're talking about the next three months, we're going to be passing legislation to address that… and we don't want people to rush out and expedite their process, so they'll get ahead of us."
Prince George's County Executive Aisha Braveboy told Washington's WTOP radio that the county council's 2021 decision to speed up the data center approval process "was a huge mistake because the residents have a stake in where these data centers are located."
"I'm in support generally of data centers," Braveboy said. "I do believe it's a really good economic tool in the right locations."
"I think we gotta look at what the land use implications are and be really thorough in these decisions," Del. Ashanti F. Martinez, D-Prince George's, said in a Sept. 18 Instagram post. "You know, at the state level we try to provide as much oversight as possible, and I'm really concerned that we are moving a little fast on the data center conversation."
Access to electricity and the price residents pay are critics' primary concerns, as the average monthly electric bill for Maryland, according to poweroutage.us, stands at $167.55. Electric bills are expected to slightly rise with the anticipated new data centers, according to a letter from the Office of People's Council for the State of Maryland.
"What we know is that no data center is going to be turned on, especially with high gigawatts, not within the next four to five years, because of all the issues with electricity and energy sourcing," Blegay said.
Maryland currently does not produce enough electricity on its own, so it relies on importing the shortfall from outside the state.
"Historically, Maryland has imported about 40% of its annual electric needs from other states," according to a 2024 fact sheet from PJM, a transmission organization that coordinates the use of wholesale electricity among 13 states and the District of Columbia.
As of last year, data centers accounted for about 4.4% of total U.S. electricity consumption, according to a report from the Department of Energy (DOE).
"(AI is) a much more significant data hog than any type of search you have today, and it's something that is exponentially growing with the types of searches Americans are doing," Michael Kratsios, director of the White House's Office of Science and Technology Policy, told a Sept. 10 hearing of the Senate Commerce, Science & Transportation Committee's science, manufacturing, and competitiveness.
The increased use of AI has provided an opening for Republicans who advocate a renewed reliance on traditional fuels to meet the energy demand. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, for example, wants "good, old-fashioned" coal and gas to provide U.S. power needs.
"When you had 94% of new power generation in America over the last four years, be it wind and solar, that probably isn't nearly enough to produce the kind of energy that we need to power the AI revolution," Moreno said at the subcommittee hearing.
But Sen. Edward Markey, D-Massachusetts, warned that "Americans' electricity bills are going to rise by as much as 25% over the next four years — 25% because of data center demand. It's not just a future fear, it's a present problem."
"So, Mr. Kratsios, do you think it's appropriate that the administration is forcing Americans to pay more on their electricity bills while using their taxpayer dollars to make the problem even worse by funding the unfettered growth of the AI industry?" Markey asked.
"I do not believe there's been an administration in American history more committed to growing power generation for the American people and lowering energy costs for everyday Americans," Kratsios responded. "And I'm proud to work for a president and administration that has that level of commitment."
In October, PG County will host another public council meeting to continue discussions about the data center. By the end of November, the Prince George's County Qualified Data Center Task Force will report its findings, giving the council six months to decide on next steps, according to the resolution.

wrong_jurisdiction.author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com
wrong_jurisdiction.content:
Hornberger to introduce citizenship check for voters

 October 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com | Section: State News 
 
 306
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Cecil County Del. Kevin Hornberger (R) says he likely has bipartisan support for a resolution he plans to bring before the Maryland General Assembly in January that would require the Maryland State Board of Elections to verify the citizenship of every registered voter in Maryland."Virginia and Colorado — both fairly 'blue' states — are already doing this," Hornberger said. "So I say, 'Hey, State of Maryland, you need to participate in this program.'"
The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlement program is an online service that verifies a benefit or license applicant's immigration status for US citizenship. It does likewise for those who are naturalized, acquired or US born, giving this information to agencies to assure only those allowed get these entitlements. That includes the right to vote, Hornberger said.
"This tells the Board of Elections to participate," Hornberger said. "I think we'll have bipartisan support."
Party affiliation is not the issue, Hornberger said, even though Democrats told Republican members of the General Assembly that this was unnecessary. "They said you guys are offering solutions to a problem that doesn't exist. Well, guess what?"
The recent arrest of an Iowa public schools superintendent — who previously resided in Maryland — is what made Hornberger pursue the SAVE Act legislation.
"He was in this country illegally and he was registered as a Democrat in Maryland," he said.
Calling Maryland "one of the largest immigration states in the country," Hornberger said the SAVE Act wouldn't carry any penalties.
"It's just saying they can't vote," he said. If the resolution gets approved, Hornberger said it would make elections fair. "Every board in Maryland would have to use the federal voter registry database to assure that everyone registered to vote in the state of Maryland are legally residents."
The bill would first go before the House Ways and Means Committee, of which Hornberger is a member.

wrong_jurisdiction.title: Lack of funding a 'recipe of frustration'
wrong_jurisdiction.author: STAFF REPORTS
wrong_jurisdiction.content:
Lack of funding a 'recipe of frustration'

 August 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORTS | Section: News 
 
 1210
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Upwards of 200 individuals gathered at the Queen Anne's County Public Schools Board of Education building in solidarity of Queen Anne's County Education Association members raising their voices against proposed employee layoffs as the board held a closed executive session Aug. 20."We teach our students to collaborate and talk together, well, let's walk the walk," Education Association President Cecilia Mitchell said about the assembly.
Marching from Centreville Elementary School to the building at 202 Chesterfield Avenue, teachers, parents, students, supporters and members of the education union wore "red for ed" against cuts proposed in an effort to balance the district's budget.
According to the meeting's agenda on the board website, the closed session was held "To consult with counsel to obtain legal advice; To conduct collective bargaining negotiations or consider matters that relate to the negotiations."
Creating "joyful noise," as Mitchell put it, the rally attendees carried signs of support for school staff and verbally chanted against cuts. In front of the building, participants inscribed chalk messages on the sidewalk.
"People love the school systems here. The future lives in that building," Mitchell said, pointing to nearby Centreville Elementary.
"It's deeply frustrating that QACPS wants to cut some of our lowest-paid educators who work directly with our students, and at the start of the year, no less. We don't know how many people, or what job titles," Mitchell said in a statement ahead of Tuesday's rally. "There are any number of ways to deal with budget problems, but not if you won't talk to your educators."
According to a press release issued by the Association, they were notified on Aug. 14 of the potential layoffs of "an unknown number of QACPS support staff, who are among the lowest-paid employees in QACPS."
The Association seeks the superintendent and school board to address the budget shortfall before pushing it on to employees, Mitchell said.
The layoffs announcement came after the school district asked Queen Anne's County educators on Aug. 12 to accept five unpaid furlough days during the 2024-25 school year.
The educators association said they asked for documentation to justify the furloughs and were "sent no response nor documentation, and then refused to meet on any of the dates offered to discuss the matter."
Seeking budget transparency, the Association has filed a formal information request, with questions including where the money was going, and what is being done that doesn't involve cutting positions, according to Mitchell.
"So, we just have two questions for Dr. Saelens. First, why are you asking us to cut our salaries if you won't ask the county for additional funding, and second, why won't QACPS answer our questions about the budget crisis like the law requires?" Mitchell said.
Other measures needed to be exhausted first before the proposed Reduction In Force and layoffs of essential support staff, she said.
Mitchell highlighted the effect layoffs would have on the livelihood of support staff, who ensure the optimal running of the school, while making up the smallest portion of school system employees, "And they make the least amount of money," she said.
According to a statement from Superintendent Patricia Saelens, the school system sought to balance the budget through attrition.
Saelens noted the "severely underfunded Blueprint For Maryland' Schools, coupled with overall inflation has created a recipe of frustration" — a deficit that Queen Anne's County is not alone in facing, she said.
As a result of that lack of attrition there is still a current shortfall of two million dollars. Saelens wrote in a letter to staff on Aug. 19, "This summer, we have worked to do a detailed budget analysis and determine what could be cut to put those funds into salaries. We have identified numerous items to help reduce the budget shortfall. We will cut scanning, tutoring and locally funded conferences. We will reduce our legal line item. We will cut school block grants by 10%."
Additionally Saelens wrote the district is canceling the Cenergistic Energy contract, and repurposing the staff tuition reimbursement line. "While these measures will help, it is simply not enough to balance the budget," she stated, "Under Maryland Law, a local board of education is prohibited from carrying a budget deficit."
Saelens contends the district met with the union on July 18 and 31 to discuss a retirement incentive and potential furlough days. The retirement incentive was not successful as only two employees took advantage, still leaving them under the attrition necessary to balance the budget.
Together with the union, Saelens said they selected dates that purposely would not impact student days. "We also determined the proposed furlough days would be for all employee units, including the superintendent and all administrative staff. These proposed five days would have avoided the need to reduce any member of our staff," she said, "We know that each of our employees are vital to the successes of students. It was our intention to keep our staff whole."
Saelens said they provided the union with all the information they requested within 24 hours, meeting again on Aug. 6 and sharing a draft MOU regarding proposed furlough days.
Given the upcoming start of the school year, we requested that they provide us with their decision by Aug. 12, Saelens said. The union responded in writing informing leadership that they "formally decline Queen Anne's County Public Schools proposal of furlough days for the 2024-2025 school year".
As a result, Reduction In Force (RIF) letters were issued on Aug. 14, in accordance with the RIF process outlined in the negotiated agreement, Saelens concluded.
Whether proposed furlough dates or RIF, the teacher's union has a ratified contract based on an offer the BOE presented to the union that was accepted, according to Mitchell.
"We must take care of each other," she said.
Showing support for fellow union members and district bus drivers, Tony Mansfield stated the rally was a "good start" and sought collaborative efforts to come up with a budget that does not include reductions and a solution that honors the contract ratified in June.
School psychologist Julie Rock, of Matapeake Middle School and Kent Island Elementary School, stated it was her job to advocate for students and the rally highlighted the invaluableness of the various support needed within the walls of the schools. "Right now, the students that need us the most are going to be losing the support," Rock said.
Standing alongside QACEA was Lori Hrinko, President of Cecil County Classroom Teachers Association. "This isn't about you wanting more, this is about what's right for our kids," Hrinko told the crowd.
Hrinko encouraged everyone to be involved in their school districts, as students represented the future generations.
QACEA is a local affiliate of the Maryland State Education Association (MSEA), which in turn is an affiliate of the National State Education Association, and Mitchell voiced appreciation of the organizations' support.
Working to promote change through action, Mitchell hoped to inspire students of all ages and showcase that change is possible.
Mitchell noted issues cannot be addressed by avoiding dialog or shifting blame, "Problems can only be solved with conversation, creative solutions and direct contact," she said.
Moving forward, Mitchell seeks to have all groups unite with the same underlying goal: identify the best interests for the good of students. "[Working] together; real numbers, real decisions," Mitchell said.
More information about QACEA can be found at https://qacea.org.
The Board of Education will next meet for a regular meeting Sept. 4 at 6 p.m.

wrong_jurisdiction.author: Connor Bolinder; connor.bolinder@chespub.com
wrong_jurisdiction.content:
Baltimore police clear homeless encampment

 August 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connor Bolinder; connor.bolinder@chespub.com | Page: A3 | Section: News 
 
 610
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On July 21, Baltimore City police, first responders and outreach workers went in full force to clear out the homeless encampment at the corner of Dundalk and Holabird Avenues.A "No Trespassing" notice was posted earlier this month, stating that the area would be cleared on July 21.The Baltimore City Mayor's Office of Homeless Services and nonprofit groups visited the site before it was cleared to connect people with resources like shelter and drug treatment. The area was cleared by noon."Members of the Baltimore County Homeless Services Division have been working closely with Baltimore City officials to address the encampment near Dundalk and Holabird Avenues," Baltimore City police said in a statement sent to the Old Dundalk Neighborhood Association. "We understand how concerning it is to see this situation in your community. As the encampment is located on city property, the Baltimore City Mayor's Office of Homeless Services is leading response efforts in coordination with other City agencies, including the Baltimore City Police Department, Baltimore City Department of Public Works, and Baltimore City Department of Transportation with support from nonprofit organizations under contract with Baltimore County to provide outreach and access to services." People began living in tents on a strip of grass in front of the Holabird Business Park earlier this year.Community groups wrote to county and city leaders for months asking for a solution, but the encampment was located just inside the city line. The Baltimore County government doesn't have any jurisdiction on that property, but county police officers are often on standby just up the street.The Old Dundalk Neighborhood Association joined with other community groups on the city-county line: Boston Courts, Norwood-Holabird and Graceland Park. In February, they wrote a letter to officials to request a solution.People living in tents longterm poses a lot of public health concerns, and city police were regularly called out to the encampment.Several people in the camp used drugs during the daytime, and panhandling at the intersection was very common.Baltimore police Precinct 12 Capt. Glenn Wiedeck and City Police Maj.Kiera Saunders had coordinated for crime calls associated with the camp. It was a welcome collaboration between the city and county law enforcement."They're actually speaking to each other right now and that didn't happen in the past," ODNA President Jess Lilli said in April.Last month, the Baltimore County Continuum of Care Homeless Roundtable hosted a job and resource fair at the Sollers Point Multipurpose Center. The Baltimore County Homeless Services Division continually works to help people who are homeless and seeking help.Baltimore County Police issued a statement promising to help connect homeless people with resources, and prevent a similar encampment from forming in Dundalk."Though this is a Baltimore City operation the Baltimore County Police Department is aware of the impact it may have on the surrounding county communities and is taking steps to offer any homeless person(s) services and resources if they attempt to migrate into Baltimore County," BCPD said."Officers will also be in place to remind any of these homeless person(s) that the camp sites they are used to in Baltimore City will not be allowed in Baltimore County." 
 
 Caption: PHOTOS BY CO NNOR BOLINDER.
 
A Baltimore City garbage truck pulls up to the homeless encampment. Workers form the Department of Public Works hauled tents, leftover belongings and trash out of the area after police cleared it out..
 
PHOTO BY CO NNOR BOLINDER.
 
Notice was posted weeks ago, alerting anyone living in the encampment that it would be cleared by city police on July 21..
 
PHOTO BY CO NNOR BOLINDER.
 
Abandoned tents and chairs are left behind after police cleared out everyone living in the homeless encampment on Dundalk Avenue.

wrong_jurisdiction.title: Police Nab Theft Suspects Who Allegedly Stole $8K in Perfume from Ulta Store
wrong_jurisdiction.author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
wrong_jurisdiction.content:
Police nab theft suspects who allegedly stole $8K in perfume from Ulta store

 April 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 471
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Five out-of-state individuals — four men and a woman — have been charged with felony theft following an alleged theft of nearly $8,000 worth of merchandise from Ulta Beauty in Prince Frederick.The incident occurred on April 4 at approximately 4:37 p.m., according to the Calvert County Sheriff's Office. Deputies responded to the store when a call went out that a theft had occurred.
According to a sheriff's office report, "Two males and one female entered the store and placed numerous colognes and perfumes into bags and fled the store. After fleeing the store, witnesses observed all three suspects enter a gray Mercury Montego that fled northbound on Route 4."
According to court documents filed by Deputy Antonio Tavares, Deputy Justin MacWilliams located the Mercury traveling northbound on Route 4, which then turned onto Route 2.
MacWilliams "initiated a traffic stop in the area of Pushaw Station Road in Sunderland. During the traffic stop, five occupants were located in the suspect vehicle along with numerous bags of perfumes and colognes in plain view. The total value of the stolen items was approximately $7,694 dollars."
In addition to the merchandise that was allegedly stolen from the Prince Frederick store, Tavares reported in charging papers that several cellphones were also confiscated.
The five arrested are identified as Yeiner Jose Rodriguez Barcelo, 27, of Bronx, N.Y., Yoncar Alberto Rainoso, 21, of Manhattan, N.Y., Estefani Andrea Urbano-Zapata, 21, of Cape Girardea, Mo., Raimil Marquez Jimenez, 25, of Washington, D.C., and Adony Josue Carana, 27, of Manhattan N.Y.
A sheriff's office press release stated that further investigation revealed Rodriguez-Barcelo was wanted on an open warrant from Pennsylvania for felony retail theft related to thefts at Ulta stores in Pennsylvania.
Court records show Carana, who was also listed with the alias Carrano, has been released after posting $10,000 bond. As of Monday, the other four remained at the Calvert detention center on a no-bond status.
A district court hearing on the charges the five are facing is scheduled for June 3. Language interpreters have been requested for four of the five defendants, court records show.
The Prince Frederick Ulta has been the scene of similar thefts over the last three years. Other Ulta stores regionally and nationally have been targets of alleged thieves. Several national news outlets have reported allegations of a possible retail theft ring in the state of California. The alleged perpetrators there stole $8 million in cosmetics from several chains, including Ulta, and then sold the products on Amazon.
It is not known at this time if the five arrested in Calvert last week are part of a larger theft ring.
Calvert County Sheriff Ricky Cox (R) issued a note of thanks in an agency press release to "the witnesses on scene that went above and beyond to promptly call 911 and provide details of the suspects and suspects' vehicle. Your efforts are greatly appreciated."

wrong_jurisdiction.author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
wrong_jurisdiction.content:
Speed cameras coming to stretch of I-95 starting July 8

 June 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 567
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Starting July 8, police in Delaware will use electronic speed cameras to help enforce speed limits in the Interstate 95 construction zone near Del. 896 in Newark.The first three weeks will be a warning period. After the warning period, registered vehicle owners receiving a first offense will receive a base violation of $20, plus an additional amount for each mile per hour over the posted work zone speed limit of 55 mph.
For example, if the captured violation occurs at a speed of 66 mph, the speed violation is $20 plus an additional $11, which accounts for $1 for each mile per hour over the speed limit. Additional fees and court costs that are tacked on to all speeding tickets in Delaware will bring the total cost up to $118.
Second and subsequent offenses are higher. These violations are civil penalties only, and no points will be assessed to drivers' licenses.
State officials first announced the program in April, saying the cameras are an important tool to make work zones safer.
"Even though we've reduced the speed limits out here in the work zone, we're still seeing people speeding through there," Delaware Department of Transportation Secretary Nicole Majeski said at the time. "It is a tight configuration, so law enforcement has difficulty pulling people over. We've also seen a spike in crashes, so we're hoping the cameras will help."
Similar to the red light cameras common throughout the state, speed cameras will take pictures of violators' license plates, and those drivers will receive a ticket in the mail. The driver must exceed the speed limit by at least 11 mph in order to receive a ticket via a speed camera.
DelDOT first used speed cameras in 2022 when the state legislature authorized a pilot program focused on an I-95 project in Wilmington.
"We saw speeds reduced significantly, both northbound and southbound, and accidents were cut in half," Majeski said. "We saw as a direct result of having those cameras that people slow down, and it really paid off."
Last year, after lobbying from Newark officials and others, the legislature expanded the program to allow cameras in work zones and residential areas throughout the state. After developing regulations and choosing a vendor, DelDOT is ready to install the first new cameras in the work zone at the I-95/Del. 896 interchange, which is in the midst of a two-year reconstruction project.
Brandon Zerilla, who is leading the project for DelDOT contractor Wagman, said earlier this year that the cameras will be a welcomed safety tool for his workers.
"These cameras have proven to reduce the speeds in the work zone, reduce crashes and increase awareness in the work zone," Zerilla said, adding that far too many drivers do not slow down while passing through the I-95 construction site.
The interchange project, which is the largest work zone in Delaware, involves building new flyover ramps from southbound Del. 896 to northbound I-95 and from southbound I-95 to southbound Del. 896. The flyovers will increase the distance between exit and entrance ramps, reducing the traffic weaving that causes crashes at the current interchange.
The project also includes widening a one-mile stretch of the interstate to provide for longer acceleration and deceleration lanes, as well as upgraded lighting, rehabilitation of 10 existing bridges, the construction of six new bridges for the flyovers, and the construction of a walking and biking bridge over the interstate.
Work began last spring and will continue through fall 2025.

wrong_jurisdiction.content:
Delaware park closed due to safety concerns, hazardous conditions

 June 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 262
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A Newark park will be closed for the foreseeable future after a recent inspection found "significant safety concerns and hazardous conditions," city officials said.One of the city's lesser-known parks, Coleman Park is located near the Maryland border, bounded by Valley Road and the Country Hills and Briarcreek neighborhoods. The main entrance is in Country Hills.
The 8.5-acre park contains walking trails but otherwise is preserved in its natural state.
The inspection found that the tree canopy near the entrance to the park consists of many black locust trees that are structurally compromised by fungal decay and pose a significant risk of falling.
The walking paths are eroded and surrounded by dense thickets of greenbrier, multiflora rose and poison ivy.
"These thorny species have overgrown the area and become entangled with large woody debris from fallen trees and limbs," City Manager Tom Coleman wrote in a memo to city council. "Significant land clearing and tree removal must be completed before we can reopen the park."
The city does not have funding for such work in the 2025 budget, according to Coleman, who did not provide any indication as to when the park might reopen.
The city's five-year capital improvement plan includes plans for broader improvements to Coleman Park, such as building a turf/meadow area, planting new trees and possibly paving the trails. However that $50,000 in funding, which is dependent on a state grant, is not budgeted until 2027.
Coleman Park was created in 1993 when Newark purchased the land for $180,000 and annexed it into the city. It is named for the family that previously owned the property.

 An incident that led to a man's arrest in June 2024 resulted in a five-count indictment this summer from a Calvert County grand jury.The defendant is identified in court papers as Edward Dewey Viens Jr., 39, of Laurel.
According to court documents, on June 5, 2024, deputies from the county's sheriff's office were initially sent to the Huntingtown area in response to a missing person report. The deputies were then dispatched to CalvertHealth Medical Center after it was learned the 32-year-old woman who had been reported missing had been located.
Viens was also at the hospital, investigators reported.
In charging papers filed by Deputy Ryan Gough, the woman claimed she had been held against her will by Viens, who was her boyfriend at the time.
Gough said Viens' accuser had bruises on her face, lacerations on her arms, neck, hands and legs, which were the result of an alleged assault by the defendant. That assault reportedly occurred while the two were riding in Viens' truck.
Gough stated in court documents that the woman told him Viens exhibited strange behavior during the ride and kept insisting the truck was being followed. She said at one point she tried to flee the truck, which led to Viens assaulting her.
Another sheriff's officer, Detective Thomas Buckler III, confirmed Viens was making strange remarks about being followed.
A search of Viens yielded four packages of suspected Suboxone.
The July 21 indictment charges Viens with one count each of kidnapping, first-degree assault, second-degree assault, possession of contraband in a place of confinement and false imprisonment.
Viens initial circuit court appearance was Monday before Judge Andrew S. Rappaport.
A pre-trial conference is scheduled for late August with a plea hearing scheduled for late September.
Prosecution of the case will be handled by Anthony R. Navalaney of the Calvert County State's Attorney's Office.
Viens is being represented by the public defenders office.

opinion_only.title: Local Lightning Rods: Social Media, National Divisions Changing Local Politics
opinion_only.author: Mike Sunnucks APG National Enterprise Editor
opinion_only.content:
Local lightning rods: Social media, national divisions changing local politics

 March 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mike Sunnucks APG National enterprise editor | Section: News 
 
 449
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Megan Cook, Russ Nelson and Ann Groves Lloyd are mayors of small towns in Maryland, Montana and Wisconsin.Nelson has been the mayor of Belgrade, Montana, for 20 years.
Karen Rose has been with Sarasota County Schools in Florida for more than three decades serving as a special education teacher, middle school principal and since 2020 on the local school board.
Over their tenures, the quartet and local officials across the country have seen the exponential growth of social media and its impacts on civil discourse, as well as the increasing intersections between divisive national politics and what's happening at the community level.
School board, city council and county commission meetings have all become venues for fights over controversial curriculums and books, COVID rules, drag shows at public libraries and national issues with advocates from the left and right looking for local debates on immigration, abortion and Israel's war in Gaza.
Rose said public comments at school board meetings can be very political and very partisan. "It's very organized," Rose said.
Social media, with its expansive reach, along with online meetings allow more residents and businesses to engage with and keep tabs on local governments and schools. That can also help bring more transparency to city halls, local law enforcement and school districts.
"The more information that we share with the public about what's happening in town, the better. We also have a live feed for all of our council, board and commission meetings. If residents aren't able to make it, they can always watch the recordings from our website," said Cook, mayor of Easton.
But social media also magnifies broader contemporary distrust of the media, government, politicians and other institutions. It can also bring rumor mills and coarse discourse.
"From a city perspective, we just wish people would pick up the phone and call us. We are constantly fighting the rumor mill," said Groves Lloyd, mayor of Lodi, Wisconsin (a small town near Madison).
Groves Lloyd identifies herself as a "progressive feminist" and "small town mayor" on her X/Twitter account where she is no fan of former president Donald Trump. But the Wisconsin mayor said she's pulled back on her progressive posts, especially on Facebook, because of the atmosphere of social media.
In Montana, Nelson, the mayor of Belgrade (which has a population approaching 13,000 people), worries all the political tensions at the local level discourages candidates for office and shortens tenures for staff and officeholders. He avoids social media altogether.
"I'm not on Facebook. I'm not on social media," said Nelson. "You can call me, or if you need me, you can text me. That's my technology."
For a more expansive look at the issue check out our story online and in our national e-edition on Monday, March 11.

opinion_only.title: 'Ride on, dear friend'
opinion_only.author: BOB FORD Special to the Star Democrat
opinion_only.content:
'Ride on, dear friend'

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BOB FORD Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Ride On Dear Friend 
 
 525
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROCK HALL — An unusually large rockfish was landed in Rock Hall on June 20 when a new striped bass-inspired bike rack was installed on Main Street to honor the memory of Ken McLaughlin, whose tireless work for the community is sorely missed.The rack, created by Greg Jetton of Gunsmoke Fabrication, calls to mind McLaughlin's fondness for pedaling around his adopted town, often doing favors or making deliveries, or dropping in to aid various non-profit organizations with their websites.
McLaughlin, who died suddenly last September at the age of 65 in the Main Street home he shared with his partner, Carol Sutera, was a retired website designer. He volunteered his expertise to help with the Friends of Eastern Neck, the Lions Club, the Mainstay, Main Street Rock Hall, as well as events including Rock Hall FallFest and Pirates & Wenches.
"This is a great addition to our town. It really speaks a lot about this community. It is very Rock Hall," said Mayor James Cook at the unveiling ceremony. "It helps the community, and that's a testament to our friend, Ken. He was active day-in and day-out to improve the lives of others. This speaks to that and his spirit lives on."
The rack was funded with help from the Kent Cultural Alliance, the Lions Club and Rock Hall Main Street. It rests on a bed of oyster shells that came from the backyard of Kent County Commission President and Rock Hall native Ron Fithian.
"And I shucked every one of them," Fithian said.
When Jetton was commissioned to build the rack, he knew what he had in mind before he found it.
"My intention was to have something like a crab or a rockfish to really make it Rock Hall," Jetton said. "It took some time, but I finally found a design I liked that would work."
The rack, located on a corner of Durocher's lot on the west side of Main Street, is made from half-inch and quarter-inch welded steel and weighs a sturdy 350 pounds.
Steve Leonard, the pastor of Raum Chapel UME on Skinner's Neck, is also co-operator of the new Rock Hall Brewing Company, which is located directly across the street from the bike rack. The brewpub hosted a small reception for those who attended the ceremony, which also served as a soft opening for the business.
"We just got the fire marshal's approval today," Leonard said. "To be part of this is an honor and it is amazing."
"Ken would have had a blast here tonight," Sutera said, as she looked around the gathering. "He'd be a little embarrassed by the attention, because he was so humble. He never made it about himself. He loved Rock Hall. We bought the house here three years ago and I was still going back and forth to Pennsylvania for work. It didn't take very long for Ken to say, 'I'm staying here. I'll see you when you get back.' He fell in love with the town."
The town returned the affection, and now his place in its memories is matched by a special spot on Main Street, with a dedication plaque that ends with these words: "Ride on, dear friend. Ride on."

Three national races top the ballot in Maryland

 October 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 393

 EASTON — Talbot, Caroline and Dorchester voters are gearing up to elect their next president, senator and congressman on Nov. 5.Republican Donald Trump and Democrat Kamala Harris are on the top of the ticket as they run for president. There are several others on the presidential ballot including Jill Stein and Robert Kennedy, Jr. (although he dropped out of the race, he is still on the ballot).
For U.S. senator there is Democrat Angela Alsobrooks and Republican Larry Hogan. Running for Congress in District 1 are Republican Andy Harris, Democrat Blane Miller III and Libertarian Joshua W. O'Brien.
For the Appellate Court of Maryland Stephen H. Kehoe is on the ballot.
There are different ways to vote.
Registered voters can vote by mail-in ballot if they do not want to go to an early voting center. You can request an early voter mail-in ballot if you have a Maryland driver's license or a MVA issued ID card. There is a mail-in ballot request form on the Maryland Board of Elections website.
Anyone who is registered to vote can vote during early voting.
The polling station for Talbot is Easton Fire Hall at 315 Aurora Park Drive in Easton. If you are in Dorchester, go to the Dorchester Election Office at 1000 Goodwill Avenue, Cambridge. Caroline County's station is at the Health and Public Services Building 403 S. Seventh St. Room 112, Denton.
You can register to vote if you are a U.S. citizen, a Maryland resident and at least 16 years old. You can register to vote Election Day at your local polling place.
These voters can satisfy the identification requirement by providing one of the following:
The voter's driver's license number, MVA ID card number or the last four digits of the voter's Social Security number, and election officials will attempt to verify this information with MVA or the Social Security Administration.A copy of a current and valid photo identification (Maryland driver's license, MVA ID card, student or employee photo ID card, military ID card, passport or any other state or federal government issued ID card).A copy of a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck or other government document that shows the voter's name and address.
Voting is a civic duty and a relatively easy one to participate in. Most voters are on the voter list in their county. After voting you can show off your "I Voted" sticker.

no_local_government_action.author: Tom McCall
no_local_government_action.content:
Hogan Visits Port Street

 October 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 358
 Words

 EASTON — Port Street got a distinguished visitor at the Neighborhood Service Center. Former Gov. Larry Hogan is running for the open U.S. Senate seat and stopped in Easton Friday to talk with people at the service center.He visited the facility on 126 Port Street and asked questions.
The Responsible Father Initiative, founded by Corey Pack and co-facilitated by Lou Dorsey, is an outreach program to help men become better fathers. It is a nonprofit and is all confidential. It provides food, clothing and first month's rent to people in need. These men gave Hogan the tour of the center.
Pack spoke to the governor about what they teach.
"We go over what is called the three E's. Emotion, energy and expression. And we talk about effective listening skills," Pack said. "We run through the 7/38/55 rule. 7% of the way we communicate is verbally. 38% is with our tone and 55% is with our body language."
The governor listened closely.
"I did not realize that," Hogan said. "That is an important lesson for me to learn."
He listened to more about the program.
"We try to develop more nurturing and caring fathers in this program. Most of the guys grew up in a home without a father. Some have been incarcerated with no contact with their children. It is great for them to see their children and establish a relationship with their children," Dorsey said.
Hogan recognized that a lot of men needed these services and saluted their dedication to helping these men flourish.
"It sounds like you guys are doing really important work here," Hogan said.
One of the Neighborhood Service Center workers asked Hogan to run for president. He smiled.
Hogan toured spaces intended for children. Then he went into the kitchen and in another room saw where they store clothes to give away.
At the end of tour, he was give two T-shirts and a coffee mug that touted the Neighborhood Service Center.
After his visit he stopped to do an interview in the parking lot. Hogan said his campaign is focused on the economy and crime.
"We are meeting voters every day," he said. "The people of Maryland know me after eight years of being governor."

too_niche.title: Eastern Shore Renters Face Challenges With Affordable Housing
too_niche.author: Maggie Trovato
too_niche.content:
Eastern Shore renters face challenges with affordable housing

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1987
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Bradford House Apartments resident Linda Johnson doesn't carry mace on her keychain anymore.She doesn't feel the need to use a key or a cell phone instead of her finger to tap the buttons of the apartment's elevator.
After years of asking apartment management to address resident safety concerns, from mold and bug infestations to a lack of security, Johnson and other Bradford House residents finally feel safe.
"I feel better every day," said Johnson, who has lived at Bradford House on Race Street in Cambridge for nearly 25 years. "I'm not angry no more."
The complex — which offers multifamily, subsidized housing for low-income individuals who are elderly or have special needs — came under new management with a new principal owner in the fall, and residents started to see changes they had requested for years be made.
But as housing problems across the Eastern Shore persist, others have not been as lucky.
A SHORE PROBLEM
With a lack of affordable housing options on the Eastern Shore and a need for better enforcement over housing standards, renters living in poor conditions often feel stuck.
In the eyes of Larry Rooths, the head of the Public Safety and Intelligence Committee for the Eastern Shore branch of the Caucus of African American Leaders, the lack of affordable housing is a national issue.
"But it seems a lot worse down here because there's so little housing," he said, "and there's no infrastructure in place for emergency services, emergency shelters."
Rooths said he's noticed landlords don't feel like they have to do much for tenants because there aren't many other places those tenants can go.
"And then the residents feel like that also," he said. "They don't want to stir up too much trouble because they know if somebody comes in and shuts the building down, where are they going?"
Rooths sees a need for housing legislation with more enforcement power so landlords address the issues residents face. He said the Shore also needs more housing infrastructure.
"If you create a situation where there's enough housing, then the landlords lose control," he said. "...If you don't like the place you're living in, you get up and move. But if there's no place to move or you can't move to another apartment building close to where you work, then it gets difficult."
The caucus is working to get tenants to form groups, which Rooths said would help them know their rights and push elected officials to make change.
"Unless there's some change in legislation or there's some increased funding to create a bigger pool of housing, this problem is going to be the same," he said.
In October, the Tenant Safety Act of 2024 went into effect in Maryland. The act, which places responsibility on landlords to provide safe dwelling for tenants, guarantees tenants can form groups.
Shore Legal Access Executive Director Meredith Girard considers Bradford House's tenant association a critical piece of its success in getting new management.
"I think the tenant association was critical to really letting the management and the court know what the issues were and how widespread it was," Girard said. "And that prompted some really important changes so that now the building is managed by a new company."
Girard said rural counties don't always have enough resources to support a rental inspection and licensing system. She said it would be great if counties on the Eastern Shore could pool their resources to form a regional housing commission.
"Where you could set some basic standards for habitability to make sure that if you're renting a unit, that the oven works, that the heat works, that the plumbing works, that the roof isn't leaking," she said.
Girard acknowledged rural landlords may also be strapped for resources. She said in some cases, landlords might not have the resources to make needed repairs.
"Which then becomes this really problematic cycle," she said.
At Bradford House, previous management said the property had been neglected before they took over in 2022.
In an April 2024 statement to The Star Democrat, Millennia Housing Management, the previous management at the complex, said it had invested more than $300,000 into the maintenance and enhancement of the "severely distressed property."
Girard said that when problems in complexes are fixed, tenants are often scared to complain about the conditions because they don't have anywhere else to go.
"And they don't want to upset their landlords," she said. "But at the same time, they need landlords to fix the things that need to be fixed."
Maryland Legal Aid Advocacy Director for the Human Right to Housing Zafar Shah said further protections against evictions are needed so tenants aren't reluctant to use the Tenant Safety Act of 2024. He said the Maryland legislature is considering a good cause eviction bill "that would protect tenants from lease non-renewal without a good reason."
"This is the big priority for renters in Maryland," he said.
NO WHERE TO GO
De'Auntte Clark came to Cambridge for peace.
In 2016, her 14-year-old son was killed after being hit by a car in Anne Arundel County. Four years later, her husband died from COVID-19.
In September 2022, Clark brought her family to the Eastern Shore for a fresh start. But since moving here, Clark has found anything but the peace she was seeking.
"I'm so numb, I can't cry," she said.
With concerns about the safety of her apartment at Calvin Mowbray Park and Stephen Camper Park in Cambridge and nowhere else to go, Clark spent more than a month living out of a van with her family.
A few days after her family moved into the complex, Clark noticed what seemed like mold in the cabinets along one of the walls in the kitchen.
Maintenance came to clean the cabinets out, but as the weather outside got colder and she turned the heat on, Clark said she started to see black spots pop up on the walls.
In December 2023, Clark's son, Keith Dezurn — who has a medical history of severe, persistent asthma — was airlifted to the University of Maryland Children's Hospital because he was struggling to breathe. He stayed in intensive care for five days, Clark said, displaying symptoms consistent with mold exposure.
Clark said on the way to the hospital in Baltimore, she could barely see anything and was crying.
"I don't want to lose another child," she said.
Ed Cafasso, a spokesperson for the property that is managed by WinnResidential, said on Jan. 15 that the health and safety of residents is WinnResidential's number one priority.
"Any time a household reports a moisture-related issue, it is treated as an emergency and remediated immediately by a professional, licensed specialist," he said.
Cafasso said over the past year, there have been seven instances at the complex that required professional mold remediation. He said there were zero reported cases of mold at the 190-apartment community as of January.
Before Clark and her family could move into a new unit at the complex this past fall, the unit was condemned. Cambridge Assistant City Manager Brandon Hesson said that in condemning the unit, the city ordered mold and moisture testing be done.
An inspection report obtained by The Star Democrat from the city showed an early November analysis found aspergillus and penicillium spore counts in the unit that were "significantly higher than the baseline count and probably indicates a source of contamination."
The unit was later removed from the city's list of condemned properties after a report by Simple Mold Solutions, which was based on the analysis, found the numbers "indicated a normal fungal environment with no elevated concentrations of airborne mold spores." The report recommended the HVAC system be cleaned to prevent mold spores from circulating.
But Clark's son's health scare was enough to make her seek housing elsewhere. The search proved to be no easy feat.
Limited affordable housing options on the Eastern Shore and across the state have made it difficult for Clark to find somewhere new to settle.
Clark said she went to multiple shelters in Howard County, where her children are currently enrolled in school, but all of them were full. She said the places she did find that had space required she live in the county for six months, which she had not.
Moving from place to place hasn't been easy on Clark's kids. She said they are scared to go back to the complex.
"They don't want to go back there, and I don't know what to do," Clark told The Star Democrat while they were living out of a van. "But at the same time, I know we can't keep living like this."
In mid-December, Clark and her family were able to secure a hotel room after living out of a van for more than a month. On Valentine's Day, they moved into a townhouse on the western shore.
"It's much better," she said. "No mold."
ZOOMING IN ON THE PROBLEM
Clark's story isn't an uncommon one when it comes to tenants of affordable housing on the Eastern Shore.
Residential issues at affordable housing complexes in Cambridge have come to a head more than once in the last two years.
In an attempt to attack the bigger issue at the local level, Cambridge has beefed up its Code Enforcement Department and is working on projects intended to increase and improve the city's housing stock.
Hesson said although the issues at housing facilities are all unique, there are common themes among them.
"There have been failures by agencies at the local, state and federal level to hold up the standards we've set for housing providers here," he said. "It's not my place to point fingers, because it isn't going to fix anything. The city is part of that structure, and we're committed to being better."
Hesson said building "strong relationships" with the governing authorities for the different housing facilities has helped achieve "significant progress."
"We've been able to draw attention to where these systems and processes have fallen short, and residents are seeing some of the early results of those efforts," he said.
PROGRESS
For Linda Johnson, those results are clear.
On Feb. 13, Johnson moved into a new unit within Bradford House Apartments. The move is not just a win for Johnson, who has been a loud and consistent voice of the Bradford House community, but proof of a new era for the apartment complex and its residents.
For years Bradford House residents expressed concerns about the safety of the building. In September 2023, the property — which was then managed by Millennia — received a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development inspection score that indicated health and safety deficiencies.
Three months later, Millennia received a debarment order from HUD, preventing the company from participating in any new business with the department.
In October, it was announced that Nuveen, an asset manager and subsidiary of financial planning firm TIAA, had been made principal owner of the apartment complex. Paths Management Services, a subsidiary of Nuveen, would manage the property.
Johnson's new digs, complete with a brand new, updated kitchen and laminate wood flooring, are a stark contrast from her previous unit.
When The Star Democrat visited some residents' homes last year, residents pointed out things like holes in ceilings, possible mold and problems with stoves. At that time, multiple residents had active rent escrow cases, where tenants pay their rent to a court, rather than to their landlord, until property issues are addressed.
The change at Bradford House isn't just visible in individual apartment units. The hallways have new flooring, the stairways are consistently clean, there is better lighting and new cameras and the community room has been renovated. Johnson said management is fixing the elevator that's been broken for more than a year.
"It's been wonderful," Johnson said. "I mean Paths came in here, they didn't talk, they worked."
Johnson is the president of the complex's tenant association, which was formed with guidance from Shore Legal Access.
"Just because we're low income people doesn't mean we have to live like that," she said.
Johnson said other renters going through housing issues should fight for what they believe in, adding that tenants have the right to withhold rent and form tenant associations.
"Your voice matters," she said.
Star Democrat reporter Konner Metz contributed to this report.

Stronger together: Rebuilding Together wraps up Rebuilding Month with appreciation lunch

 May 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 444
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Wrapping up National Rebuilding Month and celebrating its first appreciation lunch following its merger, Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore recognized volunteers and supporters at the Centreville United Methodist Church April 26.Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore provides free, critical home repairs for income eligible homeowners in Kent and Queen Anne's counties the whole month of April kicked projects into high gear to provide vital repair needs across the area, completing six projects including fresh off of two that very Saturday, said co-President Larisa Thomas.
Providing more resources and personnel to help more residents, the recent merge of the Kent and Queen Anne's counties departments has made Rebuilding Together even stronger together, Thomas said.
Thomas started as a volunteer swinging a hammer 15 years ago and credited the non-profit as making a difference in local lives.
Before rebranding, Rebuilding Together originated nationally as Christmas in April in 1973 and started in Queen Anne's County in 1994 and in Kent Count in 2004, according to Executive Director Genevieve Croker in a presentation to the Queen Anne's County Commissioners April 22.
Keeping the human aspect along with the housing aspect, Rebuilding Together recognizes everyone has the right to live comfortably, and works to repair homes, revitalize communities, and rebuild lives, Croker said.
All work is done at no cost to the homeowners who meet the income limits and other criteria. Typical projects can include painting, installing ramps and grab bars, repairing floors, plumbing, electrical, and other areas needed to ensure safe and healthy housing for homeowners.
"We say what we're going to do," Community Service Coordinator Cory Palmer said.
Rebuilding Together seeks to establish safe homes and communities for all and addresses the housing crisis by improving property values and preserving affordable housing stock, noting it is often cheaper to repair a home than build a new one and help aging homeowners age in place, Croker said.
Helen Fisher, of Crumpton, was one such homeowner utilizing volunteer services including smoke detector installation, outside lighting installation, and improved home skirting. At the appreciation luncheon, Fisher credited volunteers as professionals who get the job done.
Rebuilding Together welcomes volunteers of all calibers, whether with repairs or behind the scenes fundraising. "There is a role available for you," Thomas said.
Palmer encouraged anyone struggling with home repair costs to apply for services, noting income requirements and guidelines can change.
Volunteer Dan Hercher, of Church Hill, recently celebrated his first completed project with Rebuilding Together. Experienced with repair work, he said he loved seeing the change made to the homes and what it means to the homeowners.
"Some people don't have the tools or resources, so it's nice to help," he said.
More information about Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore can be found at rebuildingtogethereasternshore.org.

Greensboro Historical Society has new location with plans to move soon

 August 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 419
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — The Greensboro Historical Society has found its new location just blocks away from its current location, where the town said in June that the historical society could not longer keep its offices and artifacts.After months of discussion, the Greensboro Town Council voted on June 5 to give the historical society 120 days to vacate the Weaver Building.
Longtime Caroline County resident William Satterfield will allow the historical society to rent his building on Sunset Avenue, which in the 1960s was a bar and a hardware store.
The historical society was first told about a potential move out of the Weaver Building in March, when officials raised the need for more space to house town agencies. The town determined the building could be used to house either the police department or the town employees' office, but the council has leaned toward moving the police department.
With the move on the horizon, historical society Acting President Robert Moser talked to society staff and members about what is needed to ensure a safe relocation.
While no official move date is set because of new location repairs, the historical society will create a packing committee; a new location cleaning and repair committee; a moving committee; and a building, management and security committee.
The committees will be made of historical society members and community members. The historical society is asking community members to donate boxes, bubble wrap and their time to help.
"We're going to reach out to people within the community, and hopefully word of mouth from friend, to friend to friend gets people out there an opportunity to come and help," Moser said.
"We've had quite a few people reach out to us in regards to letting us know when the move is going to happen or what they can do and how they can help us facilitate the move," he said.
In addition to the move, the historical society is set to hold its biggest fundraiser of the year on Sept. 19.
The 22nd annual Greater Greensboro Open golf tournament is low on sign-ups right now, Moser said, but the historical society hopes for good participation to help with costs at the new location.
"It is our largest fundraiser in the year, which is going to be very important for us now since we have different utilities, internet and all that stuff that was provided to us through the town for the past seven years is now going to be our responsibility to pay," Moser said.
If you are interested in helping the Historical Society with moving, contact Rdmoser60@gmail.com.
